## NGFB in the industry

NGFB is **added** to the industry rather than carved out of existing banks,
following the Post 1 convention of adding a bank the size of the average large
bank. Reported banks keep their own books; market shares are measured against
the augmented industry, the reported sector plus NGFB. NGFB's history is
back-cast from its jump-off book with its drawn share-dynamics parameters
(Stage 2) and the realised regimes and sector growth, so it "lives through"
2008–2026 the way a bank with those parameters would have.

```{r shares-chart}
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: "Market shares of the augmented industry (reported sector plus NGFB). NGFB's line is its back-cast; the peer groups are reported BA900 data."
show_p <- c(cards = "Credit cards", personal_other = "Personal and other retail", mortgages_res = "Residential mortgages",
            corp_all = "Corporate loans and overdrafts", nmd = "Non-maturity deposits", beh_term = "Term deposits")
sh <- N$shares[N$shares$product %in% names(show_p), ]
sh$product <- factor(show_p[sh$product], levels = show_p)
sh$entity <- factor(sh$entity, levels = names(ent_col))
ggplot(sh, aes(date, share, colour = entity)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ product, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ent_col) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "share of augmented industry")
```

```{r shares-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
sx <- N$shares[N$shares$product %in% names(show_p) & N$shares$date %in% as.Date(c("2008-06-30", "2016-06-30", as.character(date0))), ]
sw <- stats::reshape(sx[, c("product", "entity", "date", "share")], idvar = c("product", "entity"), timevar = "date", direction = "wide")
guard(identical(names(sw)[1:2], c("product", "entity")), "shares twin column order")
names(sw) <- c("product", "entity", "2008Q2", "2016Q2", qlab(date0))
sw$product <- show_p[sw$product]; sw <- sw[order(sw$product, sw$entity), ]
for (k in 3:5) sw[[k]] <- pct(sw[[k]])
twin(sw)
```

At the jump-off NGFB holds `r pct(N$shares$share[N$shares$entity == "NGFB" & N$shares$product == "cards" & N$shares$date == date0], 0)`
of the augmented industry's credit cards and
`r pct(N$shares$share[N$shares$entity == "NGFB" & N$shares$product == "personal_other" & N$shares$date == date0], 0)`
of personal loans, against `r pct(N$shares$share[N$shares$entity == "NGFB" & N$shares$product == "mortgages_res" & N$shares$date == date0], 0)`
of residential mortgages. A bank the size of the average large bank with an
unsecured-heavy mix is necessarily a large card and personal lender; this is
the consequence of the canonical seed noted above, not a forecast.

## Calibration to the sector

```{r calibration}
#| echo: false
cal <- N$calibration
ck <- cal$checks
gv <- function(rx) ck$value[grepl(rx, ck$item)]
guard(abs(gv("NII vs BA120 after") - 1) < 1e-6, "NII calibration")
guard(abs(cal$liq$check[["lcr"]] - CFG$lcr_sector) < 1e-8 && abs(cal$liq$check[["nsfr"]] - CFG$nsfr_sector) < 1e-8,
      "liquidity calibration")
win <- range(cal$window)
```

The engine prices loans and deposits with the sector's own BA120 yields and
costs (projected by Stage 1), applies the sector's credit-loss ratio through
relative loss multipliers by product, and the sector's fee and cost ratios.
The remaining free parameters are pinned to the sector at the last BA120
quarter, `r qlab(cal$date)`:

| Parameter | Value | How it is set |
|---|---|---|
| Credit risk-weight scale | `r num(gv("credit RWA scale"), 3)` | BA900 sector book × BA200 asset-class risk weights reproduces BA200 credit RWA |
| Non-credit RWA | `r pct(gv("non-credit RWA") / 100)` of assets | BA700 total RWA less BA200 credit RWA |
| CET1 / book equity | `r num(gv("CET1 / book equity"), 3)` | BA700 CET1 over BA100 ordinary equity |
| Effective tax rate | `r pct(gv("effective tax rate"))` | BA120, last three years |
| HQLA earning share | `r pct(gv("HQLA earning share"))` | 1 − cash and central-bank balances / HQLA (BA100) |
| Wholesale spread over the 3-month benchmark | `r num(gv("wholesale spread"), 2)` pp | solved: engine NII = BA120 NII over `r qlab(win[1])`–`r qlab(win[2])` (`r rbn(gv("NII target") * 1e6)`), when the benchmark was JIBAR |
| LCR run-off scalar | `r num(cal$liq$k_lcr, 3)` | solved: sector LCR proxy = `r pct(CFG$lcr_sector, 1)` (Prudential Authority, June 2025) |
| NSFR required-funding scalar | `r num(cal$liq$k_nsfr, 3)` | solved: sector NSFR proxy = `r pct(CFG$nsfr_sector, 1)` |

: Calibration to the sector. {.striped}

Two checks are worth stating plainly. First, the engine's *gross* interest
income and expense on the BA900 balance sheet come out `r pct(gv("interest income vs") - 1, 0)`
and `r pct(gv("interest expense vs") - 1, 0)` above BA120's, while NII matches with
a plausible wholesale spread. BA900 carries trading-book positions on both
sides of the balance sheet whose interest BA120 books in trading revenue (its
own "allocated to trading" lines are R`r num(sum(P$spnl$ie_trading_alloc[P$spnl$date %in% cal$window]) / 1e6, 0)` bn of
expense and R`r num(sum(P$spnl$ii_trading_alloc[P$spnl$date %in% cal$window]) / 1e6, 0)` bn of income over the window), so the
excess is close to net-neutral and is reported rather than calibrated away.
Second, one quarter of BA120 call-deposit cost (`r qlab(cc_out)`,
`r num(cc_val, 1)`%) is a one-off outlier that the Stage 1 impulse dummies
flag; it is replaced by the window median before calibrating. Left in, it
drives the solved wholesale spread to `r sprintf("%+.2f", N$calibration$wholesale_spread_raw)` pp over JIBAR
(see [What didn't work](#what-didnt-work)).

### Liquidity

```{r liquidity}
#| echo: false
lfs <- cal$liq$sector_factors; lfn <- attr(N$chars_ngfb, "liquidity")$deposit_factors
lq <- merge(lfs[, c("line", "runoff", "asf", "financial_share", "retail_share")],
            lfn[, c("line", "runoff", "asf")], by = "line", suffixes = c("_s", "_n"))
lq <- lq[match(c("beh_operational", "beh_savings", "beh_notice", "beh_term"), lq$line), ]
q0 <- res$baseline$ngfb$run$quarterly
kt(data.frame(Line = lab_line[lq$line], `Financial depositors` = pct(lq$financial_share, 0),
              `Retail depositors` = pct(lq$retail_share, 0),
              `30-day run-off, sector` = pct(lq$runoff_s, 1), `30-day run-off, NGFB pool` = pct(lq$runoff_n, 1),
              `ASF, sector` = pct(lq$asf_s, 0), `ASF, NGFB pool` = pct(lq$asf_n, 0), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrr", caption = "Depositor-weighted Basel III factors by behavioural deposit line, before the sector scalars. Depositor shares are the sector's at the calibration date.")
```

BA900 crosses depositors with contractual buckets, and the Basel III run-off
and stable-funding factors depend on both, so each behavioural deposit line
carries the balance-weighted factor of the depositors who hold it: fund
managers' call money runs off at 100% inside 30 days, household savings at
10%. Unadjusted, these proxies put the sector's LCR at
`r pct(cal$liq$raw[["lcr"]], 0)` and NSFR at `r pct(cal$liq$raw[["nsfr"]], 0)`
against the published `r pct(CFG$lcr_sector, 0)` and `r pct(CFG$nsfr_sector, 0)`; one scalar
each absorbs what BA900 cannot see (the 30-day slice of term deposits,
operational status, committed facilities, derivatives). NGFB, with more HQLA
and less wholesale funding than the sector, starts at an LCR of
`r pct(q0$lcr[1], 0)` and an NSFR of `r pct(q0$nsfr[1], 0)`.

# Stage 1: macro to the industry

## Method

Each sector target $y$ (a product's volume growth, a spread over its reference
rate, a deposit cost, the credit-loss ratio, fee income or costs over assets)
gets an autoregressive distributed-lag (ARDL) model

$$ y_t = c + \rho\, y_{t-1} + \sum_j \beta_j\, x_{j,t-l_j} + \varepsilon_t , $$

chosen by a disciplined search rather than by hand:

1. every subset of up to `r CFG$max_k` macro drivers, at most one per economic
   group, each at one lag in `r min(CFG$lags)`–`r max(CFG$lags)` quarters;
2. a specification survives only if every driver carries its a-priori sign in
   the short run **and** in the long-run multiplier $\beta/(1-\rho)$, with a
   Newey–West $|t| \ge 1$ and $|\rho| < 0.98$;
3. survivors are ranked by **dynamic** pseudo-out-of-sample RMSE: from each
   expanding-window origin (the first after `r CFG$min_train` quarters) the
   model is re-estimated and simulated `r CFG$h_oos` quarters ahead on the
   realised macro path, which is how a scenario uses it (perfect foresight:
   the macro path is known, and nothing in the framework forecasts it); an
   AR(1), which has no macro channel, is the benchmark;
4. the projection averages all sign-valid specifications with BIC weights
   (Bayesian model averaging), which gives each driver a posterior inclusion
   probability (PIP) and a model-averaged long-run multiplier.

Deposit-cost models must contain the repo rate, so their long run is anchored
to it, and may also contain its quarterly change, so the impact of a rate move
and its long-run pass-through are estimated separately (an ARDL(1,1)). For
current accounts and savings deposits the repo rate enters as two partial
sums, of increases and of decreases, so that hikes and cuts can pass through
differently; for the commercial-mortgage and card spreads its change is split
into rises and falls the same way; and term-deposit growth may respond more
to GDP growth below zero than above it (a contraction kink). Every one of these
refinements was adopted by the rule in the next chapter, and the values not yet
published at the jump-off (GDP, unemployment and house prices lag the policy
rate by a quarter) come from each scenario, not from carrying the last
observation forward. One-off outliers
(AR(1) innovations beyond four MADs) get impulse dummies; the two COVID
quarters get dummies in the volume models only, so the credit-loss models keep
the 2020 stress signal. Ratio targets (pricing, credit, fees and costs) carry
an intercept correction: the mean residual of the last four unflagged
quarters shifts the projected path, which protects against structural drift
the sample average does not know about.

## Results

```{r s1-table}
#| echo: false
s1 <- S1$summary
s1 <- s1[order(match(s1$family, c("volume", "credit", "pnl", "pricing")), s1$target), ]
kt(data.frame(Target = s1$label, Family = s1$family, `Selected drivers [lag]` = s1$spec,
              n = s1$n, R2 = num(s1$r2, 2), `OOS RMSE` = num(s1$rmse_oos, 2), `AR(1) RMSE` = num(s1$rmse_ar, 2),
              Skill = pct(s1$skill, 0), `Valid specs` = paste0(s1$n_valid, " / ", s1$n_specs), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lllrrrrrr",
   caption = sprintf("Stage 1 satellites. Skill = 1 − OOS RMSE / AR(1) RMSE, simulated %d quarters ahead along the realised macro path from every origin. The selected specification is the best out of sample; projections average all valid specifications.", CFG$h_oos))
```

Three patterns stand out.

* **Prices are the best-identified part of the system.** Deposit costs and
  loan spreads respond to the policy rate with high fit and real
  out-of-sample skill (median `r pct(median(s1$skill[s1$family == "pricing"]), 0)` over the AR(1)), which is what a
  rate scenario mostly needs.
* **Credit losses are driven by growth.** The single best out-of-sample
  specification for the credit-loss ratio uses house-price growth, but the
  model average, which is what the projections use, puts a PIP of
  `r num(S1$bma$pip[S1$bma$target == "clr" & S1$bma$driver == "gdp_yy"], 2)` on GDP growth, with a long-run
  multiplier of `r num(S1$bma$long_run[S1$bma$target == "clr" & S1$bma$driver == "gdp_yy"], 3)` pp of loans per point of growth;
  house prices and the repo rate enter with low PIPs and unemployment not at
  all.
* **Volumes are hard.** Quarterly volume growth is noisy; the macro models
  beat the AR(1) for `r sum(s1$skill[s1$family == "volume"] > 0)` of the
  `r sum(s1$family == "volume")` volume targets, mostly modestly (median
  `r pct(median(s1$skill[s1$family == "volume"]), 0)`, with personal loans the exception at
  `r pct(s1$skill[s1$target == "g_personal_other"], 0)`), and residential mortgages not at all
  (`r pct(s1$skill[s1$target == "g_mortgages_res"], 0)`).

```{r s1-bma}

bm <- S1$bma
bm <- bm[bm$pip >= 0.5, ]
bm$label <- S1$summary$label[match(bm$target, S1$summary$target)]
bm <- bm[order(match(bm$target, s1$target), -bm$pip), ]
kt(data.frame(Target = bm$label, Driver = bm$driver, PIP = num(bm$pip, 2),
              `Long-run multiplier (model average)` = num(bm$long_run, 3),
              `Long-run multiplier (when included)` = num(bm$long_run_cond, 3), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llrrr", caption = "Drivers with posterior inclusion probability of at least 0.5. Multipliers are in the target's units per unit of the driver (pp per pp; growth targets in annualised percent). For current accounts and savings deposits, repo_pos and repo_neg are the cumulative hikes and cuts; for the commercial-mortgage and card spreads, d_repo_pos and d_repo_neg are the quarter's rise or fall.")
```

## Deposit pass-through: Stage 1 against Post 1

```{r betas}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Pass-through of a permanent 1 pp repo move to each behavioural deposit line: Post 1's one-month slopes against Stage 1's response in the first quarter and after three years, for hikes and for cuts (model average). The engine uses Stage 1's full dynamics."
pt <- MC$pass_through
bmix <- line_pricing_map()[c("beh_operational", "beh_savings", "beh_notice", "beh_term")]
resp <- function(l, mv_, q) { w <- bmix[[l]]$cost
  sum(vapply(names(w), function(k) w[[k]] * pt$response[pt$target == k & pt$move == mv_ & pt$quarter == q], 0)) }
bb <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(bmix), function(l) data.frame(
  line = l, post1 = ngfb_canonical()$deposit_beta[[l]], q1 = resp(l, "hike", 1),
  y3_hike = resp(l, "hike", CFG$horizon), y3_cut = resp(l, "cut", CFG$horizon))))
guard(bb$y3_hike[bb$line == "beh_savings"] > bb$y3_cut[bb$line == "beh_savings"] + 0.1,
      "savings: hikes pass through more than cuts")
guard(resp("beh_term", "hike", 4) > 0.95, "term money reprices fully within a year")
bl <- rbind(data.frame(line = bb$line, kind = "Post 1: one-month slope", beta = bb$post1),
            data.frame(line = bb$line, kind = "Stage 1: first quarter", beta = bb$q1),
            data.frame(line = bb$line, kind = "Stage 1: three years, hikes", beta = bb$y3_hike),
            data.frame(line = bb$line, kind = "Stage 1: three years, cuts", beta = bb$y3_cut))
bl$line <- factor(lab_line[bl$line], levels = rev(lab_line[names(bmix)]))
bl$kind <- factor(bl$kind, levels = unique(bl$kind))
ggplot(bl, aes(beta, line, colour = kind, shape = kind)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(ink[["muted"]], unname(pal$categorical[c(1, 2, 3)]))) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 16, 17, 25)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0, 1), colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "pass-through of a 1 pp repo move", y = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), shape = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

```{r betas-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(data.frame(Line = lab_line[bb$line], `Post 1 one-month` = num(bb$post1, 2), `Stage 1, first quarter` = num(bb$q1, 2),
                `Stage 1, three years (hikes)` = num(bb$y3_hike, 2), `Stage 1, three years (cuts)` = num(bb$y3_cut, 2),
                check.names = FALSE))
```

Post 1 reported one-month contemporaneous slopes on offered rates (book
average about 0.44) and noted that "the long-run cumulative pass-through is
higher". Stage 1 works on BA120-implied *book* costs over a quarter. With the
refined models, more of a rate move reaches deposit costs within the quarter
than the earlier version allowed (`r num(bb$q1[bb$line == "beh_operational"], 2)` for
operational deposits and `r num(bb$q1[bb$line == "beh_savings"], 2)` for savings), and
term money reprices fully within a year. Savings deposits are asymmetric:
after three years `r pct(bb$y3_hike[bb$line == "beh_savings"], 0)` of a hike has passed
through but only `r pct(bb$y3_cut[bb$line == "beh_savings"], 0)` of a cut, so cuts squeeze the
sector's savings margin by more than hikes widen it. Faster pass-through means a smaller
deposit endowment, which is why NGFB's hedge now more than offsets it (see
[Sensitivities](#sensitivities)).

# Is ARDL the right tool, and where do asymmetries belong? {#is-ardl-the-right-tool}

```{r mc-setup}
#| include: false
cw <- MC$cw; bnd <- MC$bounds; dyn <- MC$dynamics; asy <- MC$asym; icx <- MC$ic
va <- MC$vol_asym; kk <- MC$kinks; cvs <- MC$convex
guard(MC$horizon == 12L && CFG$h_oos == 12L, "the model checks are written for twelve-quarter conditional simulations")
n_cw <- sum(cw$ph < 0.10); n_cw5 <- sum(cw$ph < 0.05)
dw <- function(k, v) stats::setNames(dyn[[v]][dyn$registry == k], dyn$target[dyn$registry == k])
dep_t <- c("c_current", "c_savings", "c_call", "c_fixed_notice", "c_ncd")
spr_t <- c("s_homeloans", "s_commercial", "s_vaf", "s_cards", "s_overdrafts", "s_term_loans")
dep_lab <- c(c_current = "Current accounts", c_savings = "Savings", c_call = "Call", c_fixed_notice = "Fixed and notice",
             c_ncd = "NCDs")
lab_of <- function(t) S1$summary$label[match(t, S1$summary$target)]
guard(all(unlist(MC$rules)), "a registry default disagrees with the adoption rule")
guard(MC$ardl11_better, "the ARDL(1,1) deposit form is adopted")
asy_ad <- asy$target[asy$adopt]
guard(setequal(asy_ad, c("c_current", "c_savings", "s_commercial", "s_cards")), "pricing asymmetry adopted for four targets")
ar <- function(t, col) asy[asy$target == t, col]
guard(ar("c_current", "beta_down") > ar("c_current", "beta_up") && ar("c_current", "p_sym") < 0.001,
      "current accounts: cuts pass through more than hikes, strongly significant")
guard(ar("s_cards", "beta_up") < -0.2 && abs(ar("s_cards", "beta_down")) < 0.1, "card yields lag rises, follow cuts")
guard(ar("c_savings", "bt_asym") < 0.6 * ar("c_savings", "bt_sym"), "savings: asymmetry cuts the two-origin error sharply")
n_asy_sig <- sum(asy$p_sym < 0.10, na.rm = TRUE)
guard(n_asy_sig > length(asy_ad), "some pricing asymmetries are significant in sample but fail a back-test")
guard(!any(va$adopt) && sum(va$p_sym < 0.10, na.rm = TRUE) <= 1, "volume asymmetry: none adopted, at most one significant")
kv <- function(t, col) kk[kk$target == t, col]
guard(setequal(kk$target[kk$adopt], "g_cards"), "the card kink is the only kink adopted")
guard(kv("g_cards", "sbt_kink") > 0.95 * kv("g_cards", "sbt_linear") && kv("g_cards", "t_kink") < 2.5,
      "the card kink passes narrowly")
guard(!kv("g_beh_term", "adopt"), "the term-deposit kink no longer passes")
guard(kv("clr", "t_kink") < -3 && kv("clr", "sbt_kink") > kv("clr", "sbt_linear") && kv("clr", "bt_kink") < kv("clr", "bt_linear"),
      "credit-loss kink: strong in sample, worse in the scenario back-test, better in the two-origin back-test")
k_ovf <- kk[kk$has_kink & is.finite(kk$t_kink) & abs(kk$t_kink) >= 1.645 & !kk$adopt & kk$target != "clr", ]
guard(sum(k_ovf$sbt_kink > 1.5 * k_ovf$sbt_linear) >= 2, "kinks significant in sample but much worse in the scenario back-test")
guard(MC$ic_level_better && !(MC$ic_tests[["eq_better_oos"]] && MC$ic_tests[["eq_better_bt"]]) &&
      (MC$ic_tests[["eq_better_oos"]] != MC$ic_tests[["eq_better_bt"]]), "the IC evidence is split; the level shift stays")
guard(MC$comb_all[["bma"]] > MC$comb_all[["comb"]] && MC$comb_all[["bma"]] > MC$comb_all[["best"]],
      "BIC model averaging beats the out-of-sample combination and the single best")
guard(MC$bounds$decision[MC$bounds$target == "c_current"] == "level relationship" &&
      MC$bounds$decision[MC$bounds$target == "c_savings"] == "no level relationship", "bounds-test claims")
cm <- satellite_bma_summary(S1$sats$s_cards)
guard(all(c("d_repo_pos", "d_repo_neg") %in% cm$driver), "the card model carries both partial sums")
```

The question deserves a direct answer, and this version asks it on a
different footing from the previous ones. The models' job is not to forecast
the macro variables, which a scenario fixes, but to get the relationship
between those variables and each balance-sheet line right. So every test
conditions on the **realised** macro path, as if it had been known (perfect
foresight), and judges a model by how well it reproduces the industry's
outcomes over the scenario horizon of **twelve quarters**:

* **(a) in sample:** the refinement's own test (a HAC Wald test of equal
  responses to rises and falls; the $t$-statistic of a kink);
* **(b) the scenario back-test:** each satellite's model average re-estimated
  at every expanding-window origin and simulated twelve quarters along the
  realised macro path, the way a scenario uses it;
* **(c) the two-origin back-test:** the whole specification search re-run on
  data up to 2019Q4 and 2021Q4 and projected twelve quarters, so that not
  even the choice of drivers sees the future.

The rule for adopting a refinement was fixed before looking at any scenario
result, and the scripts enforce it: it enters the production models only if
it passes **all three**. Earlier versions selected and scored models one to
four quarters ahead, a horizon that rewards short-run persistence; twelve
quarters rewards the macro relationship, which is what a three-year scenario
runs on.

## Why ARDL

* **Scenarios are conditional projections.** A scenario fixes the macro path;
  the models must say what the industry does *given* that path. Single-equation
  models conditioned on exogenous drivers do exactly that, and under perfect
  foresight nothing about the drivers has to be predicted. A VAR would model
  the macro variables too, which is precisely the exercise this framework
  leaves out.
* **Seventy quarters is a small sample.** An AR(1) term plus at most three
  drivers is about as much structure as 2008–2025 can support, and the sign
  restrictions stop the search from fitting noise with economically wrong
  coefficients.
* **The long run is interpretable.** An ARDL in levels is an error-correction
  model in disguise: $\beta/(1-\rho)$ is the steady-state effect of a driver,
  which is what a three-year projection converges to.
* **Asymmetries fit in naturally.** Splitting a driver into its rises and falls,
  or adding a kink below zero growth, keeps the model linear in its
  parameters. Such regime-dependent models are risky when the regime must be
  forecast; under perfect foresight the scenario says which regime it is in,
  so they are usable whenever the data support them.
* **It is the supervisors' workhorse.** The Federal Reserve models 20 of the 24
  core components of pre-provision net revenue in its supervisory stress test
  with autoregressive models of ratios, and ECB research argues for averaging
  over many satellite equations rather than hand-picking one (Gross and
  Población, 2015), which is what the model averaging here does.

## What was tested

```{r mc-table}
#| echo: false
n_kink_sig <- sum(kk$has_kink & is.finite(kk$t_kink) & abs(kk$t_kink) >= 1.645)
tested <- data.frame(
  Refinement = c("Does knowing the macro path help? (Clark–West against the AR(1))",
                 "Level relationship (Pesaran–Shin–Smith bounds test)",
                 "Impact and long-run pass-through estimated separately (ARDL(1,1) for deposit costs)",
                 "Asymmetric pricing: rate rises and cuts pass through differently",
                 "Asymmetric volumes: books respond differently to rate rises and falls",
                 "Contraction kinks: credit losses and volumes more sensitive to growth below zero",
                 "Intercept correction as a level shift or in the equation",
                 "Model averaging against the five best out of sample and the single best"),
  Verdict = c(sprintf("%d of %d satellites at 10%%, twelve quarters ahead", n_cw, nrow(cw)),
              "confirmed for current accounts only",
              "adopted: better for most deposit costs in both back-tests",
              sprintf("significant for %d of %d pricing targets; adopted for %d (current accounts, savings, commercial mortgages, cards)",
                      n_asy_sig, nrow(asy), length(asy_ad)),
              sprintf("significant for %d of %d volume targets and adopted for none", sum(va$p_sym < 0.10, na.rm = TRUE), nrow(va)),
              sprintf("significant for %d of %d targets; adopted for card lending only", n_kink_sig, sum(kk$has_kink)),
              "evidence split between the two tests: the level shift stays",
              "BIC model averaging kept"),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kt(tested, align = "ll", caption = "Refinements tested in analysis/08_model_checks.R, each with the macro path known and simulated twelve quarters ahead.")
```

### Does knowing the macro path help?

An AR(1) has no macro channel: it projects each series from its own past.
If the satellites beat it when the macro path is known, the relationship
carries information; if not, the macro drivers are decoration. With some
4,000 specifications searched per target, a winner can beat the benchmark by
luck, so the Clark–West test asks whether the improvement is larger than the
noise that a bigger model adds when its extra coefficients are truly zero.

```{r mc-cw}
#| echo: false
cwt <- cw[order(match(cw$family, c("pricing", "credit", "pnl", "volume")), cw$ph), ]
kt(data.frame(Target = lab_of(cwt$target), Family = cwt$family,
              `Skill vs AR(1), 12 quarters` = pct(cwt$skill, 0), `Clark-West p, 1 quarter` = num(cwt$p1, 3),
              `Clark-West p, 12 quarters` = num(cwt$ph, 3), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llrrr", caption = sprintf("One-sided p-values; %d expanding-window origins per target, each simulated along the realised macro path. With %d tests at 10%%, about %.0f would pass by chance.",
                                      median(cw$origins), nrow(cw), 0.1 * nrow(cw)))
```

`r n_cw` of `r nrow(cw)` satellites pass at 10% (`r n_cw5` at 5%), far more than the
`r round(0.1 * nrow(cw))` that chance would deliver.

### Is a deposit cost tied to the repo rate in the long run?

A levels regression of one persistent series on another can be spurious. The
Pesaran–Shin–Smith bounds test asks whether a level relationship exists
without having to know whether the series are stationary; its critical values
are simulated here for the actual sample size.

```{r mc-bounds}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(`Deposit cost` = dep_lab[bnd$target], F = num(bnd$F, 2),
              `5% bounds, I(0) / I(1)` = paste(num(bnd$i0_95, 2), "/", num(bnd$i1_95, 2)),
              Decision = bnd$decision, `F, asymmetric` = num(bnd$F_asym, 2),
              `5% bounds, asymmetric` = paste(num(bnd$i0_95_asym, 2), "/", num(bnd$i1_95_asym, 2)),
              `Decision, asymmetric` = bnd$decision_asym, check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrlrrl", caption = "Bounds test, unrestricted intercept and no trend, one lag of the differences, impulse dummies as controls. Critical values from 4,000 simulations at the sample size. 'Asymmetric': the repo rate split into cumulative rises and cuts.")
```

The test confirms a long-run anchor for current accounts and cannot find one
for the other categories. Part of that is low power in `r bnd$n[1]` quarters;
part is real: the composition of each BA120 category drifts (digital banks'
savings products, the mix of corporate and retail call money), so the level
relationship moves. These deposit costs are best modelled through their
response to rate *changes*, which is well identified, with a long run pinned
down weakly, and that is what the next refinement does.

### Deposit-cost dynamics and asymmetric pricing

The original search allowed the repo level *or* its change in a deposit-cost
equation, never both, which forces the impact of a rate move and its long-run
pass-through into one geometric profile. Letting both enter (an ARDL(1,1))
separates them. On top of it, the asymmetric registry splits the repo rate
(deposit costs) or its change (loan spreads over prime) into rises and falls,
so that hikes and cuts can pass through at different speeds.

```{r mc-asym}
#| echo: false
pt <- c(dep_t, spr_t)
kt(data.frame(Target = lab_of(pt),
              `Response to rises` = num(asy$beta_up[match(pt, asy$target)], 2),
              `Response to falls` = num(asy$beta_down[match(pt, asy$target)], 2),
              `Symmetry rejected (p)` = num(asy$p_sym[match(pt, asy$target)], 3),
              `Scenario back-test: symmetric / asymmetric` = paste(num(dw("ardl11", "rmse_sbt")[pt], 3), "/", num(dw("asym", "rmse_sbt")[pt], 3)),
              `Two-origin back-test: symmetric / asymmetric` = paste(num(dw("ardl11", "bt_mean")[pt], 3), "/", num(dw("asym", "bt_mean")[pt], 3)),
              Adopted = ifelse(pt %in% asy_ad, "asymmetric", "symmetric"), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrl", caption = "Pricing models (percentage points). Responses: impact coefficients on the rises and falls of the policy-rate driver in the leading symmetric specification, with the HAC Wald test of their equality. Back-tests: RMSE over twelve quarters along the realised macro path; two-origin: mean of 2019Q4 and 2021Q4 with the whole search re-run.")
```

Asymmetry passes all three tests for `r length(asy_ad)` of the `r nrow(asy)` pricing models:

* **Current accounts** pass rate cuts through more than rises (impact
  `r num(ar("c_current", "beta_down"), 2)` against `r num(ar("c_current", "beta_up"), 2)`,
  $p$ < 0.001): banks cut the few transactional rates they pay quickly and raise them slowly.
* **Savings deposits**: symmetry is rejected at `r num(ar("c_savings", "p_sym"), 3)` and the
  two-origin back-test error falls from `r num(ar("c_savings", "bt_sym"), 2)` to
  `r num(ar("c_savings", "bt_asym"), 2)` pp, the largest improvement in the table.
* **Commercial mortgages and cards**: loan yields over prime lag rate rises
  and follow cuts; for cards the response to a rise is `r num(ar("s_cards", "beta_up"), 2)`
  against `r num(ar("s_cards", "beta_down"), 2)` to a fall, so card margins compress in a
  hiking cycle and recover when it turns.

`r n_asy_sig - length(asy_ad)` more pricing models show significant asymmetry in sample but do
not improve both back-tests; partial sums trend, so a model that uses them
can drift when simulated far from its sample, which is what the back-tests
are there to catch.

### Do volumes respond asymmetrically to rate rises and falls?

```{r mc-vol}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(Target = lab_of(va$target), `Leading specification` = va$base_spec,
              `Rises / falls (impact)` = ifelse(is.finite(va$p_sym), paste(num(va$beta_up, 2), "/", num(va$beta_down, 2)), "—"),
              `Symmetry rejected (p)` = ifelse(is.finite(va$p_sym), num(va$p_sym, 3), "no rate driver"),
              `Scenario back-test: symmetric / asymmetric` = paste(num(va$sbt_sym, 2), "/", num(va$sbt_asym, 2)),
              `Two-origin: symmetric / asymmetric` = paste(num(va$bt_sym, 2), "/", num(va$bt_asym, 2)), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llrrrr", caption = "Volume growth (annualised, percent): the four-quarter change in the repo rate split into rises and falls.")
```

No. The data cannot tell a volume response to rate rises from one to rate
falls: at most one book shows a significant difference in sample, and the
asymmetric registry projects no better. Volumes respond to rates slowly and
through income and house prices, and seventy quarters with four rate cycles
are too few to split that response by direction.

### Contraction kinks: credit losses and volumes

```{r mc-kinks}
#| echo: false
kz <- kk[kk$has_kink, ]
kt(data.frame(Target = lab_of(kz$target), `Kink: t (leading spec.)` = ifelse(is.finite(kz$t_kink), num(kz$t_kink, 1), "not selected"),
              `Posterior inclusion` = num(kz$pip_kink, 2),
              `Scenario back-test: linear / kink` = paste(num(kz$sbt_linear, 2), "/", num(kz$sbt_kink, 2)),
              `Two-origin: linear / kink` = paste(num(kz$bt_linear, 2), "/", num(kz$bt_kink, 2)),
              Adopted = ifelse(kz$adopt, "yes", "no"), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrl", caption = "Targets with GDP growth among their drivers, with GDP growth below zero added as a candidate (its sign the same as growth's). Posterior inclusion: the BIC weight of the specifications that contain the kink.")
```

The kink is the classic asymmetry in credit, and the data find it: in the
credit-loss model each point of contraction adds far more to losses than a
point of growth subtracts ($t$ = `r num(kv("clr", "t_kink"), 1)` in the leading specification,
inclusion `r num(kv("clr", "pip_kink"), 2)`). It also improves the two-origin back-test
(`r num(kv("clr", "bt_linear"), 3)` to `r num(kv("clr", "bt_kink"), 3)` pp), but worsens the scenario back-test across all
origins (`r num(kv("clr", "sbt_linear"), 3)` to `r num(kv("clr", "sbt_kink"), 3)`): before 2020 it had only 2009 to
learn the kink from, and at most origins it overshoots. It fails the rule and
stays a scenario sensitivity (see [Model risk in the scenarios](#scenarios)),
an important one. Kinks in several volume models are significant in sample and
much worse out of it (personal and corporate loans' scenario back-test errors
roughly double), the signature of overfitting two recessions. **Card
lending** passes all three tests, narrowly ($t$ = `r num(kv("g_cards", "t_kink"), 1)`, scenario
back-test `r num(kv("g_cards", "sbt_linear"), 2)` to `r num(kv("g_cards", "sbt_kink"), 2)`, two-origin
`r num(kv("g_cards", "bt_linear"), 2)` to `r num(kv("g_cards", "bt_kink"), 2)`): in a contraction, card balances slow by more
than growth alone predicts, as lenders tighten unsecured credit. In the
previous version the kink passed for term deposits instead; with the equity
series corrected ([A broken equity series](#equity-break)) term deposits fail
both back-tests (scenario `r num(kv("g_beh_term", "sbt_linear"), 1)` to `r num(kv("g_beh_term", "sbt_kink"), 1)`). Verdicts this close
to the line move with the data, which is why the rule is fixed in advance and
re-applied rather than argued case by case.

### The intercept correction

```{r mc-ic}
#| echo: false
ict <- icx[order(match(icx$family, c("credit", "pnl", "pricing")), icx$target), ]
kt(data.frame(Target = lab_of(ict$target), AR = num(ict$rho, 2),
              `RMSE, no correction` = num(ict$rmse_no_ic, 3), `RMSE ratio, level shift` = num(ict$ratio, 2),
              `RMSE ratio, in the equation` = num(ict$ratio_equation, 2), `Diebold-Mariano p (level)` = num(ict$p, 3),
              check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrr", caption = "The correction (mean residual of the last four unflagged quarters), evaluated twelve quarters ahead at every expanding-window origin. Ratios below one favour the correction. AR: the autoregressive coefficient of the selected model.")
```

Two forms compete: adding the recent residual to the equation's intercept,
where it compounds through the autoregressive term to roughly
$\text{ic}/(1-\rho)$, or shifting the projected path by it. At twelve quarters
the evidence is split: across the expanding-window origins the level shift is
neutral (median RMSE ratio `r num(stats::median(icx$ratio), 2)`) where the equation form loses
(`r num(stats::median(icx$ratio_equation), 2)`), while the equation form wins the two-origin back-test. The level shift is the incumbent
and the rule requires a challenger to win both, so it stays. It is worth
`r ubps(mr["baseline", "core"] - mr["baseline", "no_ic_credit"])` of NGFB's baseline ROE through the credit-loss ratio
alone, the largest single modelling assumption behind the *level* of ROE here.

### Model averaging, selection or combination?

```{r mc-comb}
#| echo: false
cb <- MC$comb
kt(data.frame(Family = cb$family, `BIC model average (used)` = pct(cb$skill_used, 0),
              `Five best out of sample, equal weights` = pct(cb$skill_comb, 0),
              `Single best out of sample` = pct(cb$skill_best, 0), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrr", caption = "Median two-origin back-test skill against no change over twelve quarters, with the whole search re-run at each origin.")
```

Selecting the specification with the best out-of-sample record is the
natural instinct, and it is wrong here: on genuinely new data the single best
specification does worst (median skill `r pct(MC$comb_all[["best"]], 0)`), an equal-weighted
average of the five best does better (`r pct(MC$comb_all[["comb"]], 0)`), and the
BIC-weighted model average does best (`r pct(MC$comb_all[["bma"]], 0)`). Ranking by
out-of-sample error over a few dozen origins overfits the ranking itself (a
winner's curse), while BIC weights spread the bet across specifications that
fit the whole sample.

## What would improve accuracy most

The tests point to the data rather than the model class. In order of likely
value:

1. **A bank's own data.** NGFB inherits the sector's pricing and loss rates.
   A real bank would replace the Stage 1 pricing with its own product pricing
   and the relative loss multipliers with its own loss history.
2. **Market data that the engine needs and the SARB does not publish.** This
   version found the structural hedge priced off a proxy that overstated swap
   rates by up to two points ([Are the numbers right?](#audit)); actual swap
   fixings exist only from 2023 in the free source used here, so the hedge
   book's history is partly back-cast.
3. **Loss data by product.** BA200 publishes no losses by product, so credit
   enters the engine as one sector ratio with assumed relative multipliers;
   impairment data by asset class would allow a product-level credit model,
   and a convex one with more than two recessions to learn from.
4. **Longer samples through structural breaks.** IFRS 9 (2018) changed how
   losses are recognised; a time-varying intercept (a state-space local
   level) is the principled version of the intercept correction once there
   is enough post-2018 data to estimate it.

Machine-learning alternatives are a poor fit: with 70 observations they
overfit, and tree-based methods cannot extrapolate beyond the historical range,
which a downside scenario routinely requires.

# Monthly frequency: does it recover the relationships better? {#monthly}

```{r m-setup}

      "deposit costs: rate effect within about a quarter")
```
