```{r m-setup}
        abs(mvm("c_savings", 2/3) - mvm("c_current", 2/3)) < 0.03 && MM$sats_m$c_savings$fit$coef[["ar1"]] > 0.9,
      "wording: equal lags, equal two-month moves, monthly savings rho near one")
```

South African banking data are richer at monthly frequency than the
quarterly models use: BA900 is a monthly return for every bank, BA120 (the
sector's income statement) is monthly, and so are the policy rate, bond
yields, inflation, the rand, equity prices, the SARB's coincident indicator
and its credit statistics. Real GDP, the unemployment rate and house prices
are not. The previous version asked whether monthly models *forecast* better
and judged them one to eight quarters ahead. With the objective restated --
good relationships between the macro variables and the balance sheet, the
macro path known -- the question changes: **does estimating at monthly
frequency recover those relationships better, judged over the twelve
quarters a scenario runs?** Three things change with it:

* **No nowcasting.** Months after the last published quarter used to be
  extrapolated from the indicators. Under perfect foresight those values
  belong to the scenario, so the monthly GDP path now stops at the last
  published quarter, and the GDP indicators are chosen by in-sample fit
  rather than by a nowcast test.
* **The horizon is the scenario's.** Every model is re-estimated at each
  origin and simulated twelve quarters (thirty-six months) along the
  realised macro path; errors are scored on the same quarterly outcomes, in
  three blocks of four quarters, and for volumes also in the *level* of the
  book after twelve quarters, which is what drives a scenario's balance sheet.
* **The scenario's GDP path is quarterly.** A monthly model estimated on
  indicator-based monthly GDP would, in a scenario, be fed the smooth monthly
  path that the scenario's quarters imply. The race therefore also scores
  monthly models estimated on that smooth path.

```{r m-data-note}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (MM$vol_source == "KBP") cat(
  "::: {.callout-warning appearance=\"simple\"}\n## Data used here\n",
  "The monthly BA900 pull (`data-raw/03_pull_monthly.bat`) had not run when this version was rendered, so the",
  "monthly *volume* comparison uses the SARB's monthly credit statistics, mapped to the six lending products.\n:::\n")
if (MM$vol_source == "BA900") {
  vm <- MM$panel_m[is.finite(MM$panel_m$g_mortgages_res), "date"]
  cat("::: {.callout-note appearance=\"simple\"}\n## Data used here\n",
      sprintf("Monthly volumes are the BA900 returns of every month from %s to %s (%d months), for the same banks as the quarterly panel, so the three monthly growth rates of a quarter average exactly to the quarterly growth rate the production models use.",
              format(min(vm) - 1, "%B %Y"), format(max(vm), "%B %Y"), length(vm) + 1L),
      "Monthly pricing, credit-loss, fee and cost ratios divide the monthly BA120 income statement by the monthly BA100 balance sheet.",
      "The quarterly ratios divide a quarter's flow by the average of its two quarter-end balances, the monthly ones each month's flow by that month's average balance, and the two differ when balances move within the quarter:",
      sprintf("by %s pp on average for savings deposits (at most %s pp), and by up to %s pp for current accounts and NCDs in 2008-09.",
              num(dgv("c_savings", "mean_abs_gap"), 2), num(dgv("c_savings", "max_abs_gap"), 2),
              num(max(dgv("c_current", "max_abs_gap"), dgv("c_ncd", "max_abs_gap")), 1)),
      "The comparison below scores every model on the production definition, and checks the monthly models on their own.\n:::\n")
}
```

## Quarterly series to monthly: the Kalman filter

A monthly model needs monthly GDP, and the monthly path has to satisfy two
conditions: its three months must add up to the published quarter, and its
shape within the quarter should come from monthly data, not from a smooth
curve drawn through the quarters. That is temporal disaggregation (Chow and
Lin, 1971; Fernández, 1981; Litterman, 1983), and its natural home is the
state-space form (Harvey and Pierse, 1984; Proietti, 2006):

$$y_t = x_t'\beta + u_t, \qquad u_t = \phi\, u_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad Y_q = \sum_{t \in q} c\, y_t ,$$

where $y_t$ is the unobserved monthly series, $x_t$ the monthly indicators,
$u_t$ the part the indicators miss, and $Y_q$ the published quarter. A
"cumulator" state adds up the months of each quarter and is observed only in
its last month; the two months in between are missing observations, which
the Kalman filter handles by skipping the update. $\beta$ is estimated by
generalised least squares on the quarters, $\phi$ by maximising the profile
likelihood, and the monthly path is the Kalman smoother's estimate, with a
standard error for every month. The same path has a closed form (the GLS best
linear unbiased predictor); the package computes both and its tests check that
they agree to machine precision.

Which indicators? Nothing is forecast, so the choice is made in sample, by
the disaggregation model's fit to the published quarters:

```{r m-tdfit}
#| echo: false
ind_lab <- c(none = "None (smooth path)", coinc = "Coincident indicator", `mfg + retail` = "Manufacturing + retail",
             `coinc + mfg + retail` = "Coincident + manufacturing + retail")
mod_lab <- c(`chow-lin` = "Chow-Lin", fernandez = "Fernández", litterman = "Litterman")
guard(all(tf_$indicators %in% names(ind_lab)) && all(tf_$model %in% names(mod_lab)), "disaggregation table labels")
kt(data.frame(Indicators = ind_lab[tf_$indicators], Model = mod_lab[tf_$model], Quarters = tf_$quarters,
              AIC = num(tf_$aic, 1), `AIC against the best` = num(tf_$d_aic, 1), phi = num(tf_$phi, 3),
              `Quarterly growth explained (R²)` = ifelse(tf_$indicators == "none", "—", pct(tf_$r2_growth, 0)),
              check.names = FALSE), align = "llrrrrr",
   caption = "Temporal disaggregation of quarterly real GDP, fitted on the published quarters. Indicators: the SARB coincident business-cycle indicator, manufacturing production and retail sales at constant prices. R²: the share of quarterly GDP growth the aggregated indicators explain.")
```

The coincident indicator with manufacturing and retail sales fits best by a
wide margin and explains `r pct(best_td$r2_growth, 0)` of quarterly GDP growth, so its monthly path
carries real information about the timing of activity within each quarter.
Among the three models, Fernández's wins: the gap between GDP and the
indicators is best treated as a random walk ($\phi = 1$; Chow-Lin's estimate
sits at `r num(tfv("coinc + mfg + retail", "chow-lin", "phi"), 3)`, the top of its range), which is why the filter
re-anchors to every published quarter. The previous version used Chow-Lin,
chosen by a nowcast test that has no place when nothing is forecast. Unemployment
(published quarterly only since the Quarterly Labour Force Survey began in
2008) and house prices have no monthly indicator here, so they get the smooth
path whose quarterly averages match (a Litterman model without regressors).
The same smooth path for GDP is what a monthly model would see in a scenario,
because a scenario's GDP path is quarterly.

```{r m-gdp}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Real GDP growth: the published quarters (annualised quarter on quarter) and the monthly path from the Kalman filter with the three indicators (annualised three-month growth), 2015-2026; the 2020 collapse and rebound run off the scale. The path stops at the last published quarter."
gm <- MM$disaggregation$gdp_monthly
gm$g3 <- 400 * (log(gm$gdp_m) - log(c(rep(NA, 3), utils::head(gm$gdp_m, -3))))
gq <- P$macro[, c("date", "gdp_qq")]
gq <- gq[gq$date >= as.Date("2015-01-01") & is.finite(gq$gdp_qq), ]
gm <- gm[gm$date >= as.Date("2015-01-01"), ]
ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_step(data = transform(gq, date = date - 91), aes(date, gdp_qq, colour = "Published quarter"), linewidth = 0.5,
            direction = "hv") +
  geom_line(data = gm, aes(date, g3, colour = "Monthly path, indicators (Kalman)"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Published quarter` = ink[["muted"]], `Monthly path, indicators (Kalman)` = ent_col[["NGFB"]]),
                      name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-15, 15)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "annualised growth (%)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Monthly against quarterly

The monthly satellites are built exactly like the quarterly ones -- the same
registry of targets, candidate drivers, economic signs and driver groups,
the same $|t| \ge 1$ and $|\rho| < 0.98$ screens, model averaging with BIC
weights -- with three changes the frequency forces: lags of 0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9
and 12 months; month-of-year dummies (and the COVID quarters month by month);
and the conditional simulations run thirty-six months ahead from quarter-end
origins. Monthly interest is annualised with the month's day count, since
interest accrues by the day.

Both frequencies forecast the *same quarterly outcomes* from the *same
origins*, re-estimated on data up to each origin and simulated along the
realised macro path for twelve quarters, exactly as in a scenario. Monthly
forecasts map into quarters exactly: three months of annualised growth
average to the quarter's growth, and day-weighted monthly interest rates sum
to the quarterly rate.

```{r m-race}
#| fig-height: 5.8
#| fig-cap: "Error of the monthly ARDL relative to the quarterly ARDL (RMSE ratio; below one, monthly is better), by target, in three blocks of the twelve-quarter conditional simulation. Same quarterly outcomes, same origins."
rr <- rw[rw$block != "h1_12", ]
rr$lab <- vapply(rr$target, function(t) S1$sats[[t]]$label %||% t, "")
rr$lab <- factor(rr$lab, levels = unique(rr$lab[order(rr$family, rr$target)]))
rr$block <- factor(blk_lab[rr$block], levels = blk_lab[1:3])
rr$family <- fam_lab[rr$family]
ggplot(rr, aes(r_m_ardl, lab, colour = family)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ block) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Volumes = ent_col[["Big Four"]], Pricing = ent_col[["NGFB"]],
                                 `Credit losses` = pal$categorical[[7]], `Fees and costs` = ink[["muted"]]),
                      breaks = unname(fam_lab), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "RMSE, monthly / quarterly (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r m-race-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
tw <- rw[rw$block == "h1_12", c("target", "q_ardl", "r_m_ardl")]
tw <- merge(tw, dm, by = "target", all.x = TRUE)
tw <- merge(tw, data.frame(target = lv12$target, lvl = lv12$m_ardl / lv12$q_ardl), by = "target", all.x = TRUE)
twin(data.frame(Target = vapply(tw$target, function(t) S1$sats[[t]]$label %||% t, ""),
                `Quarterly RMSE, 1-12 q` = num(tw$q_ardl, 3), `Monthly / quarterly, 1-12 q` = num(tw$r_m_ardl, 2),
                `Monthly / quarterly, level after 12 q` = ifelse(is.finite(tw$lvl), num(tw$lvl, 2), "—"),
                `Diebold-Mariano (positive favours monthly)` = num(tw$dm_stat, 2), `p-value` = num(tw$p_value, 3),
                check.names = FALSE), "Table view: monthly against quarterly over twelve quarters, with Diebold-Mariano tests on the twelve-quarter path error")
```

```{r m-findings-guards}
#| include: false
guard(med("pricing", "m_ardl") > 1.1 && all(vapply(c("h1_4", "h5_8", "h9_12"), function(b) med("pricing", "m_ardl", b) > 1.1, TRUE)),
      "pricing: monthly worse in every block")
guard(abs(med("volume", "m_ardl") - 1) < 0.06 && abs(lvr - 1) < 0.06, "volumes: no systematic difference, in growth or in level")
guard(med("credit", "m_ardl") < 1 && med("pnl", "m_ardl") < 1 && all(dm$p_value[dm$target %in% c("clr", "nir_assets", "opex_assets")] > 0.10),
      "credit and costs: better monthly, not significantly")
fav_m <- dm$target[which(dm$p_value < 0.10 & dm$dm_stat > 0)]; fav_q <- dm$target[which(dm$p_value < 0.10 & dm$dm_stat < 0)]
guard(setequal(fav_m, c("g_corp_all", "g_beh_term", "s_cards", "s_overdrafts")) && length(fav_q) == 5, "the significant DM tests")
sm_worse <- dms$target[which(dms$p_value < 0.10 & dms$dm_stat < 0)]; sm_better <- dms$target[which(dms$p_value < 0.10 & dms$dm_stat > 0)]
guard(length(sm_worse) >= 3 && length(sm_better) <= 1, "the smooth GDP path a scenario implies makes the monthly models worse")
guard(med_own("pricing") > 1.1, "pricing: monthly is worse on its own definition too")
lag1_m <- vapply(c("g_corp_all", "g_beh_term"), function(t) { x <- MM$panel_m[[t]][MM$panel_m$date >= MM$m_args$sample_from]
  x <- x[is.finite(x)]; stats::cor(x[-1], x[-length(x)]) }, 0)
guard(all(lag1_m < 0), "lumpy books: month-to-month growth reverses")
bw <- DY$multipliers[DY$multipliers$shock == "repo_up" & abs(DY$multipliers$quarters - 12) < 1e-9, ]
bw$w <- bw$hi - bw$lo
bwr <- function(rx) { z <- bw[grepl(rx, bw$target), ]
  stats::median(z$w[z$set == "monthly"][match(unique(z$target), z$target[z$set == "monthly"])] /
                z$w[z$set == "production"][match(unique(z$target), z$target[z$set == "production"])], na.rm = TRUE) }
band_ratio <- c(dep = bwr("^c_"), vol = bwr("^g_"))
guard(all(band_ratio < 0.8), "monthly multiplier bands are narrower")
```

**Monthly estimation does not recover the relationships better, and the new
objective strengthens that answer.** Over the twelve quarters a scenario runs:

* **Pricing**, where monthly data were expected to help most, is worse
  monthly in every block: the median monthly model's error is
  `r num(med("pricing", "m_ardl"), 2)` times the quarterly model's over twelve quarters
  (`r num(med("pricing", "m_ardl", "h1_4"), 2)`, `r num(med("pricing", "m_ardl", "h5_8"), 2)` and `r num(med("pricing", "m_ardl", "h9_12"), 2)` in the three blocks), and
  `r num(med_own("pricing"), 2)` times on the monthly models' own definition of the quarterly rate.
* **Volumes** show no systematic difference: `r num(med("volume", "m_ardl"), 2)` in growth and
  `r num(lvr, 2)` in the level of the book after twelve quarters.
* **Credit losses and costs** are a little better monthly (`r num(med("credit", "m_ardl"), 2)` and
  `r num(med("pnl", "m_ardl"), 2)`), but not significantly.
* Of the `r nrow(dm)` Diebold–Mariano tests on the twelve-quarter path error,
  `r length(fav_m)` favour the monthly model at 10% (corporate loans and term deposits, whose
  lumpy flows partly reverse the next month, and the card and overdraft
  spreads) and `r length(fav_q)` the quarterly (the home-loan, vehicle-finance and term-loan
  spreads, current accounts and NCDs).

The test above flatters the monthly models in one respect. They are estimated
on a monthly GDP path built from monthly indicators, but a scenario's GDP path
is quarterly, so in use they would be fed the smooth monthly path the
quarters imply. Estimated on that smooth path, as they would have to be for
consistency, the monthly models do worse again for the GDP-driven targets
(significantly for `r length(sm_worse)` of `r nrow(dms[is.finite(dms$p_value), ])`, better for
`r length(sm_better)`): what monthly GDP adds is the timing of activity within the
quarter, and a scenario does not have it. Under perfect foresight the other
argument for monthly data, that the latest month is more timely, disappears
too: the scenario supplies the macro path, and nothing needs to be nowcast.

Why monthly estimation does not help is a matter of signal and noise. The
signal in these series is slow: a deposit book reprices over quarters, a credit
cycle turns over years, and the policy rate moves only at the six MPC meetings
a year, so monthly timing adds a few weeks of resolution at most. The noise is
per observation: month-end balances, interest posted unevenly across months,
provisions booked at quarter and year ends. Tripling the observations triples
the noise draws without adding much independent information about slow
dynamics, and in the monthly pricing models the autoregressive coefficient sits
close to one (`r num(MM$sats_m$c_savings$fit$coef[["ar1"]], 2)` for savings deposits), where small estimation errors
compound over a thirty-six-month simulation. Quarterly aggregation is not a
loss of information here; it is a filter. The monthly models *look* more
precise -- their 90% parameter bands on the three-year response to a rate rise
are `r pct(1 - band_ratio[["dep"]], 0)` narrower for deposit costs and `r pct(1 - band_ratio[["vol"]], 0)` narrower for volumes -- but the
bands assume the extra observations are independent information, and the
simulation test shows they are not.

**So the production models stay quarterly.** Monthly data keep two uses that
need no macro forecast: the latest month of BA900 and BA120 measures the bank's
own jump-off book before the quarter closes (corporate loans and term deposits
above all, where a large month partly reverses the next: first-order
autocorrelation of monthly growth `r num(lag1_m[["g_corp_all"]], 2)` and `r num(lag1_m[["g_beh_term"]], 2)`), and monthly multipliers show the first weeks of a rate
cycle that quarterly models report as one number (below).

## Is ARDL still the right tool at monthly frequency?

The same race includes the two alternatives that make most sense when the lag
dimension grows from five quarters to thirteen months: **polynomial
distributed lags** (Almon), in which each driver enters through a quadratic
lag profile over 0-12 months, so a rate change can be spread over a year with
three parameters instead of thirteen, the sign restriction applying to the
sum of the lag weights; and **Bayesian shrinkage**, the single-equation
version of a Bayesian VAR with exogenous drivers, in which every candidate
driver enters at every lag, coefficients are shrunk towards zero with a prior
variance that falls with the lag (a Minnesota prior), and the tightness is set
by the marginal likelihood -- shrinkage instead of selection, and no signs.

```{r m-classes}
#| echo: false
ct <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("h1_4", "h9_12", "h1_12"), function(b) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fam_lab), function(f)
  data.frame(`Quarters ahead` = blk_lab[[b]], Family = fam_lab[[f]],
             `ARDL, quarterly` = "1.00", `PDL, quarterly` = num(med(f, "q_pdl", b), 2),
             `Shrinkage, quarterly` = num(med(f, "q_shrink", b), 2), `AR(1), quarterly` = num(med(f, "q_ar1", b), 2),
             `ARDL, monthly` = num(med(f, "m_ardl", b), 2), `PDL, monthly` = num(med(f, "m_pdl", b), 2),
             `Shrinkage, monthly` = num(med(f, "m_shrink", b), 2), `AR(1), monthly` = num(med(f, "m_ar1", b), 2),
             check.names = FALSE)))))
no_pdl_q <- unique(rw$target[is.na(rw$q_pdl)])
kt(ct, align = "llrrrrrrrr",
   caption = paste0("Median error by model class, relative to the quarterly sign-restricted ARDL average (below one is better), twelve-quarter simulations along the realised macro path. Same quarterly outcomes and origins for every model. PDL: polynomial distributed lags.",
                    if (length(no_pdl_q)) sprintf(" No quarterly PDL specification for %s survives the sign and t screens, so that median covers the other volume targets.",
                                                  tolower(paste(plab[sub("^g_", "", no_pdl_q)], collapse = " and "))) else ""))
guard(all(vapply(c("q_pdl", "q_shrink", "m_pdl", "m_shrink"), function(k) med("pricing", k) > 1.1, TRUE)),
      "ARDL beats PDL and shrinkage in pricing at both frequencies")
guard(med("volume", "q_ar1") < 1 && med("volume", "m_ar1") < 1, "the AR(1) matches the macro models' accuracy for volumes")
```

**Yes.** Within each frequency the sign-restricted ARDL average is the most
accurate macro model for pricing, ahead of both alternatives: polynomial lags
impose a smooth lag profile that deposit repricing does not have (it is a
jump at the MPC meeting followed by a tail), and shrinkage keeps every
driver at every lag with small, often wrong-signed coefficients that add noise.
For volumes a plain AR(1) is as accurate over twelve quarters as any macro
model (median ratio `r num(med("volume", "q_ar1"), 2)`, and `r num(med("volume", "m_ar1"), 2)` monthly): a loan book's path is mostly
its own momentum. But an AR(1) has no macro channel, so it cannot answer a
scenario, and the Clark–West tests in the previous chapter find the macro
information in the volume models significant twelve quarters ahead for most
books even where it does not lower the mean squared error; the satellites are
held to economic signs for exactly that reason.

A VAR would not change this. In a scenario the macro path is set from
outside, so the object needed is the distribution of each banking variable
*conditional on* that path. A VAR's conditional forecast (Waggoner and Zha,
1999) equals the ARDL's when the macro block does not respond to the banking
variables within the horizon; otherwise the VAR adds equations for macro
variables that the scenario then overrides. The VAR's real advantage, joint
dynamics, matters for unconditional forecasting, not for scenario analysis.

Mixed-frequency regressions (MIDAS; Ghysels, Santa-Clara and Valkanov, 2004)
solve a different problem: a target observed only quarterly, with drivers
observed monthly. Here the targets are monthly too, so the monthly ARDL uses
strictly more information than a MIDAS regression of the quarterly target on
monthly drivers would, and the polynomial lags above are MIDAS's weighting
scheme applied at a single frequency.

## How the lags are chosen and how the sign restrictions work

Each satellite is a model average over a disciplined search, not a single
regression. For a target $y$ with candidate drivers $x_j$:

1. **Specifications.** Every subset of at most `r CFG$max_k` drivers, at most one
   from each economic group (the repo level and its change never compete in
   one equation, unless the target's registry allows both), each at **one**
   lag chosen from a grid -- 0 to 4 quarters (0 to 12 months monthly):
   $y_t = c + \rho\, y_{t-1} + \sum_j \beta_j x_{j,t-\ell_j} + \varepsilon_t$.
   One lag per driver keeps the parameter count down; the AR term $\rho$
   spreads the effect over time, so the response to a permanent change in
   $x_j$ is $0$ before $\ell_j$ and then
   $\beta_j(1 + \rho + \dots + \rho^{h-\ell_j})$, converging to the long-run
   multiplier $\beta_j / (1 - \rho)$.
2. **Sign restrictions.** A specification survives only if every driver's
   short-run coefficient $\beta_j$ *and* long-run multiplier
   $\beta_j/(1-\rho)$ carry the sign economics requires (a higher repo rate
   cannot raise mortgage demand; higher unemployment cannot lower credit
   losses), where the registry fixes one, with $|t_{\text{HAC}}| \ge 1$, and
   $|\rho| < 0.98$. This is a restriction on the *model space*, not on a
   structural shock as in a sign-restricted VAR: it removes specifications
   whose estimated effects contradict the direction economics requires.
   Where theory is ambiguous the sign is left free: the policy rate for
   cards and corporate credit (a hike damps new borrowing but raises
   drawdowns on existing facilities as cash flow tightens) and for
   non-maturity deposits (higher rates draw money into savings and notice
   accounts and push it out to term deposits).
3. **Selection.** Survivors are ranked by dynamic pseudo-out-of-sample error
   -- re-estimated at each origin and simulated twelve quarters ahead along the
   realised macro path (thirty-six months for the monthly models) -- and the
   most parsimonious within 2% of the best is the selected specification.
4. **Averaging.** Projections average every surviving specification with BIC
   weights, an approximation to posterior model probabilities (Raftery,
   1995), so lag uncertainty is carried into the scenario rather than
   resolved by fiat.

Home loans show how this works. Of the
`r format(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "n_specs"), big.mark = ",")` candidate specifications,
`r sgv("g_mortgages_res", "sign_valid")` survive the screens. The model average puts
`r pct(sum(hl_d4), 0)` of its weight on the four-quarter change in the repo rate, spread
over lags of two quarters (`r pct(hl_d4[["2"]], 0)`), three (`r pct(hl_d4[["3"]], 0)`) and four
(`r pct(hl_d4[["4"]], 0)`); the one-quarter change and the repo level carry the rest of
the rate weight, also at two to four quarters, and specifications with house
prices carry `r pct(hpi_w("g_mortgages_res"), 0)`. No single lag is imposed: a rate rise starts
to slow home-loan growth after about two quarters and keeps slowing it for
well over a year (at most `r pct(hl_rate_early, 0)` of the weight sits on lags of zero or
one quarter). The selected specification, the four-quarter
change at a two-quarter lag, is the most parsimonious within 2% of the best
out-of-sample error; the scenarios use the average.

```{r m-signs}
#| echo: false
sg <- stats::aggregate(cbind(n_specs, rejected_sign, rejected_t, rejected_rho, sign_valid) ~ family, sgc, sum)
wf <- stats::aggregate(cbind(wrong_weight_free, ratio = rmse_free / rmse_restricted) ~ family, sgc, stats::median)
sg <- merge(sg, wf, by = "family")
kt(data.frame(Family = fam_lab[sg$family], Specifications = format(sg$n_specs, big.mark = ","),
              `Fail a sign` = pct(sg$rejected_sign / sg$n_specs, 0), `Fail the t screen` = pct(sg$rejected_t / sg$n_specs, 0),
              `Fail the ρ screen` = pct(sg$rejected_rho / sg$n_specs, 0), `Survive` = format(sg$sign_valid, big.mark = ","),
              `Wrong-sign weight, unrestricted` = pct(sg$wrong_weight_free, 0),
              `RMSE, unrestricted / restricted` = num(sg$ratio, 2), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrrr",
   caption = "What the restrictions remove, quarterly production models. The last two columns re-run the search with every sign left free: the share of the model-average weight that lands on specifications with at least one economically wrong sign, and the out-of-sample error of that average relative to the restricted one (twelve-quarter simulations along the realised macro path); both are medians across the family's targets.")
```

The restrictions matter exactly where the data are misleading. For pricing,
the data and economics agree: without the restriction almost no weight lands
on a wrong sign and accuracy is unchanged. For volumes they disagree. In home
loans `r pct(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "rejected_sign") / sgv("g_mortgages_res", "n_specs"), 0)` of
the `r format(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "n_specs"), big.mark = ",")` specifications fail a sign, and with the signs left free
`r pct(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "wrong_weight_free"), 0)` of the model weight goes to specifications in which a higher
repo rate *raises* mortgage growth. That is not a finding about mortgages;
it is the SARB at work: it hikes into credit booms and cuts into slumps, so in
the raw data rates and credit growth rise together. The unrestricted average
learns that correlation and forecasts worse out of sample
(`r num(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "rmse_free"), 2)` against `r num(sgv("g_mortgages_res", "rmse_restricted"), 2)`), and in a scenario it
would turn a hike into a lending boom. Personal loans and the credit-loss ratio
tell the same story: left free, `r pct(sgv("g_personal_other", "wrong_weight_free"), 0)` and `r pct(sgv("clr", "wrong_weight_free"), 0)` of the model weight goes to
wrong signs, and the free averages are less accurate over twelve quarters
(`r num(sgv("g_personal_other", "rmse_free"), 2)` against `r num(sgv("g_personal_other", "rmse_restricted"), 2)` for personal loans, `r num(sgv("clr", "rmse_free"), 3)` against
`r num(sgv("clr", "rmse_restricted"), 3)` for credit losses). Judged as a scenario uses them, the
restrictions cost nothing where the data agree with economics and improve
accuracy where they do not.

```{r m-lags}
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Where the rate effect sits: the model-averaged lag (in quarters) of the policy-rate drivers in each satellite, quarterly production models and monthly models (monthly volumes are shown only when they come from BA900). Larger points: more of the model weight on that driver."
lp_rate <- DY$lag_profile[DY$lag_profile$driver %in% c("repo", "d_repo", "d4_repo", "real_repo", "repo_pos",
                                                         "repo_neg", "d_repo_pos", "d_repo_neg"), ]
if (MM$vol_source == "KBP") lp_rate <- lp_rate[!(lp_rate$freq == "month" & grepl("^g_", lp_rate$target)), ]
lp_rate$lab <- vapply(lp_rate$target, function(t) S1$sats[[t]]$label %||% t, "")
lp_rate$freq <- ifelse(lp_rate$freq == "quarter", "Quarterly", "Monthly")
ggplot(lp_rate, aes(lag, lab, colour = freq)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = w), alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 4), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Quarterly = ent_col[["Big Four"]], Monthly = ent_col[["NGFB"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "model-averaged lag of the rate driver (quarters)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Deposit costs carry their rate effect within about a quarter at both
frequencies. Retail loan books are the opposite: the monthly models put
almost all of their rate weight at the longest lag the grid allows, twelve
months, for home loans and personal loans (both at `r num(lagw_avg("g_mortgages_res", "month"), 1)` quarters), and
the quarterly models, whose grid
reaches the same year, at `r num(lagw_avg("g_mortgages_res", "quarter"), 1)` and
`r num(lagw_avg("g_personal_other", "quarter"), 1)` quarters. Both frequencies say a rate change takes
the best part of a year to reach a retail loan book; at the boundary, the
monthly grid cannot say whether it takes longer.

## Dynamic multipliers: what a rate move does to each line

A dynamic multiplier is the path of a line after a shock, all else equal.
Because the satellites average several specifications whose rate drivers
include the level, its one- and four-period changes, the real rate and the
partial sums of hikes and cuts, the multipliers are computed by simulation:
each model is projected along a flat macro path and along the same path with
the shock, every derived driver recomputed (a repo shock moves prime, the
3-month floating rate, the real rate, the changes and the partial sums
together), and the difference
is the multiplier. Bands redraw the coefficients of the averaged
specifications from their HAC covariance (5th to 95th percentile).

```{r m-mult-vol}
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-cap: "A permanent 100 bps rise in the repo rate: the level of sector balances, percent difference from no change, quarterly production models with a 90% parameter band (all else equal: the macro path is otherwise unchanged)."
vt <- c("g_mortgages_res", "g_mortgages_com", "g_vaf", "g_cards", "g_personal_other", "g_corp_all", "g_nmd", "g_beh_term")
mv1 <- mu[mu$set == "production" & mu$shock == "repo_up" & mu$target %in% vt, ]
mv1$lab <- factor(plab[sub("^g_", "", mv1$target)], levels = plab)
ggplot(mv1, aes(quarters, effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = ent_col[["NGFB"]], alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(colour = ent_col[["NGFB"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12)) +
  labs(x = "quarters after the rise", y = "balance, % difference")
```

```{r m-mult-vol-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
tv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vt, function(t) data.frame(Line = plab[sub("^g_", "", t)],
  `After 1 year` = sprintf("%+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 4)), `After 2 years` = sprintf("%+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 8)),
  `After 3 years` = sprintf("%+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 12)),
  `90% band, 3 years` = sprintf("%+.2f to %+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 12, col = "lo"), mval(t, "repo_up", 12, col = "hi")),
  check.names = FALSE)))
twin(tv, "Table view: balances after a permanent 100 bps rise in the repo rate (% difference)")
```

Loan books respond slowly and personal loans most: three years after a
permanent 100 bps rise, personal loans are
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_personal_other", "repo_up", 12)))`% smaller than they would have been, vehicle and asset finance
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_vaf", "repo_up", 12)))`%, cards `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_cards", "repo_up", 12)))`% and home loans
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_mortgages_res", "repo_up", 12)))`%, with little happening in the first year. Corporate loans
edge up after a hike (`r sprintf("%+.1f", mval("g_corp_all", "repo_up", 1))`% in the first quarter, as companies draw on existing
facilities) and their band spans zero at three years, which is why the
registry leaves their rate sign free. Term deposits
*grow* (`r sprintf("%+.1f", mval("g_beh_term", "repo_up", 12))`%): savers move into fixed deposits when rates are high. These are partial
effects with the rest of the macro path held fixed; in a scenario a hike also
slows GDP and raises unemployment, which add their own effects through the
other drivers.

```{r m-mult-price}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "A permanent 100 bps change in the repo rate: deposit costs and loan spreads over their reference rates (percentage points), quarterly production models. Solid: a rise; dashed: a cut (shown with its sign reversed, so that a symmetric response would overlap)."
pt <- c("c_current", "c_savings", "c_call", "c_fixed_notice", "c_ncd", "s_homeloans", "s_vaf", "s_cards")
mp <- mu[mu$set == "production" & mu$target %in% pt & mu$shock %in% c("repo_up", "repo_down"), ]
mp$effect[mp$shock == "repo_down"] <- -mp$effect[mp$shock == "repo_down"]
mp$lab <- factor(tlab[mp$target], levels = tlab[pt])
mp$shock <- ifelse(mp$shock == "repo_up", "Rise", "Cut (sign reversed)")
ggplot(mp, aes(quarters, effect, linetype = shock)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(colour = ent_col[["NGFB"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Rise = "solid", `Cut (sign reversed)` = "22"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "quarters after the change", y = "percentage points") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Deposit costs reprice at very different speeds. Call deposits move almost at
once (`r num(mval("c_call", "repo_up", 1), 2)` pp in the first quarter after a 100 bps rise); savings and
current accounts move part of the way (`r num(mval("c_savings", "repo_up", 1), 2)` and
`r num(mval("c_current", "repo_up", 1), 2)`); NCDs only as they roll over (`r num(mval("c_ncd", "repo_up", 1), 2)` at first,
`r num(mval("c_ncd", "repo_up", 4), 2)` after a year). After three years fixed and notice deposits and NCDs
have passed through almost fully (`r num(mval("c_fixed_notice", "repo_up", 12), 2)` and `r num(mval("c_ncd", "repo_up", 12), 2)`)
and current accounts least (`r num(mval("c_current", "repo_up", 12), 2)`). Savings deposits show the asymmetry:
a 100 bps rise adds `r num(mval("c_savings", "repo_up", 12), 2)` pp to their cost after three years, a 100 bps
cut takes off only `r num(abs(mval("c_savings", "repo_down", 12)), 2)` pp, which is what squeezes the savings
margin in an easing cycle. Loan yields are set off prime, which moves one for one
with the repo rate, so their spreads dip on impact (the book reprices with a
lag) and close within a year or two: vehicle and asset finance by
`r num(abs(mval("s_vaf", "repo_up", 1)), 2)` pp at first and cards by `r num(abs(mval("s_cards", "repo_up", 1)), 2)` pp.

### The first months, seen monthly

The quarterly models report the first quarter as one number. The monthly
models, estimated on the same lines with the same signs, show what happens
inside it.

```{r m-mult-freq}
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-cap: "A permanent 100 bps rise in the repo rate, monthly models (line, month by month) against the quarterly production models (points, one per quarter): deposit costs in percentage points, balances in % difference. The first three years."
ft <- c("c_call", "c_savings", "c_current", "c_fixed_notice", "c_ncd", "g_cards", "g_mortgages_res", "g_nmd")
mf <- mu[mu$shock == "repo_up" & mu$target %in% ft & mu$set %in% c("production", "monthly"), ]
mf$lab <- factor(tlab[mf$target], levels = tlab[ft])
mf$set <- ifelse(mf$set == "production", "Quarterly", "Monthly")
ggplot(mf, aes(quarters, effect, colour = set)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = mf[mf$set == "Monthly", ], linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = mf[mf$set == "Quarterly", ], size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Monthly = ent_col[["NGFB"]], Quarterly = ent_col[["Big Four"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "quarters after the rise", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r m-mult-freq-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
tf <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ft, function(t) data.frame(Line = tlab[[t]],
  `Month 1` = sprintf("%+.2f", mvm(t, 1/3)), `Month 2` = sprintf("%+.2f", mvm(t, 2/3)),
  `Quarter 1, monthly` = sprintf("%+.2f", mvm(t, 1)), `Quarter 1, quarterly` = sprintf("%+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 1)),
  `Year 3, monthly` = sprintf("%+.2f", mvm(t, 12)), `Year 3, quarterly` = sprintf("%+.2f", mval(t, "repo_up", 12)),
  check.names = FALSE)))
twin(tf, "Table view: monthly against quarterly multipliers (deposit costs in pp, balances in %)")
```

Call deposits have repriced `r ubps(mvm("c_call", 2/3) / 100)` two months after a 100 bps
rise. NCDs barely move in the first month (`r bps(mvm("c_ncd", 1/3) / 100)`) and then
reprice `r ubps(mvm("c_ncd", 2/3) / 100)` in the second as certificates roll over; fixed and
notice deposits follow the same pattern. Savings and current accounts have
each moved about `r ubps(mean(c(mvm("c_savings", 2/3), mvm("c_current", 2/3))) / 100)` after two months. After three years the monthly and quarterly models are within
`r num(max(abs(vapply(dep5, function(t) mvm(t, 12) - mval(t, "repo_up", 12), 0))), 2)` pp of each other on every
deposit line, so for NII over a scenario the frequency hardly matters; for the
first quarter of a rate cycle -- the quarter an ALCO is usually asked about --
the monthly profile is the better guide. For balances the two frequencies
agree on unsecured lending (cards `r sprintf("%+.1f", mvm("g_cards", 12))`% monthly against
`r sprintf("%+.1f", mval("g_cards", "repo_up", 12))`% quarterly after three years) and on the timing of home
loans, which slow only from the second year (the monthly response is smaller,
`r sprintf("%+.1f", mvm("g_mortgages_res", 12))`% against `r sprintf("%+.1f", mval("g_mortgages_res", "repo_up", 12))`%). They differ on
non-maturity deposits, where the monthly model finds no effect to speak of (`r sprintf("%+.1f", mvm("g_nmd", 12))`% after three years) and the
quarterly model a gradual outflow (`r sprintf("%+.1f", mval("g_nmd", "repo_up", 12))`%),
both with bands that span zero: volume elasticities remain the least well
identified part of Stage 1.

```{r m-mult-gdp}
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "GDP growth one percentage point lower, permanently: the sector's credit-loss ratio (percentage points) and loan balances (% difference), quarterly production models."
gt <- c("clr", "g_mortgages_res", "g_vaf", "g_cards", "g_personal_other", "g_corp_all")
mg2 <- mu[mu$set == "production" & mu$shock == "gdp_down" & mu$target %in% gt, ]
mg2$lab <- ifelse(mg2$target == "clr", "Credit-loss ratio (pp)", paste0(plab[sub("^g_", "", mg2$target)], " (%)"))
ggplot(mg2, aes(quarters, effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = sc_col[["downside"]], alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(colour = sc_col[["downside"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12)) +
  labs(x = "quarters after the shock", y = NULL)
```

Growth works through credit quality and volumes rather than pricing: a
percentage point less GDP growth raises the sector's credit-loss ratio by
`r num(mval("clr", "gdp_down", 12), 2)` pp after three years (NGFB's unsecured-heavy book multiplies that) and
takes `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_cards", "gdp_down", 12)))`% off card balances and
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(mval("g_corp_all", "gdp_down", 12)))`% off corporate loans.

### A model-free check: local projections

Local projections (Jordà, 2005) estimate the response to a repo change
horizon by horizon, without the ARDL's geometric decay. The comparison feeds
the ARDL the same repo path the projections find (a rate change is followed
by further changes in the same direction).

```{r m-lp}
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-cap: "Response to a 1 pp repo change: local projection (points, 90% band) and the ARDL along the same repo path (line), quarterly. Deposit costs in percentage points; balances in % (the level of the book)."
lpq <- DY$lp[DY$lp$freq == "quarter", ]
lpq$lab <- factor(tlab[lpq$target], levels = unique(tlab[lpq$target]))
ggplot(lpq, aes(h)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = ink[["muted"]], width = 0, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(y = lp), colour = ink[["muted"]], size = 1.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ardl), colour = ent_col[["NGFB"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ lab, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 4, 8, 12)) +
  labs(x = "quarters after the change", y = NULL)
```

For savings and fixed deposits the two agree closely: the savings-deposit
model's response four quarters on is `r num(lpv("c_savings", 4, "ardl"), 2)` pp against the local
projection's `r num(lpv("c_savings", 4, "lp"), 2)`. Current accounts are the exception: along the same
repo path the local projection finds `r num(lpv("c_current", 4, "lp"), 2)` pp after four quarters and the
model `r num(lpv("c_current", 4, "ardl"), 2)`, below the projection's band. If the projection is right,
current-account costs follow the policy rate more closely than the model
assumes, which would make NGFB somewhat more liability-sensitive than
reported. For loan volumes they disagree, and instructively. The
local projection says home-loan balances are *higher* after a rise
(`r sprintf("%+.1f", lpv("g_mortgages_res", 4, "lp"))`% four quarters on): it measures the correlation between rate
changes and credit growth, and the SARB raises rates when credit is strong. It
is model-free but not identification-free; the sign restriction is what
identifies the causal direction in the satellites. A clean test would need
monetary-policy shocks measured directly, for example from the movement of
interest-rate futures around MPC announcements.

# Stage 2: banks relative to the industry

## Regimes and the share model

```{r regimes}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "The repo rate with the macro regimes used in Stage 2. Contraction takes priority (real GDP down on a year earlier), then hiking or easing (the repo rate up or down at least 25 bps over two quarters)."
rgm <- S2$regimes
reg_col <- c(contraction = "#e34948", hiking = "#eb6834", easing = "#1baf7a", neutral = "#c3c2b7")
mm <- merge(rgm, P$macro[, c("date", "repo")], by = "date")
mm$start <- mm$date - 91
ggplot(mm) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = start, xmax = date, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = regime), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(date, repo), colour = ink[["primary"]], linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = reg_col) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "repo rate (%)")
```

For each peer group (and, internally, each large bank) and product, the
annualised change in log market share is

$$ 400\,\Delta \log s_{t} = a + \delta_{\text{contr}}\, C_t + \delta_{\text{hike}}\, H_t + \delta_{\text{ease}}\, E_t + \kappa\,(g^{\text{sector}}_t - \bar g) + e_t , $$

Read it left to right. The 400 turns a quarterly change in log share into
percentage points a year: four quarters, times a hundred. $a$ is the
structural drift, how fast the group gains or loses share in an ordinary
quarter, which for some groups is a decade-long march summarised in one
number. $C_t$, $H_t$ and $E_t$ are switches that turn on in contraction,
hiking and easing quarters, so each $\delta$ is the extra drift in that regime
compared with a neutral quarter, the base. The $\kappa$ term asks whether the
group grows faster than the market when the market is booming, meaning sector
growth $g^{\text{sector}}_t$ above its average $\bar g$, and slower when it is
not: $\kappa > 0$ is a pro-cyclical share, growing faster than the market in
booms and shrinking faster in busts. $e_t$ is everything else: a new app, a
new chief executive, a weekend the core banking system spent offline.

The regimes are defined mechanically, with contraction taking priority. A
quarter is a contraction if real GDP is lower than a year earlier. Otherwise
it is hiking or easing if the repo rate has moved up or down by at least
25 bps over two quarters, and otherwise it is neutral. The sample has `r sum(rgm$regime == "contraction")`
contraction, `r sum(rgm$regime == "hiking")` hiking, `r sum(rgm$regime == "easing")` easing and
`r sum(rgm$regime == "neutral")` neutral quarters from `r qlab(min(rgm$date))`.

```{r s2-groups}
#| echo: false
keep_p <- c("cards", "personal_other", "mortgages_res", "corp_all", "nmd", "dep_retail", "beh_term")
prod_lab <- c(show_p, dep_retail = "Retail deposits (households)", vaf = "Vehicle and asset finance",
              mortgages_com = "Commercial mortgages")
cg <- S2$coef_groups[S2$coef_groups$product %in% keep_p, ]
cg$cell <- ifelse(is.finite(cg$t), sprintf("%+.1f (%.1f)", cg$est, cg$t), sprintf("%+.1f", cg$est))
dr <- cg[cg$param == "(Intercept)", c("product", "entity", "cell")]
dwd <- stats::reshape(dr, idvar = "product", timevar = "entity", direction = "wide")
names(dwd) <- sub("^cell\\.", "", names(dwd))
for (g in c("Big Four", "Challengers", "Specialists", "Other")) if (!g %in% names(dwd)) dwd[[g]] <- NA
dwd[is.na(dwd)] <- "—"
dwd$product <- prod_lab[dwd$product]
dwd <- dwd[match(prod_lab[keep_p], dwd$product), ]
kt(dwd[, c("product", "Big Four", "Challengers", "Specialists", "Other")], align = "lrrrr",
   caption = "Structural share drift a by peer group: percent a year of share growth, HAC t-statistics in brackets (— where a group's share is too small to model).")
```

```{r s2-groups-full}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cwd <- stats::reshape(cg[, c("entity", "product", "param", "cell")], idvar = c("entity", "product"),
                      timevar = "param", direction = "wide")
names(cwd) <- sub("^cell\\.", "", names(cwd))
cwd <- cwd[, c("product", "entity", "(Intercept)", "contraction", "hiking", "easing", "kappa")]
names(cwd) <- c("Product", "Group", "Drift a", "Contraction", "Hiking", "Easing", "Cycle kappa")
cwd$Product <- prod_lab[cwd$Product]
twin(cwd[order(cwd$Product, cwd$Group), ], "All share-model coefficients (percent a year; HAC t in brackets; kappa per point of sector growth)")
```

The structural drifts carry the clearest message: over 2008–2026 the
Challengers took share at double-digit rates in cards, retail deposits and
non-maturity deposits (all with $t > 2.5$), and the Big Four ceded it slowly
but significantly in cards, retail deposits and mortgages. Regime effects are
mostly imprecise, as is to be expected with only `r sum(rgm$regime == "contraction")`
contraction quarters, which is why they are pooled across banks and then
truncated before they reach NGFB.

## Who takes share from whom

```{r who-gains}
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-cap: "Average change in market share by regime, percentage points a year, with NGFB in the mix. Positive (blue) is a gain."
rs <- N$regime_share
rs <- rs[rs$product %in% c(names(show_p), "dep_retail"), ]
rs$product <- factor(prod_lab[rs$product], levels = rev(prod_lab[c(names(show_p), "dep_retail")]))
rs$entity <- factor(rs$entity, levels = names(ent_col))
rs$regime <- factor(rs$regime, levels = c("contraction", "hiking", "easing", "neutral"))
lim <- max(abs(rs$ds_pp_yr), na.rm = TRUE)
ggplot(rs, aes(entity, product, fill = ds_pp_yr)) +
  geom_tile(colour = ink[["surface"]], linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ regime, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = div_lo, mid = div_mid, high = div_hi, midpoint = 0, limits = c(-lim, lim),
                       name = "pp a year") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.title = element_text(colour = ink[["secondary"]]),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank())
```

```{r who-gains-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
rw <- stats::reshape(data.frame(product = as.character(rs$product), entity = as.character(rs$entity),
                                regime = as.character(rs$regime), v = sprintf("%+.2f", rs$ds_pp_yr)),
                     idvar = c("product", "entity"), timevar = "regime", direction = "wide")
names(rw) <- sub("^v\\.", "", names(rw))
twin(rw[order(rw$product, rw$entity), ], "Table view (pp a year)")
```

Net share changes do not say who lost to whom: a two-point gain could come
from one competitor or from all of them. The flow matrices below use a
labelled convention, giving each gainer's gain to the losers in proportion to
their losses.

```{r flows}
#| echo: false
fm <- function(key) {
  M <- N$flows[[key]]
  d <- data.frame(`gains` = rownames(M), round(M, 2), check.names = FALSE)
  d[rowSums(abs(M)) > 0, , drop = FALSE]
}
f1 <- fm("cards contraction"); f2 <- fm("nmd hiking")
guard(abs(sum(N$flows[["cards contraction"]]) -
          sum(pmax(rs$ds_pp_yr[rs$regime == "contraction" & rs$product == "Credit cards"], 0))) < 1e-8,
      "flow matrix does not allocate the gains")
kt(f1, caption = "Credit cards in contractions: share gained (rows) from each loser (columns), pp a year.")
kt(f2, caption = "Non-maturity deposits in hiking regimes: share gained (rows) from each loser (columns), pp a year.")
```

In contractions the Big Four lose card share to the Challengers and to
NGFB; in hiking regimes non-maturity deposits move from the Big Four towards
the Specialists, with NGFB and the Challengers smaller gainers. NGFB's rows follow from its drawn
parameters below, so they describe the kind of bank NGFB is, not data about
any real bank.

## NGFB's share parameters

```{r ngfb-draw}
#| echo: false
ph <- S2$population_hyper
ph <- ph[ph$product %in% c("cards", "personal_other", "nmd"), ]
ph$product <- prod_lab[ph$product]
kt(data.frame(Product = ph$product, Parameter = ph$param, `Population mean` = num(ph$mu, 2),
              `Between-bank s.d.` = num(ph$tau, 2), `s.e. of mean` = num(ph$se_mu, 2),
              Banks = ph$k, NGFB = num(ph$ngfb, 2), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llrrrrr", caption = sprintf("Random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) pooling across the six large banks and NGFB's posterior-predictive draw (seed %d), truncated at the same central probability mass as Post 1. Only pooled hyperparameters are shown.", CFG$seed))
```

The bank layer needs more than peer-group averages, because NGFB has to be a
plausible *single* bank. So the six large banks' equations are also estimated
one by one and pooled into a population with a random-effects estimator
(DerSimonian and Laird 1986). Each bank's estimate $\hat\theta_b$ of a
parameter is treated as the population mean, plus the bank's genuine
difference from it, plus estimation noise:

$$\hat\theta_b \;=\; \mu \;+\; u_b \;+\; \varepsilon_b, \qquad u_b \sim N(0,\tau^2), \qquad \varepsilon_b \sim N(0,\mathrm{se}_b^2).$$

The noise variances are known, because every estimate comes with its standard
error. So whatever spread between the banks' estimates is left over beyond
what noise can explain is genuine difference between banks, $\tau^2$.
DerSimonian and Laird estimate it by the method of moments, and the
population mean $\mu$ is then a weighted average that trusts the precisely
estimated banks more than the noisy ones. A new member of the population,
such as NGFB, draws its parameters from $N(\mu,\,\tau^2 + \mathrm{se}_\mu^2)$:
the population mean, spread by both the genuine differences between banks and
the uncertainty about the mean itself. The same population supplies the
yardsticks for [where NGFB should lean in](#share-strategy) and for its
[macro-adjusted scorecards](#performance): par (the mean) and the frontier
(the 80th percentile of the predictive distribution).

Each parameter is pooled across the six large banks with a random-effects
(DerSimonian–Laird) estimator, and NGFB's vector is drawn from the posterior
predictive $N(\mu, \tau^2 + \text{se}_\mu^2)$, truncated to the same central
probability mass as Post 1 (radius `r num(unique(S2$population_hyper$radius), 2)` in five
dimensions). Only pooled quantities with at least four banks are used. NGFB's
**structural drift is switched off** in all projections: a drawn drift of a
few percent a year compounds into large, arbitrary share gains or losses
over a horizon, and the question here is how NGFB responds to the *cycle*.

# The engine {#engine}

Each quarter the engine does what a bank's planning model does, line by line.
Every book grows with the industry's growth for that product, adjusted by
NGFB's share dynamics from Stage 2, and wholesale funding balances the books,
which is what a bank actually does at the margin. Then comes the income
statement, starting with net interest income:

$$\text{NII}_t \;=\; \sum_{i\,\in\,\text{assets}} \bar B_{i,t}\,\frac{y_{i,t}}{4} \;-\; \sum_{j\,\in\,\text{liabilities}} \bar B_{j,t}\,\frac{c_{j,t}}{4} \;+\; H_t .$$

That is average balance $\bar B$ times rate, a quarter at a time, for every
asset (at yield $y$) and every liability (at cost $c$), plus $H_t$, the
structural hedge's net settlement. Loans earn prime or the three-month
benchmark plus the industry's projected spreads, deposits cost the industry's
projected deposit costs, and HQLA earn roughly the Treasury bill rate. The
hedge term deserves its own line, because it is where most of the rate risk
is made and lost:

$$H_t \;=\; \sum_{i} N_i\,\frac{F_i - f_t}{4} .$$

Each tranche $i$ of the receive-fixed hedge earns its fixed rate $F_i$ and
pays the floating benchmark $f_t$ on its notional $N_i$. In the plan one
twentieth of the book matures every quarter and is replaced at the then
five-year swap rate (or at the tenor a lever chooses), so the book's average
fixed rate drifts slowly while the floating rate moves at the speed of the
Monetary Policy Committee. The gap between the two is the hedge carry, and it
is the whole story of how a structural hedge makes or loses money.

Below NII the engine is plain accounting, the part nobody presents at
conferences and every number depends on:

$$\text{NI}_t \;=\; (1-\tau)\big(\text{NII}_t + \text{NIR}_t - \text{Opex}_t - \text{Imp}_t\big), \qquad \text{ROE}_t \;=\; \frac{4\,\text{NI}_t}{\tfrac12\,(E_{t-1}+E_t)} .$$

Fees ($\text{NIR}$) and operating costs follow the industry's ratios to
assets. Impairments are the industry's credit-loss ratio scaled up or down by
product, unsecured highest and home loans lowest, because no return publishes
losses by product. Net income is profit after tax at rate $\tau$. In the plan
half of it is paid out and the rest retained, so equity rolls forward as
$E_t = E_{t-1} + \text{NI}_t - \text{dividends}_t$, and ROE is annualised net
income over average equity. The CET1 ratio is CET1 over risk-weighted assets,
with the bond books' OCI reserve when they are held at fair value; the LCR and
NSFR are proxies built from BA900's depositor-by-maturity matrix and
calibrated to the ratios the Prudential Authority publishes for the sector
([Calibration to the sector](#calibration-to-the-sector)); the leverage ratio
is CET1 over on-balance-sheet assets; and the PV01 of the hedge and bond books
gives the change in the economic value of equity (EVE) for a parallel rate
shock. Every ROE in this report is the average over the twelve quarters from
2026Q3 to 2029Q2 unless it says otherwise.

One more piece of plumbing has become topical. JIBAR, the three-month rate
that floating loans, wholesale funding and the hedge's floating leg have
referenced for a generation, publishes its last fixing on 31 December 2026, so
somebody in every treasury already knows how they are spending New Year's Eve.
From 2027Q1 the engine's floating benchmark is compounded ZARONIA plus the
fixed 16.19 bp fallback spread, so `r B(nw(tr$n_post))` of the twelve projected quarters
are priced off JIBAR's successor. [JIBAR's end](#jibar-end) has what that does.

# Scenarios {#scenarios}

```{r scen-table}
#| echo: false
lib <- c(SC$library, list(downside_cuts = SC$variants$downside_cuts$scenario))
guard(sum(lib$downside$gdp_yy < 0) >= 8 && max(lib$downside$cpi_yy) > 6 && max(lib$upside$gdp_yy) > 2.9,
      "scenario narratives")
guard(att_r("downside_cuts") / att_r("downside") > 0.35 && att_r("downside_cuts") / att_r("downside") < 0.65,
      "the variant loses about half")
kt(data.frame(Scenario = sc_long[names(lib)], Narrative = vapply(lib, function(s) attr(s, "narrative") %||% "", ""),
              Probability = c(pct(CFG$scenario_weights[scen], 0), "variant"), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llr", caption = "The three scenarios, and the downside's policy-rate variant. Probabilities are judgemental and are used only for the probability-weighted positioning.")
```

The baseline starts from the realised data at `r qlab(date0)` and follows the
SARB's own guidance for the next year: the repo rate at 7.25% after the
September 2026 increase, inflation above 5% around the turn of the year and
back at the 3% target (adopted with a one-point tolerance band in November
2025) by late 2027, after which the policy rate eases gradually to a
`r num(CFG$anchors$repo, 2)`% neutral level. Growth converges to about
`r num(CFG$anchors$gdp_yy, 1)`%. The upside and the downside are shocks layered on
the baseline with build-up, hold and decay profiles; the derived variables
(prime, the 3-month floating benchmark, curve slope, swap curve, real rates,
rate changes and their partial sums) are recomputed from the shocked paths, so
every scenario is internally consistent. The floating benchmark is 3-month
JIBAR until its last fixing on 31 December 2026 and compounded ZARONIA plus
the 16.19 bp fallback spread from 2027Q1 ([JIBAR's end](#jibar-end)), so ten
of the twelve projected quarters are priced off ZARONIA.

The **downside** is deliberately stagflationary. The SARB's own 2023 common
scenario stress test built its domestic adverse scenario the same way: a
higher country risk premium and a sharply weaker rand push inflation up, the
SARB tightens, government bond yields reprice and the economy contracts. The
alternative, a demand-led recession in which inflation falls and the SARB
cuts (2009, 2020), is run as a **variant** with the same real shock, because
for a hedged bank the policy response decides the sign of the rate effect.

```{r macro-paths}
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: "Macro paths by scenario (history in grey). The dashed line is the downside's variant with rate cuts."
mv_lab <- c(repo = "Repo rate (%)", gov10y = "10-year government yield (%)", cpi_yy = "CPI inflation (% y/y)",
            gdp_yy = "Real GDP (% y/y)", unemp = "Unemployment rate (%)", hpi_yy = "House prices (% y/y)")
hh <- P$macro[P$macro$date <= date0 & P$macro$date > date0 - 365 * 3, c("date", names(mv_lab))]
hl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(mv_lab), function(v) data.frame(date = hh$date, var = v, value = hh[[v]])))
sl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lib), function(k) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(mv_lab), function(v)
  data.frame(date = lib[[k]]$date, var = v, value = lib[[k]][[v]], scenario = k)))))
hl$var <- factor(mv_lab[hl$var], levels = mv_lab); sl$var <- factor(mv_lab[sl$var], levels = mv_lab)
sl$scenario <- factor(sl$scenario, levels = names(sc_col))
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = hl[is.finite(hl$value), ], aes(date, value), colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_line(data = sl, aes(date, value, colour = scenario, linetype = scenario), linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ var, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sc_col, labels = sc_short) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(baseline = "solid", upside = "solid", downside = "solid", downside_cuts = "22"),
                        labels = sc_short) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

```{r macro-twin}

#| results: asis

  s <- lib[[k]]
  data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[[k]], `Repo, peak` = num(max(s$repo), 2), `Repo, end` = num(utils::tail(s$repo, 1), 2),

}))
```

## What the scenarios do to the industry and to NGFB

```{r roe-dots}
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-cap: "Three-year average ROE by scenario: NGFB with its hedge, NGFB without it, and the BA900 sector through the same engine (unhedged)."
rl <- rbind(data.frame(scenario = sumtab$scenario, who = "NGFB", roe = sumtab$ngfb),
            data.frame(scenario = sumtab$scenario, who = "NGFB without hedge", roe = sumtab$ngfb_nohedge),
            data.frame(scenario = sumtab$scenario, who = "Sector (unhedged)", roe = sumtab$sector))
rl$scenario <- factor(sc_short[rl$scenario], levels = rev(sc_short))
ggplot(rl, aes(roe, scenario, colour = who)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(NGFB = ent_col[["NGFB"]], `NGFB without hedge` = "#86b6ef",
                                 `Sector (unhedged)` = ink[["secondary"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = "ROE, three-year average", y = NULL)
```

```{r attribution}
#| echo: false
aa <- att[att$metric %in% c("roe", "net_income"), ]
aa <- aa[order(match(aa$scenario, c("upside", "downside", "downside_cuts")), aa$entity, aa$metric == "net_income"), ]
fmt <- function(v, m) ifelse(m == "roe", bps(v), srbn(v, 1))
kt(data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[aa$scenario], Entity = aa$entity, Metric = ifelse(aa$metric == "roe", "ROE", "Net income, 3 years"),
              Volume = fmt(aa$volume, aa$metric), `Pricing (incl. hedge)` = fmt(aa$pricing, aa$metric),
              Credit = fmt(aa$credit, aa$metric), `Fees and costs` = fmt(aa$fees_costs, aa$metric),
              Interaction = fmt(aa$interaction, aa$metric), Total = fmt(aa$total, aa$metric), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lllrrrrrr", caption = "Change against the baseline, by channel: three-year average ROE and three-year net income. Each channel swaps one block of engine inputs from the scenario into the baseline run; the interaction is the residual.")
```

The industry is an **endowment play**. Without a hedge, its deposits and
capital earn more when rates rise, so in the downside the higher repo path
adds `r bps(att_r("downside", "Sector", "pricing"))` to the sector's ROE and offsets the credit
losses (`r bps(att_r("downside", "Sector", "credit"))`); in the upside the cuts take
`r bps(att_r("upside", "Sector", "pricing"))` away and the better credit picture only partly
compensates. NGFB is a **credit play**, and in this version a slightly
**liability-sensitive** one. Its unsecured-heavy book makes credit its largest channel
(`r bps(att_r("downside", "NGFB", "credit"))` in the downside, `r bps(att_r("upside", "NGFB", "credit"))` in the upside),
and its receive-fixed hedge, sized for slower deposit repricing than the
refined models now find, more than offsets its endowment: higher rates cost it
`r ubps(att_r("downside", "NGFB", "pricing"))` in the downside, and lower rates add
`r ubps(att_r("upside", "NGFB", "pricing"))` in the upside. In net income the downside
costs NGFB `r urbn(att_r("downside", m = "net_income"))` over three years
(`r urbn(-att_r("downside", "NGFB", "credit", "net_income"))` of it credit), while the sector,
`r num(sumtab["baseline", "sector_ni"] / base$ni, 1)` times NGFB's size in earnings, makes
`r srbn(att_r("downside", "Sector", m = "net_income"))`.

The **variant** shows how much rides on the policy response. With the same
contraction but rate cuts, the hedge earns `r bps(att_r("downside_cuts", "NGFB", "pricing"))` for
NGFB, which loses `r ubps(att_r("downside_cuts"))` in total, about half the stagflationary
loss, while the unhedged sector loses `r ubps(att_r("downside_cuts", "Sector"))`. A
structural hedge protects against the downturns of 2009 and 2020; it does
not protect against a downturn that comes with hikes.

NGFB's *level* of ROE sits below the sector's (`r pct(base$ngfb)` against
`r pct(base$sector)` in the baseline), because its unsecured-heavy book carries higher credit
losses (`r pct(base$clr, 2)` of loans against `r pct(base$sector_clr, 2)`). The hedge narrows the gap: without
it NGFB would earn `r pct(base$ngfb_nohedge)`. Its receive-fixed book carries an average fixed rate
of `r num(SC$hedge0$fixed0, 2)`%, struck at actual swap rates over the past five years, against a
floating leg averaging `r num(mean(res$baseline$scenario$float3m), 2)`% over the horizon (JIBAR to December 2026, then
compounded ZARONIA plus 16.19 bp, which is what the converted swaps pay), while new swaps are struck
close to that benchmark (the 5-year JIBAR swap traded `r num(A0$spreads$spread[A0$spreads$col == "swap5y"], 2)` pp above 3-month JIBAR on average in
2023–2026). The carry is the value of a position taken when rates were higher,
not a free lunch: it is what the hedge pays for giving up the upside in a
hiking cycle. In the previous version the hedge appeared to lift NGFB above
the sector; that was a swap proxy that overstated the book's rate (see
[Are the numbers right?](#audit)).

```{r roe-paths}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "NGFB's quarterly ROE and cumulative net income by scenario."
rp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(allr), function(k) { q <- allr[[k]]$ngfb$run$quarterly
  data.frame(date = q$date, roe = q$roe, ni = cumsum(q$net_income), scenario = k) }))
rp$scenario <- factor(rp$scenario, levels = names(sc_col))
p1 <- ggplot(rp, aes(date, roe, colour = scenario, linetype = scenario)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sc_col, labels = sc_short) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(baseline = "solid", upside = "solid", downside = "solid", downside_cuts = "22"),
                        labels = sc_short) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "annualised ROE")
p2 <- ggplot(rp, aes(date, ni / 1e6, colour = scenario, linetype = scenario)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sc_col, labels = sc_short) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(baseline = "solid", upside = "solid", downside = "solid", downside_cuts = "22"),
                        labels = sc_short) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "cumulative net income (R bn)")
if (requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, ncol = 2, guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "top"))
} else print(p1)
```

```{r roe-paths-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
rpw <- stats::reshape(data.frame(Quarter = qlab(rp$date), scenario = sc_short[as.character(rp$scenario)],
                                 v = paste0(pct(rp$roe), " / ", rbn(rp$ni, 1))),
                      idvar = "Quarter", timevar = "scenario", direction = "wide")
names(rpw) <- sub("^v\\.", "", names(rpw))
twin(rpw, "Table view: quarterly ROE / cumulative net income")
```

Capital and liquidity are not the constraint in any scenario: NGFB's CET1
ratio never falls below `r pct(min(sumtab$cet1_min))` (management floor
`r pct(CFG$cet1_min)`), and its LCR proxy never below `r pct(min(sumtab$lcr_min), 0)`
(floor `r pct(CFG$lcr_min, 0)`).

## Model risk in the scenarios

```{r model-risk}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[mr$scenario], `Core ROE` = pct(mr$core),
              `Credit losses convex in a contraction` = paste0(pct(mr$convex), " (", bps(mr$convex - mr$core), ")"),
              `No intercept correction on credit losses` = paste0(pct(mr$no_ic_credit), " (", bps(mr$no_ic_credit - mr$core), ")"),
              `Core net income` = rbn(mr$core_ni, 1), `Convex: net income` = srbn(mr$convex_ni - mr$core_ni),
              `No credit correction: net income` = srbn(mr$no_ic_credit_ni - mr$core_ni), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrr", caption = "NGFB's three-year average ROE and net income under two alternative credit models (changes against the core in brackets).")
```

Two credit-model choices deserve a flag. If losses are
convex in a contraction (the kinked model from the model checks), growth above
zero no longer lowers them, so the upside's credit benefit shrinks
(`r bps(mr["upside", "convex"] - mr["upside", "core"])` of ROE), while the downside barely changes because its
two years of negative growth produce about the same losses either way. And the
intercept correction on the credit-loss ratio, which carries the industry's
recent better-than-modelled loss experience forward, is worth
`r ubps(mr["baseline", "core"] - mr["baseline", "no_ic_credit"])` of ROE in every scenario: it moves the
level of NGFB's returns, not the differences between scenarios, and not the
positioning.

# Sensitivities {#sensitivities}

```{r sens-chart}
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "NGFB's three-year average ROE response to one-variable shocks around the baseline, by channel. The dot is the total."
sh_lab <- c(repo_up_100 = "Repo +100 bps", repo_down_100 = "Repo −100 bps", gdp_down_1 = "GDP growth −1 pp",
            unemp_up_2 = "Unemployment +2 pp", hpi_down_10 = "House prices −10% (year 1)",
            zar_weaker_10 = "Rand 10% weaker (year 1)", gov10y_up_100 = "10-year yield +100 bps",
            cpi_up_1 = "CPI +1 pp")
ch_lab <- c(volume = "Volume", pricing = "Pricing (incl. hedge)", credit = "Credit", fees_costs = "Fees and costs",
            interaction = "Interaction")
sl2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ch_lab), function(k) data.frame(shock = sens$shock, channel = k, v = sens[[k]])))
sl2$shock <- factor(sh_lab[sl2$shock], levels = rev(sh_lab)); sl2$channel <- factor(ch_lab[sl2$channel], levels = ch_lab)
tot <- data.frame(shock = factor(sh_lab[sens$shock], levels = rev(sh_lab)), v = sens$total)
ggplot(sl2, aes(1e4 * v, shock, fill = channel)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = tot, aes(1e4 * v, shock), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.4, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(unname(pal$categorical[1:4]), ink[["muted"]])) +
  labs(x = "change in ROE (bps)", y = NULL)
```

```{r sens-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(data.frame(Shock = sh_lab[sens$shock], Total = bps(sens$total), `Net income, 3 years` = srm(sens$net_income),
                Volume = bps(sens$volume), Pricing = bps(sens$pricing), Credit = bps(sens$credit),
                `Fees and costs` = bps(sens$fees_costs), `NIM` = bps(sens$nim), `Credit-loss ratio` = bps(sens$clr),
                `CET1, end` = bps(sens$cet1_end), `Total without hedge` = bps(snh[sens$shock, "total"]), check.names = FALSE))
```

The sensitivities answer "how exposed are we" one variable at a time
(one basis point of ROE is about `r urm(bp1)` of net income a year):

* **Rates.** ±100 bps on the repo path moves NGFB's ROE by
  `r bps(sens["repo_up_100", "total"])` / `r bps(sens["repo_down_100", "total"])`
  (`r srm(sens["repo_up_100", "net_income"])` / `r srm(sens["repo_down_100", "net_income"])` of net income over three years).
  Without the hedge the same shocks would move it by
  `r bps(snh["repo_up_100", "total"])` / `r bps(snh["repo_down_100", "total"])`. The hedge,
  `r pct(hedge_ratio0)` of non-maturity deposits, was sized in Post 3 for slower
  deposit repricing than the refined Stage 1 models find, so it now more than
  neutralises the endowment and leaves NGFB modestly liability-sensitive; the
  ratio that would leave first-year NII unchanged by a parallel move is
  `r pct(A0$neutral_ratio, 0)` (see [Are the numbers right?](#audit)). A
  rate rise also costs `r ubps(sens["repo_up_100", "credit"])` through credit losses.
* **Growth.** One point less GDP growth for three years costs
  `r ubps(sens["gdp_down_1", "total"])` (`r srm(sens["gdp_down_1", "net_income"])`), almost all of it
  through credit losses (`r bps(sens["gdp_down_1", "credit"])`). This is NGFB's
  largest single exposure.
* **House prices** matter through mortgage and VAF pricing and credit
  (`r bps(sens["hpi_down_10", "total"])` for a 10% fall in the first year).
* **Inflation** helps a little (`r bps(sens["cpi_up_1", "total"])` per point)
  because fee income tracks nominal activity.
* **Unemployment** has essentially no effect (`r bps(sens["unemp_up_2", "total"])`):
  no credit-loss specification with unemployment survives the sign and
  t-tests, so the engine has no unemployment channel. Unemployment is not
  harmless; the South African series is too slow-moving and too noisy, given
  GDP, to identify one.

# Positioning before the scenario arrives

## The optimisation problem

The decision is a set of balance-sheet moves made at the jump-off: transfers
of one percent of total assets from HQLA (the liquidity numeraire) into a
lending book, from wholesale funding into a deposit category, or a change in
the receive-fixed hedge of one percent of the non-maturity deposit (NMD) base.
The full engine is the source of truth; around the status quo it is close to
linear in the moves, so for every scenario $s$ the ROE gradient $G_s$ and the
gradients of the CET1 and LCR troughs and of net income come from central
finite differences.

A naive optimiser would simply maximise the engine's ROE. Even with the
execution costs below it grows every lending book out of HQLA, pushes
`r raw_up` of the six to their upper bound and claims `r ubps(raw_gain)` of
probability-weighted ROE: the engine prices new volume at the book's
*average* yield, loss rate and cost ratio, and holds equity fixed, so any risk
asset looks better than HQLA. That static attractiveness is a franchise and
capacity question (marginal pricing, cost to serve, adverse selection) that
public data cannot price. The positioning question is different: *what should
change because scenario X is coming?*

The answer used here treats the status quo as optimal under the baseline (the
balance sheet reflects the bank's central plan). That reveals an implied
marginal cost for every move, $c = G_{\text{baseline}}$, in the same way
Black and Litterman back out implied returns from market weights. Positioning
then trades on how a scenario changes each move's value:

$$ \max_x \; \sum_s w_s \big(R_s + (G_s - c)\,x\big) \;-\; \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\, \mathrm{Var}_w\!\big(R + G x\big) \;-\; \tfrac12\, x' K x $$

subject to the CET1 floor (`r pct(CFG$cet1_min)`), the LCR floor
(`r pct(CFG$lcr_min, 0)`) and move bounds, where $K$ is an execution cost:
pricing concessions and acquisition costs to grow a book within a year,
attrition to shrink it. With one scenario treated as certain ($w_X = 1$,
$\lambda = 0$) and no constraint binding, the problem separates move by move
and has a closed form:

$$ x_k^{*} = \frac{G_{X,k} - c_k}{2\,\kappa_k}, \qquad \text{net gain} = \sum_k \frac{(G_{X,k} - c_k)^2}{4\,\kappa_k}, $$

where $\kappa_k$ is the execution cost of a one-unit move. Every result is
re-run through the full engine and reported net of $c'x$ and
$\tfrac12 x'Kx$, in ROE and in net income (the implied cost in net-income
terms is the net-income gradient under the baseline, so the status quo is
optimal in both). The quadratic programme's linear prediction and the engine
agree to within `r ubps(max(abs(O$own - O$pred)), 2)` of ROE.

```{r moves-table}
#| echo: false
c0 <- O$implied_cost
short_line <- c(hqla = "HQLA", wholesale_other = "Wholesale funding")
kt(data.frame(Move = mv$label, From = ifelse(is.na(mv$from), "—", short_line[mv$from]),
              Unit = ifelse(mv$unit == "hedge", "1% of NMD", "1% of assets"),
              Bounds = sprintf("%+.1f to %+.1f", mv$lower, mv$upper),
              `Execution cost of a 1-unit move` = ubps(mv$cost, 1),
              `Engine ROE gain per unit, baseline (= implied cost)` = bps(c0, 1),
              `Net income per unit, baseline` = srm(O$implied_ni), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lllrrrr", caption = "Moves, bounds and costs. The last two columns are what the engine says each move earns under the baseline before any marginal cost (net income over three years); the optimiser treats them as the move's implied marginal cost.")
```

The hedge is bounded by policy (a hedge ratio of roughly 25–75% of NMD) and
penalised for deviating from Post 3's variance-optimal ratio rather than for
transaction costs, which are negligible for swaps.

In plain terms: $x$ is the vector of moves, $R_s$ the ROE in scenario $s$ if
nothing moves, $w_s$ the scenario probabilities, and $(G_s - c)$ the extra
value one unit of each move adds in scenario $s$ over and above the baseline.
The middle term penalises spreading the outcomes across scenarios, with
$\lambda$ setting how much; a bank that cares only about the average sets
$\lambda = 0$. The last term is the execution cost, and it is quadratic, so a
two-unit move costs four times a one-unit move, which is roughly how
franchises behave when you try to rush them. With one scenario treated as
certain, each move's problem is to maximise $(G_{X,k} - c_k)\,x_k - \kappa_k x_k^2$:
the benefit rises in a straight line and the cost in a parabola, and the best
move is where one more unit adds exactly as much benefit as cost. Move in the
direction the scenario shifts the move's value, by an amount proportional to
how far it shifts it, and inversely proportional to how expensive the move is
to execute. The implied cost $c$ is what keeps this honest: instead of asking
the model what the balance sheet should be, it asks what the model must
believe for the current balance sheet to be right, and trades only on
departures from that.

Take the hedge, because it does most of the work. Under the baseline one more
point of hedge earns `r B(bps(h_c, 1))` of ROE, so that is its implied cost. Under the
downside it earns `r B(bps(h_G, 1))`, because the floating leg it pays reprices up with
the hikes. The net gradient is `r B(bps(h_G - h_c, 1))` a point and the execution cost
`r B(ubps(h_k, 1))` per point squared, so the optimum is
$`r B(sprintf("%.2f", 1e4 * (h_G - h_c)))` / (2 \times `r B(sprintf("%.1f", 1e4 * h_k))`) = `r B(sprintf("%.1f", h_x))`$ points of
non-maturity deposits, taking the hedge from `r B(pct(N$hedge_ratio))` to `r B(pct(N$hedge_ratio + h_x / 100))`.

## How the problem is solved, step by step {.steps}

For every scenario the same eight steps run, in `analysis/05_scenarios.R` and
`analysis/06_optimise.R`:

1. **Project the scenario.** The macro path drives the Stage 1 sector models
   (volumes, spreads, deposit costs, credit losses, fees, costs) and the
   Stage 2 share models (NGFB's growth relative to the sector, by regime).
2. **Run the status quo.** The engine projects NGFB's balance sheet, P&L,
   capital and liquidity quarter by quarter: ROE $R_s$, net income, CET1 and
   LCR troughs.
3. **Measure the gradients.** Each move is made at ±0.5 units and the engine
   re-run: $G_{s,k} = (\text{ROE}^{+} - \text{ROE}^{-})/1$, and likewise for
   net income, CET1 and LCR.
4. **Back out the implied costs.** $c_k = G_{\text{baseline},k}$: the plan is
   built for the baseline, so at the margin no move adds value there.
5. **Net gradient.** $G_{s,k} - c_k$ is what scenario $s$ changes about the
   value of move $k$.
6. **Solve.** The quadratic programme (`quadprog`'s dual active-set method)
   maximises net gradient times moves less execution cost, subject to the
   bounds and the CET1 and LCR floors. When nothing binds the solution is the
   closed form above, one line per move.
7. **Re-run and bridge.** The engine is re-run with the moves, which captures
   everything the linear model misses (moves compound with growth, equity
