JIBAR has not ceased yet, but almost all of the projection lies beyond it. The
SARB's Market Practitioners Group set the timetable on
`r format(jt$announced, "%e %B %Y")`:

| Date | Milestone |
|---|---|
| `r format(jt$announced, "%e %B %Y")` | Cessation announced; the credit adjustment spread (CAS) for 3-month JIBAR fixed at 16.19 bp, the five-year median of 3-month JIBAR less compounded ZARONIA |
| `r format(jt$new_contracts_banned, "%e %B %Y")` | No new JIBAR-linked contracts, except trades that reduce existing JIBAR exposure |
| 20–21 November 2026 | Cleared JIBAR swaps converted to ZARONIA overnight-index swaps at the clearing houses: the fixed rate is kept and the floating leg pays compounded ZARONIA plus 16.19 bp, with a cash payment for any valuation difference |
| `r format(jt$last_fixing, "%e %B %Y")` | Last publication of JIBAR; contracts that still reference it fall back to compounded ZARONIA plus the CAS |

: The JIBAR transition. Loans follow the Market Practitioners Group's conventions: ZARONIA compounded in arrears with a five-business-day lookback, plus the CAS and the contractual margin. {.striped}

`r tr$n_post` of the twelve projected quarters (2027Q1 to 2029Q2) therefore fall
after the last fixing, and from this version the engine prices them that way.
Its 3-month floating benchmark -- the reference for corporate term loans,
interbank lending, floating-rate securities, wholesale funding and the
hedge's floating leg -- is JIBAR to 2026Q4 and compounded ZARONIA plus 16.19 bp
from 2027Q1. ZARONIA follows the policy rate at the median spread of the last
eight quarters of daily data (`r sprintf("%+.2f", tr$spreads[["zaronia"]])` pp), and a quarter's average
of daily ZARONIA is its compounded rate up to convexity well under a basis point.
At a given policy rate the successor sits `r ubps(tr$switch_level / 100, 1)` above JIBAR
(`r sprintf("%+.2f", tr$spreads[["jibar"]])` pp over the policy rate in the panel), and against a run that keeps JIBAR to
2029, NGFB's ROE moves by `r bps(swe["baseline", "d_roe"], 1)` in the baseline (`r srm(swe["baseline", "d_nii"])` of NII over three
years) and by no more than `r ubps(max(abs(swe$d_roe)), 1)` in any scenario. That is no accident: the CAS is the long-run median of the basis it
replaces. Over the 36 months of daily data, 3-month JIBAR traded `r num(jz[["mean"]], 2)` pp above
ZARONIA on average, between `r num(jz[["min"]], 2)` and `r num(jz[["max"]], 2)` pp, and the CAS sits at the median:

```{r au-basis}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "3-month JIBAR less ZARONIA, monthly averages of daily fixings, against the fixed fallback spread of 16.19 bp. Source: rbond.co.za (CC BY 4.0), SARB Market Practitioners Group."
mo <- A$monthly
bz <- data.frame(date = mo$date, basis = 100 * (mo$jibar3m_rb - mo$zaronia))
ggplot(bz, aes(date, basis)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100 * jt$cas, colour = div_lo, linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "22") +
  annotate("text", x = min(bz$date), y = 100 * jt$cas + 1.2, label = "fallback spread, 16.19 bp", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.1, colour = div_lo) +
  geom_line(colour = ent_col[["NGFB"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "basis points")
```

```{r au-basis-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(data.frame(Month = format(bz$date, "%b %Y"), `JIBAR less ZARONIA (bp)` = num(bz$basis, 1), check.names = FALSE))
```

What the transition changes is risk, not level:

* **The basis stops floating.** A 3-month term rate carries the market's
  expected policy move over the coming quarter and the banks' term and credit
  premium; over `r format(min(jrh$date), "%Y")`–`r format(max(jrh$date), "%Y")` 3-month JIBAR's quarterly spread over the policy rate ranged from
  `r num(min(jrh$spread), 2)` to `r num(max(jrh$spread), 2)` pp (median `r num(tr$jibar_repo$median, 2)`). ZARONIA compounded in arrears carries neither,
  and the CAS is fixed. Floating-rate assets will no longer reprice ahead of an
  expected hike, nor pick up a widening bank-credit premium in a stress; nor will
  floating funding or the hedge's floating leg pay it. NGFB pays the benchmark
  on net -- floating assets of `r rbn(ex[["assets"]])` against floating funding of `r rbn(ex[["funding"]])` and a
  hedge notional of `r rbn(ex[["hedge"]])` -- so each 10 bp of basis widening cost it about
  `r urm(tr$basis_10bp)` of annual NII under JIBAR, and costs nothing from 2027. Funding stress
  does not disappear: it moves into the spreads at which NCDs and notes are
  issued over the overnight rate.
* **The spread is at risk on the asset side.** Converted and fallback
  contracts keep the 16.19 bp, but loans that are re-papered onto ZARONIA are
  priced in negotiation, and a borrower quoted "ZARONIA plus the old margin"
  has gained the CAS. If NGFB lost it on every floating-rate asset from 2027Q1,
  ROE would fall by `r ubps(-crx("baseline"))` in the baseline (`r urbn(-crx("baseline", col = "d_nii"))` of NII over three
  years), and by `r ubps(-crx("baseline", "assets_and_funding"))` if its floating funding were re-priced the same way. Pricing
  new ZARONIA business at all-in parity -- ZARONIA plus the CAS plus the
  margin -- is worth that much.
* **The hedge is unaffected.** The clearing houses keep each swap's fixed
  rate and pay ZARONIA plus 16.19 bp on the floating leg, so the book's carry is
  unchanged. A new receive-fixed hedge is a ZARONIA swap, struck about 16.19 bp
  below the JIBAR swap rate while the basis trades at the CAS, and earns the
  same carry against ZARONIA as the engine's JIBAR-equivalent quote against
  ZARONIA plus 16.19 bp.

```{r au-cas}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[unique(cr$scenario)],
              `Floating assets lose the CAS: ROE` = bps(cr$d_roe[cr$case == "assets"]),
              `NII, 3 years` = srbn(cr$d_nii[cr$case == "assets"]),
              `Assets and floating funding lose it: ROE` = bps(cr$d_roe[cr$case == "assets_and_funding"]),
              `NII, 3 years ` = srbn(cr$d_nii[cr$case == "assets_and_funding"]), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrr", caption = sprintf("The spread at risk: 16.19 bp off the rate of every floating-rate asset (%s) from 2027Q1, and off floating funding (%s) as well. An upper bound: converted and fallback contracts keep the spread.",
                                       paste(c(corporate_loans = "corporate term loans", interbank = "interbank lending", other_securities = "floating-rate securities")[tr$lines_assets], collapse = ", "),
                                       "wholesale funding"))
```

# More levers: what else ties in with the macro view {#levers}

```{r lv-setup}
#| include: false
LV <- rd("levers.rds")
lvs <- LV$summary; lvl <- LV$levers; rcv <- LV$ratio_curve; rbest <- LV$ratio_best
lv <- function(l, s, col) lvs[lvs$lever == l & lvs$setting == s, col]
lvx <- function(l, s, k, col) lvl[lvl$lever == l & lvl$setting == s & lvl$scenario == k, col]
hq <- LV$hqla; rownames(hq) <- hq$scenario
sc4 <- c("baseline", "upside", "downside", "downside_cuts")
asw <- LV$asset_swap; rownames(asw) <- asw$scenario
as_set <- "A quarter of HQLA in asset-swapped 5-year bonds"
bsm <- rd("audit.rds")$bs_model
buf <- LV$buffer
buf_set <- function(tg) sprintf("LCR %.0f%% at the jump-off", 100 * tg)
bx <- function(tg, k, col) buf[buf$setting == buf_set(tg) & buf$scenario == k, col]
whs0 <- N$engine_bs$balance[N$engine_bs$line == "wholesale_other"]
as_size <- LV$theta * LV$H0
br0 <- res$baseline$ngfb$inputs$rates; bill_gap <- mean(float_rate(br0) - br0$tbill)
per10 <- vapply(LV$lcr_targets, function(tg) 1e4 * bx(tg, "baseline", "d_roe") / (bx(tg, "baseline", "release") / 1e7), 0)
guard(all(per10 > 8 & per10 < 10), "the buffer saves about nine basis points per R10 bn")
## the claims in the asset-swap and buffer sections
guard(all(asw$d_roe > 0.003) && max(asw$d_roe) - min(asw$d_roe) < 0.001,
      "the asset swap pays about the same in every scenario")
guard(asw["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"] == min(asw$d_cet1_oci_min) &&
      abs(asw["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"]) < abs(hq["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"]) / 3,
      "the asset swap's worst OCI hit is in the downside and a fraction of the duration book's")
guard(bsm$beta < 0.25 && bsm$kappa > 0.2 && bsm$kappa < 0.35 && bsm$kappa_d1 < 0.15, "the spread model's numbers in the text")
guard(LV$as_jo$bs < bsm$bs_mean - 0.3 && LV$as_jo$bs > bsm$bs_min, "today's spread sits at the tight end of its range")
bs_widen_max <- max(vapply(seq_along(bsm$fit$bs5), function(i) max(bsm$fit$bs5[i:nrow(bsm$fit)] - bsm$fit$bs5[i]), 0))
guard(bs_widen_max > 0.1 && bs_widen_max < 0.5, "the largest widening in the swap data is a fraction of 100 bps")
frac_word <- function(r) { r <- round(abs(r)); guard(r >= 2 && r <= 10, "no word for a ratio of %s", r)
  c("half", "third", "quarter", "fifth", "sixth", "seventh", "eighth", "ninth", "tenth")[r - 1] }
bft <- utils::tail(bsm$fit, 4)
guard(all(bft$bs5 < bft$fitted), "the spread model overstates the spread in the most recent months")
guard(all(diff(vapply(LV$lcr_targets, function(tg) bx(tg, "baseline", "d_roe"), 0)) > 0) &&
      all(buf$lcr_min > CFG$lcr_min) && all(buf$nsfr_min > 1.1) && max(LV$release_share) * N$engine_bs$balance[N$engine_bs$line == "hqla"] < whs0,
      "a smaller buffer pays more, stays above the floors and repays no more than the wholesale book")
```

The optimiser in [Positioning](#positioning-before-the-scenario-arrives) moves
the balance sheet's mix. A bank's ALCO has more levers than that, and most of
them are rate, spread, liquidity and capital decisions that a macro view
should drive directly. This chapter runs each through the full engine in every
scenario (and the downside's variant with cuts), against NGFB's plan, with the
swap curve corrected in [Are the numbers right?](#audit), in the order an ALCO
sets them: the **structural hedge** that converts the deposit franchise's rate
sensitivity (how much of it, and at what tenor maturing swaps are reinvested);
the **liquidity book** (whether the buffer sits in bills, ten-year bonds or
asset-swapped bonds, and how large it is); **capital** (payout and
distribution); and deposit pricing. The macro paths are known in each
scenario; the question is which settings pay in which world, and which pay
across them, using the same judgemental probabilities as the robust
positioning (baseline `r pct(LV$weights[["baseline"]], 0)`, upside
`r pct(LV$weights[["upside"]], 0)`, downside `r pct(LV$weights[["downside"]], 0)`).
The [strategy lab](#lab) then replays every lever across sixty historical
macro paths, and the [risk-budgeted optimiser](#risk-budget) sets them together.

## A strategy map: which macro signal drives which lever {#strategy-map}

```{r lv-map}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(
  Lever = c("Hedge ratio", "Reinvestment tenor", "10-year bonds in HQLA", "Asset-swapped bonds", "Size of the buffer", "Payout",
            "Unsecured growth"),
  Decision = c("share of non-maturity deposits received fixed", "tenor of the swaps that replace maturing tranches",
               "share of the buffer's bills in 10-year government bonds", "share in 5-year government bonds swapped to floating",
               "Treasury bills released to repay wholesale funding", "share of profit paid out", "card and personal-loan growth"),
  `Premium it earns` = c("fixed over floating: a view on the policy path", "the swap curve's term premium",
                         "the term premium and the fiscal premium", "the fiscal premium alone",
                         "wholesale funding's cost over the bills' yield", "equity returned: a smaller ROE denominator",
                         "volume and margin"),
  `Macro signal (rule)` = c("policy rate against neutral (R1)", "policy rate against neutral (R2)", "the curve's slope (R3)",
                            "the 5-year bond–swap spread (R6)", "stress: GDP or the rand (R7)", "growth and CET1 (R4)",
                            "the labour market (R5)"),
  `Risk it takes` = c("rates rise", "today's rates locked in for longer", "the 10-year yield rises",
                      "the spread widens", "less liquidity going into a stress", "a thinner cushion into a downturn",
                      "credit losses"),
  `Where the risk shows` = c("NII, EVE", "EVE", "OCI and CET1, HQLA at market, EVE", "OCI and CET1, HQLA at market",
                             "LCR, NSFR", "CET1", "profit, CET1"),
  check.names = FALSE),
  align = "llllll", caption = "The strategy map. Each rule reads the previous quarter's data with parameters set in advance as round numbers ([Strategy lab](#lab)). Payout and unsecured growth also have static settings; every lever's static settings are in the tables below.")
```

Read down, the map is the order of an ALCO's decisions: first how much of the
deposit franchise's rate sensitivity to convert to fixed, then how to hold
the liquidity that regulation requires and how much of it to hold, then how
much capital to keep. Read across, it says why each lever has its own macro
signal: each earns a different premium, and a premium is worth collecting
when it is large. A receive-fixed hedge pays when the policy rate falls below
the swap rate struck, so its signal is the policy rate against neutral; a
ten-year bond earns the term premium, largest when the curve is steep; an
asset-swapped bond earns only the fiscal premium, largest when sovereign
stress has widened the bond–swap spread; surplus liquidity is insurance,
worth most going into a stress; retained capital is worth most going into a
downturn. And it says why the levers have to be chosen under limits: every
setting that earns more takes a risk the three-year ROE does not price, and
the risks land in different places -- the hedge and the bond book in the
economic value of equity, the bond books in OCI and CET1 and in the market
value of the buffer, a smaller buffer in the LCR and NSFR, a higher payout in
CET1. The [risk-budgeted optimiser](#risk-budget) puts one limit on each.

```{r lv-table}
#| echo: false
ord <- c("Hedge ratio", "Reinvestment tenor", "Equity hedge", "HQLA duration", "Asset swap", "Liquidity buffer", "Payout",
         "Distribution", "Deposit pricing", "Combined")
lt <- lvs[lvs$lever %in% ord, ]
lt <- lt[order(match(lt$lever, ord), -lt$d_roe_weighted), ]
show <- !(lt$lever == "Hedge ratio" & !(lt$setting %in% c("0%", "25%", "35%", "65%", "80%")))
lt <- lt[show, ]
kt(data.frame(Lever = lt$lever, Setting = lt$setting, Baseline = bps(lt$d_roe_baseline), Upside = bps(lt$d_roe_upside),
              Downside = bps(lt$d_roe_downside), `Downside with cuts` = bps(lt$d_roe_cuts),
              `Probability-weighted` = bps(lt$d_roe_weighted), `Net income, weighted, 3 years` = srbn(lt$d_ni_weighted),
              `CET1 trough` = pct(lt$cet1_min), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llrrrrrrr", caption = "Change in NGFB's three-year average ROE against the plan, by lever and scenario. Probability-weighted: baseline, upside and downside at the judgemental weights (the variant carries no weight). CET1 trough: the lowest quarter across the three weighted scenarios.")
```

```{r lv-guards}

guard(rbest[["weighted"]] == max(rcv$ratio) && rbest[["downside"]] == min(rcv$ratio) && rbest[["stable"]] == min(rcv$ratio),
      "hedge ratio: corner solutions, the weighted best at the top, the downside and stability at zero")

guard(all(lvl$d_roe[lvl$lever == "Reinvestment tenor" & lvl$setting == "3 years"] < 0), "three-year reinvestment loses everywhere")
```

## The hedge ratio is a rate view

```{r lv-ratio}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "NGFB's three-year average ROE against the structural hedge ratio, by scenario. Changes are made at the jump-off with 5-year swaps (receive fixed to add, pay fixed to offset); the existing book's locked-in carry stays either way. Dotted lines: the plan's ratio and the ratio at which first-year NII does not move with a parallel rate shift."
rl2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sc4, function(k) data.frame(ratio = rcv$ratio, roe = rcv[[c(baseline = "baseline", upside = "upside", downside = "downside", downside_cuts = "cuts")[[k]]]], scenario = k)))
rl2$scenario <- factor(rl2$scenario, levels = names(sc_col))
ggplot(rl2, aes(ratio, roe, colour = scenario, linetype = scenario)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(hedge_ratio0, neutral_r), colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "13") +
  annotate("text", x = c(neutral_r, hedge_ratio0), y = max(rl2$roe) + 0.002, label = c("rate-neutral", "plan"),
           size = 3.1, colour = ink[["secondary"]], hjust = c(1.05, -0.05)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sc_col, labels = sc_short) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(baseline = "solid", upside = "solid", downside = "solid", downside_cuts = "22"), labels = sc_short) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(0.1)) +
  labs(x = "hedge ratio, % of non-maturity deposits", y = "ROE, three-year average")
```

```{r lv-ratio-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(data.frame(`Hedge ratio` = pct(rcv$ratio, 0), Baseline = pct(rcv$baseline, 2), Upside = pct(rcv$upside, 2),
                Downside = pct(rcv$downside, 2), `Downside with cuts` = pct(rcv$cuts, 2),
                `Probability-weighted` = pct(rcv$weighted, 2), check.names = FALSE))
```

A receive-fixed swap earns its fixed rate and pays the floating benchmark
(JIBAR, and from 2027 compounded ZARONIA plus 16.19 bp), so more hedge pays in
every scenario in which the benchmark falls below the swap rate it was struck
at, and costs in every scenario in which it rises above it. ROE is therefore
linear in the hedge ratio, and the best ratio is a corner: as much hedge as
policy allows if the view is the baseline (`r bps(lvx("Hedge ratio", "80%", "baseline", "d_roe"))` at 80% of
non-maturity deposits), the upside (`r bps(lvx("Hedge ratio", "80%", "upside", "d_roe"))`) or a downturn with cuts
(`r bps(lvx("Hedge ratio", "80%", "downside_cuts", "d_roe"))`), and none if the view is the stagflationary downside
(`r bps(lvx("Hedge ratio", "0%", "downside", "d_roe"))` at 0%). At the judgemental weights more hedge wins
(`r bps(lv("Hedge ratio", "80%", "d_roe_weighted"))` at 80%), because the 5-year swap at the jump-off (`r num(LV$swap5_jo, 2)`%) priced the
SARB's 2026 increases but not the baseline's point of cuts by 2028. That is a
bet on the bank's rate view against the market's, and it should be sized as
one, not as a structural decision: the ratio that leaves first-year NII
unchanged by a parallel move is `r pct(neutral_r, 0)`, and the ROE range across the three
weighted scenarios is narrowest with no hedge at all (`r pp(rcv$range[rcv$ratio == 0], 1)` against
`r pp(rcv$range[abs(rcv$ratio - 0.5) < 1e-9], 1)` at 50%).

## Reinvestment tenor: the term premium

```{r lv-tenor}
#| echo: false
tt <- lvl[lvl$lever == "Reinvestment tenor", ]
ten_set <- c("3 years", "5 years", "7 years", "10 years")
kt(data.frame(Tenor = ten_set,
              Baseline = bps(vapply(ten_set, function(x) lvx("Reinvestment tenor", x, "baseline", "d_roe"), 0)),
              Upside = bps(vapply(ten_set, function(x) lvx("Reinvestment tenor", x, "upside", "d_roe"), 0)),
              Downside = bps(vapply(ten_set, function(x) lvx("Reinvestment tenor", x, "downside", "d_roe"), 0)),
              `Downside with cuts` = bps(vapply(ten_set, function(x) lvx("Reinvestment tenor", x, "downside_cuts", "d_roe"), 0)),
              `Book PV01 after three years` = paste0("R", num(pv$pv01 / 1e3, 0), nb, "m per bp"),
              `PV01 against the plan` = spct(pv$vs_plan, 0), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrr", caption = "Change in ROE when maturing hedge tranches are reinvested at each tenor instead of five years, and the receive-fixed book's PV01 at the end of the horizon (the value change for a 1 bp parallel move).")
```

One twentieth of the hedge matures every quarter, so within three years
three-fifths of the book is reinvested. At ten years instead of five each
reinvested tranche earns the swap curve's term premium, about
`r num(A0$spreads$spread[A0$spreads$col == "swap10y"] - A0$spreads$spread[A0$spreads$col == "swap5y"], 1)` pp a year more over 2023–2026,
which is worth `r bps(lv("Reinvestment tenor", "10 years", "d_roe_weighted"))` of ROE in every scenario alike. It is not free:
the book's PV01 rises by `r pct(pv$vs_plan[pv$tenor_q == 40], 0)`, so the economic value of equity becomes
more sensitive to rates and the IRRBB limits bind sooner, and the bank locks
today's rates in for longer. Seven years is the halfway house
(`r bps(lv("Reinvestment tenor", "7 years", "d_roe_weighted"))`, `r spct(pv$vs_plan[pv$tenor_q == 28], 0)` PV01).

## HQLA duration: the term and fiscal premia

```{r lv-hqla}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[hq$scenario], `ROE` = bps(hq$d_roe), `Net income, 3 years` = srbn(hq$d_ni),
              `10-year yield, change over the horizon` = sprintf("%+.2f pp", hq$gov10y_change),
              `CET1 through OCI: worst quarter` = bps(hq$d_cet1_oci_min), `CET1 through OCI: end` = bps(hq$d_cet1_oci_end),
              check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrr", caption = sprintf("A quarter of the earning HQLA (%s) moved from Treasury bills into 10-year government bonds at the jump-off. The carry runs through NII; at fair value through OCI the price change along each scenario's 10-year yield runs through CET1 (modified duration of the bond's remaining life, after tax). Held at amortised cost there is no OCI effect, but the economic exposure is the same.",
                                       rbn(LV$theta * N$pricing$hqla$scale * N$engine_bs$balance[N$engine_bs$line == "hqla"])))
```

NGFB's liquidity buffer sits in Treasury bills and cash. Level 1 government
bonds count the same towards the LCR, and South Africa's curve pays about two
points for the duration: the 10-year bond yielded `r num(LV$gov10_jo, 2)`% in the jump-off quarter
against `r num(P$macro$jibar3m[P$macro$date == date0], 2)`% for three-month JIBAR, and bills yield a little less than the 3-month benchmark.
The bonds are bought at that jump-off yield in every scenario. Moving a quarter of the buffer adds
`r bps(lv("HQLA duration", hq_set, "d_roe_weighted"))` of ROE at the scenario weights, most where the long yield falls
(`r bps(hq["downside_cuts", "d_roe"])` in a downturn with cuts) and least in the stagflationary downside
(`r bps(hq["downside", "d_roe"])`). The price is the same fiscal risk the premium compensates: at
the downside's peak the bonds' mark-to-market costs `r ubps(-hq["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"])` of CET1 if held at
fair value through OCI, and a sovereign shock larger than the scenarios'
(2015 and 2020 both moved the long bond by more) would cost more. This is a
lever to size against a view on the long bond -- its term and fiscal premia --
not on the policy rate. The next lever keeps the fiscal premium and hedges
away the rest.

## Asset-swapped bonds: the fiscal premium without the duration {#asset-swap}

**What it is.** A ten-year bond held for liquidity earns two premia over
bills: the *term premium*, the reward for interest-rate risk, and the
*fiscal premium* South African government bonds pay over the swap curve, the
reward for sovereign and supply risk. An asset swap separates them. NGFB
buys a 5-year government bond for the buffer and, against it, pays fixed on a
5-year swap of the same notional: the swap's fixed leg passes the bond's
coupon on, its floating leg pays the benchmark back. What is left is a
floating-rate asset that yields the benchmark plus the bond's yield over the
swap rate -- the *bond–swap spread*, $bs = y^{\text{bond}}_{5} - s_{5}$. Against the
Treasury bills it replaces, each rand earns

$$ \text{carry} = \underbrace{y^{\text{bond}}_{5} - s_{5}}_{\text{bond–swap spread, locked at purchase}} + \underbrace{\left(f_t - y^{\text{bill}}_t\right)}_{\text{bills' discount to the benchmark}} , $$

with $f_t$ the floating benchmark (3-month JIBAR, then compounded ZARONIA
plus 16.19 bp). In the jump-off quarter the 5-year bond yielded
`r num(LV$as_jo$gov5y, 2)`% against a 5-year swap of `r num(LV$as_jo$gov5y - LV$as_jo$bs, 2)`%, a spread of
`r num(LV$as_jo$bs, 2)` pp; bills yield about `r num(bill_gap, 2)` pp less than the benchmark. So the pickup is
about `r num(LV$as_jo$bs + bill_gap, 1)` pp a year, and none of it depends on where the policy rate goes.

**What it does to the risk measures.**

* *Economic value of equity.* None: the swap carries the bond's interest-rate
  sensitivity away, so the position adds nothing to the EVE budget -- which is
  why it matters when the levers are chosen together.
* *Spread.* What is left is credit-spread risk in the banking book: if the
  fiscal premium widens, the bond falls against the swap. With the bond at
  fair value through OCI and the swap designated as a fair-value hedge of its
  rate risk, the rate parts offset in profit and loss and the spread part
  sits in the OCI reserve, and so in CET1; a sale recycles it to profit or
  loss. The book's spread PV01 is `r paste0("R", num(LV$as_spv01 / 1e3, 1), nb, "m")` per basis point: a 100 bps
  widening at the jump-off -- more than `r num(floor(1 / bs_widen_max), 0)` times the largest widening since the
  swap data begin in late 2023 -- would cost `r ubps(LV$as_shock100)` of CET1 after tax.
* *Liquidity.* A government bond is Level 1 like a bill, so buying it does not
  move the LCR; but HQLA count at market value, so a widening lowers the
  buffer. A rate-driven fall in the bond's price does not, because the cleared
  swap pays it back daily as cash variation margin.

**How the spread moves with the macro picture.** A scenario carries the
10-year yield and the benchmark but no swap curve that prices the policy
path (its swap rates are the benchmark plus constant spreads), so the spread
is modelled. Both curves price the expected policy path, so a policy-driven
move should leave their difference alone; the spread should take a share of
the rest of the long bond's move -- the fiscal premium and global yields:

$$ \Delta bs_t = \kappa \left[\Delta y^{\text{gov}}_{10,t} - \beta\, \Delta f_t\right]. $$

The 10-year yield moves by $\beta$ = `r num(bsm$beta, 2)` for each point of the benchmark (three-year
changes since 2005, HAC *t* = `r num(bsm$beta_t, 1)`): the long end barely follows the policy rate.
And the 5-year bond–swap spread takes $\kappa$ = `r num(bsm$kappa, 2)` of the 10-year's remaining move
(monthly levels, `r format(bsm$from, "%B %Y")` to `r format(bsm$to, "%B %Y")`, *t* = `r num(bsm$kappa_t, 1)`, $R^2$ = `r num(bsm$kappa_r2, 2)`): about a quarter of a fiscal or
global move in the long bond shows up in the spread, and the rest moves the
swap curve with it. Month-on-month changes give a smaller `r num(bsm$kappa_d1, 2)`, short-run noise
that does not accumulate; for a book held for years the level relationship
is the relevant one, and the larger number is the more prudent for risk. The
scenarios' own swap curve would have loaded every change in the government
curve's slope onto the spread -- a five-point policy cut would have widened it by
up to five points, which is not what spreads do. The model misses the most
recent months, when swap rates rose faster than bond yields as the market
began to price the SARB's hikes, and the spread compressed further than the
long bond's level implies.

```{r lv-bs-fit}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "The 5-year bond–swap spread, monthly, against the spread model's fit: a share κ of the 10-year yield net of β times the benchmark. The spread compressed from about 1.4 pp in late 2023 to under 0.7 pp as the long bond rallied."
bf <- bsm$fit
bl <- rbind(data.frame(date = bf$date, value = bf$bs5, series = "5-year bond less 5-year swap"),
            data.frame(date = bf$date, value = bf$fitted, series = "fitted"))
ggplot(bl, aes(date, value, colour = series, linetype = series)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`5-year bond less 5-year swap` = ent_col[["NGFB"]], fitted = ink[["secondary"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`5-year bond less 5-year swap` = "solid", fitted = "22"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "pp") + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r lv-bs-fit-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(data.frame(Month = format(bf$date, "%Y-%m"), `Bond-swap spread (pp)` = num(bf$bs5, 2), `Fitted (pp)` = num(bf$fitted, 2),
                `10-year yield (%)` = num(bf$gov10y, 2), `3-month JIBAR (%)` = num(bf$jibar3m, 2), check.names = FALSE))
```

```{r lv-as}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[asw$scenario], ROE = bps(asw$d_roe), `NII, 3 years` = srbn(asw$d_nii),
              `Net income, 3 years` = srbn(asw$d_ni), `Spread at its widest` = sprintf("%.2f pp", asw$spread_max),
              `Spread at the end` = sprintf("%.2f pp", asw$spread_end),
              `CET1 through OCI: worst quarter` = bps(asw$d_cet1_oci_min), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrr", caption = sprintf("A quarter of the earning HQLA (%s) moved from Treasury bills into 5-year government bonds at the jump-off, each with a pay-fixed 5-year swap against it, the spread locked at %s pp. The carry runs through NII; the spread's mark-to-market through the OCI reserve and CET1. Against the plan.",
                                       rbn(as_size), num(LV$as_jo$bs, 2)))
```

**What it earns.** A quarter of the buffer (`r rbn(as_size)`) in asset-swapped bonds adds
`r ubps(min(asw$d_roe))` to `r ubps(max(asw$d_roe))` of ROE in every scenario, about `r rbn(mean(asw$d_ni), 1)` of net income over three
years, because its income does not depend on the policy path. The
stagflationary downside's sovereign stress widens the spread to
`r num(asw["downside", "spread_max"], 2)` pp at its worst, which costs `r ubps(asw["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"])` of CET1 through OCI -- about a
`r frac_word(hq["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"] / asw["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"])` of the ten-year book's `r ubps(hq["downside", "d_cet1_oci_min"])`, for `r pct(lv("Asset swap", as_set, "d_roe_weighted") / lv("HQLA duration", hq_set, "d_roe_weighted"), 0)` of its return. The
ten-year book earns more because it also collects the term premium, and the
term premium is paid for interest-rate risk the asset swap does not take.

**The macro link.** The lever is a view on the fiscal premium, not on the
policy rate. Its rule (R6, [Strategy lab](#lab)) holds none below a 0.5 pp
spread, a quarter of earning HQLA at 1 pp and half at 1.5 pp or more: it buys
the premium after sovereign stress has widened it and lets it go as it
compresses. Today's spread is at the tight end of its range -- `r num(LV$as_jo$bs, 2)` pp against
`r num(bsm$bs_mean, 2)` pp on average since late 2023, after the long bond's 2024–26 rally -- so the rule
would start small.

**What else it risks.** The spread can widen more than the model's quarter
of a fiscal move (2015 and March 2020 were sharp); the bond and the swap can
diverge for reasons other than the fiscal premium (a bond trading special in
repo, a maturity mismatch); an asset swap is harder to unwind in a stress
than a bill; and it adds to the bank's single largest credit exposure, the
sovereign.

## The size of the buffer: what surplus liquidity costs {#buffer}

```{r lv-buffer}
#| echo: false
tgs <- LV$lcr_targets
kt(data.frame(`LCR at the jump-off` = pct(tgs, 0),
              `Bills released` = rbn(vapply(tgs, function(tg) bx(tg, "baseline", "release"), 0), 1),
              `Share of wholesale funding repaid` = pct(vapply(tgs, function(tg) bx(tg, "baseline", "release"), 0) / whs0, 0),
              Baseline = bps(vapply(tgs, function(tg) bx(tg, "baseline", "d_roe"), 0)),
              Upside = bps(vapply(tgs, function(tg) bx(tg, "upside", "d_roe"), 0)),
              Downside = bps(vapply(tgs, function(tg) bx(tg, "downside", "d_roe"), 0)),
              `Net income, weighted, 3 years` = srbn(vapply(tgs, function(tg) lv("Liquidity buffer", buf_set(tg), "d_ni_weighted"), 0)),
              `Lowest LCR` = pct(vapply(tgs, function(tg) min(buf$lcr_min[buf$setting == buf_set(tg)]), 0), 0),
              `Lowest NSFR` = pct(vapply(tgs, function(tg) min(buf$nsfr_min[buf$setting == buf_set(tg)]), 0), 0),
              check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrrrr", caption = sprintf("Treasury bills released from the buffer at the jump-off to repay wholesale funding, sized to the LCR proxy shown (the plan starts at %s, its lowest quarter %s). Change in ROE against the plan; lowest LCR and NSFR across the four scenarios. Fees, costs and non-credit RWA are unchanged: bills held or sold do not change the cost base.",
                                         pct(LV$lcr0, 0), pct(min(LV$plan_liq$lcr_min), 0)))
```

**What it is.** NGFB's buffer is larger than its rules require: its LCR proxy
starts at `r pct(LV$lcr0, 0)` against the `r pct(CFG$lcr_sector, 0)` the sector publishes and the `r pct(CFG$lcr_min, 0)` NGFB sets as its own floor.
The buffer sits in Treasury bills, and at the margin it is funded with
wholesale funding, so every rand of surplus earns the bill rate and costs the
wholesale rate. Over the baseline that negative carry averages `r num(LV$buf_spread, 2)` pp a year:
about `r paste0("R", num(LV$buf_spread * 10, 0), nb, "m")` before tax for each R1`r nb`bn of surplus. Releasing bills and repaying
wholesale funding with them saves it. In the engine the released bills leave
the HQLA line, the wholesale balance falls by the same amount, and the line
loses the bills' full yield on them; fee income, operating costs and
non-credit RWA stay as they were.

**What it earns.** Cutting the LCR to 180%, 170% or 160% at the jump-off releases
`r rbn(bx(1.8, "baseline", "release"), 0)`, `r rbn(bx(1.7, "baseline", "release"), 0)` or `r rbn(bx(1.6, "baseline", "release"), 0)` and adds `r bps(bx(1.8, "baseline", "d_roe"))`, `r bps(bx(1.7, "baseline", "d_roe"))` or `r bps(bx(1.6, "baseline", "d_roe"))` of baseline ROE --
about nine basis points per R10`r nb`bn, the same in every scenario because
the saving is a spread, not a rate view. The lowest LCR across the scenarios is
then `r pct(min(buf$lcr_min[buf$setting == buf_set(1.6)]), 0)`, still well above the floor, and the NSFR `r pct(min(buf$nsfr_min[buf$setting == buf_set(1.6)]), 0)`. The binding limit is
not a ratio but the wholesale book itself: at 160% NGFB repays
`r pct(bx(1.6, "baseline", "release") / whs0, 0)` of its wholesale funding, and releasing more would leave bills with nothing
dear to repay.

**The macro link.** Liquidity is insurance, and insurance is worth most
before a stress. The buffer's rule (R7, [Strategy lab](#lab)) holds an LCR of
170% in calm quarters and rebuilds it to 185% after a quarter in which GDP
contracted or the rand lost more than 15% over the year -- the signals that
came before the funding stresses of 2008, 2015–16 and 2020.

**What else it risks.** The engine does not stress run-offs, funding spreads
or the price a forced seller of assets gets, so it shows the release's
saving but not what the surplus buys: room to absorb a deposit run without
selling, and a wholesale programme that stays in the market. Repaying
wholesale funding also shortens the bank's market presence, which is costly
to rebuild, and lowers the NSFR, because wholesale funding counts as half
stable. The release is a size decision to take against the bank's own
liquidity stress test, not against the LCR alone.

## Capital and deposit pricing

```{r lv-capital}
#| echo: false
cap_rows <- lvs[lvs$lever %in% c("Payout", "Distribution", "Deposit pricing", "Equity hedge", "Combined"), ]
cap_rows <- cap_rows[order(match(cap_rows$lever, c("Payout", "Distribution", "Equity hedge", "Deposit pricing", "Combined")), cap_rows$setting), ]
kt(data.frame(Lever = cap_rows$lever, Setting = cap_rows$setting, Baseline = bps(cap_rows$d_roe_baseline),
              Downside = bps(cap_rows$d_roe_downside), `Probability-weighted` = bps(cap_rows$d_roe_weighted),
              `Net income, weighted` = srbn(cap_rows$d_ni_weighted), `CET1 trough` = pct(cap_rows$cet1_min, 2), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llrrrrr", caption = "Capital, the equity hedge, deposit pricing and the levers combined. CET1 trough: lowest quarter across the weighted scenarios, before any OCI effect of the HQLA bonds.")
```

* **Capital.** NGFB starts at a CET1 ratio of `r pct(LV$cet1_0, 1)` and builds capital
  through the horizon at a 50% payout. Returning the `r rbn(LV$excess, 1)` above a 12.5% target
  at the jump-off adds `r bps(lv("Distribution", dist_set, "d_roe_weighted"))` of ROE (net income falls by less than
  equity), and a 70% payout adds `r bps(lv("Payout", "70% of earnings", "d_roe_weighted"))` with the CET1 trough at
  `r pct(lv("Payout", "70% of earnings", "cet1_min"), 1)`, close to the `r pct(CFG$cet1_min, 1)` floor. Payout is the natural
  macro-contingent lever: more in the upside, less going into the downside.
* **A hedge of equity**, half of it received fixed for five years, is worth
  `r bps(lv("Equity hedge", "Half of equity, 5 years", "d_roe_weighted"))` at the weights (`r bps(lv("Equity hedge", "Half of equity, 5 years", "d_roe_downside"))` in the downside): it is the same rate bet as a
  higher hedge ratio, on a smaller notional.
* **Deposit pricing.** Passing 10% less of each policy-rate rise and 10% more
  of each cut to non-maturity deposit rates than the sector does adds
  `r bps(lv("Deposit pricing", dep_set, "d_roe_weighted"))` at the weights. It is an upper bound: the share models do not
  price the deposits it would lose, and Stage 1 already finds the sector
  passing cuts through faster than rises on current accounts.

**Together**, ten-year reinvestment, a quarter of HQLA in ten-year bonds and
the capital distribution add `r bps(lv("Combined", cmb_set, "d_roe_weighted"))` of ROE at the scenario weights
(`r bps(lv("Combined", cmb_set, "d_roe_downside"))` in the downside), taking the baseline from `r pct(base$ngfb)` to
`r pct(base$ngfb + lv("Combined", cmb_set, "d_roe_baseline"))`. Before any mark-to-market the CET1 ratio stays above the floor in every
scenario (trough `r pct(min(LV$combo$cet1_min), 1)`). Held at fair value through OCI, the bonds' price fall at
the downside's peak would take it to about `r pct(min(LV$combo$cet1_min_fvoci), 1)`, below the `r pct(CFG$cet1_min, 1)` floor: the
three levers fit together only with the bonds at amortised cost, or with a
smaller distribution. Each of them takes a risk the engine's three-year ROE
does not price -- duration in the hedge book, the fiscal premium in the
buffer, and a thinner capital cushion -- which is why they are presented as
levers to size, not as free money.

## A playbook by view

```{r lv-playbook}
#| echo: false
best_of <- function(l, k) { z <- lvl[lvl$lever == l & lvl$scenario == k, ]; z$setting[which.max(z$roe)] }
pb <- data.frame(Lever = c("Hedge ratio", "Reinvestment tenor", "10-year bonds in HQLA", "Asset-swapped bonds", "Size of the buffer", "Payout"),
                 check.names = FALSE)
for (k in sc4) pb[[sc_short[[k]]]] <- c(best_of("Hedge ratio", k), best_of("Reinvestment tenor", k),
                                         ifelse(hq[k, "d_roe"] > 0, "a quarter of HQLA", "bills"),
                                         ifelse(asw[k, "d_roe"] > 0, "a quarter of HQLA", "bills"),
                                         sub(" at the jump-off", "", best_of("Liquidity buffer", k)),
                                         best_of("Payout", k))
pb$`Robust (weighted)` <- c(sprintf("structural: near the rate-neutral %s; above it only as a sized rate view", pct(neutral_r, 0)),
                            lvs$setting[lvs$lever == "Reinvestment tenor"][which.max(lvs$d_roe_weighted[lvs$lever == "Reinvestment tenor"])],
                            "sized to the view on the long bond and the CET1 room",
                            "sized to the view on the fiscal premium and the spread-risk appetite",
                            "as small as the bank's own liquidity stress test allows",
                            "as high as the CET1 floor allows going into a downturn")
kt(pb, align = "lllllll", caption = "The setting of each lever that maximises NGFB's three-year ROE if each scenario were known to arrive, and at the judgemental weights. The engine's ROE does not price duration, fiscal, liquidity or capital-cushion risk; the last column says how to size each.")
```

The pattern is the one the positioning chapter found for the balance-sheet
mix: what the view changes is above all the *rate* position. The hedge ratio
flips with the SARB's response, while the term-premium levers (reinvestment
tenor and ten-year bonds) pay in every scenario and are limited by risk
appetite rather than by the view. So do the two new levers, more cleanly
still: the asset swap and a smaller buffer collect spreads -- the fiscal
premium, the gap between wholesale funding and bills -- that do not depend on
the policy path at all, and their limits are spread risk and liquidity, not
the outlook.

# Strategy lab: positioning across sixty macro histories {#lab}

```{r lab-setup}
#| include: false
LB <- rd("lab.rds")
ld <- LB$dist; lb <- LB$lab; lfr <- LB$frontier; li <- LB$info; lpar <- LB$params
d0 <- ld[ld$phi == 0, ]; rownames(d0) <- d0$strategy
d5 <- ld[ld$phi == 0.5, ]; rownames(d5) <- d5$strategy
n_ep <- nrow(li)
rl <- c(R1 = "R1 hedge ratio with the policy rate", R2 = "R2 reinvestment tenor with the policy rate",
        R3 = "R3 HQLA duration with the curve's slope", R4 = "R4 payout with growth and capital",
        R5 = "R5 unsecured growth with the labour market", R6 = "R6 asset swap with the bond-swap spread",
        R7 = "R7 liquidity buffer with stress", all = "All seven rules",
        oracle = "Best static hedge ratio with hindsight")
g0 <- function(k, col) d0[k, col]
g5 <- function(k, col) d5[k, col]
st_lab <- function(r, t) sprintf("%.0f%% at %d years", 100 * r, t)
plan_st <- st_lab(lpar$plan_ratio, 5)
guard(plan_st %in% rownames(d0) && abs(g0(plan_st, "d_roe_mean")) < 1e-6, "the static grid holds the plan")
li$d_repo_avg <- li$repo_mean - lpar$repo_jo
lup <- sum(li$d_repo_avg > 0.25); ldn <- sum(li$d_repo_avg < -0.25); lfl <- n_ep - lup - ldn
pe <- lb[lb$strategy == "Plan" & lb$phi == 0, ]
pe_ep <- pe[pe$kind == "episode", ]
pe_ep <- merge(pe_ep, li[, c("episode", "d_repo_avg", "gdp_mean", "d_unemp", "start")], by.x = "path", by.y = "episode")
drv <- stats::setNames(LB$drivers$coef, LB$drivers$term)
roe_q <- function(p) unname(stats::quantile(pe_ep$roe, p))
worst_ep <- pe_ep[which.min(pe_ep$roe), ]
best_ep <- pe_ep[which.max(pe_ep$roe), ]
## the static frontier
lfr$tenor_lab <- paste(lfr$tenor, "years")
sd_min <- lfr[which.min(lfr$roe_sd), ]
lab_rules <- c(rl[c("R1", "R2", "R3", "R4", "R5", "R6", "R7", "all")])
as25 <- "25% of HQLA in asset-swapped 5-year bonds"; buf170 <- "Buffer at an LCR of 170%"
## realised gains and losses on the bond books (recycled from OCI to profit)
r3g <- lb[lb$phi == 0 & lb$kind == "episode" & lb$strategy == rl[["R3"]], ]
r3g <- merge(r3g, li[, c("episode", "d_repo_avg")], by.x = "path", by.y = "episode")
r3_gain_up <- mean(r3g$gains[r3g$d_repo_avg > 0.25]); r3_gain_dn <- mean(r3g$gains[r3g$d_repo_avg < -0.25])
st_share <- mean(vapply(LB$rule_paths[LB$kind == "episode"], function(z) mean(z$stress), 0))
p10 <- st_lab(lpar$plan_ratio, 10)
th0 <- LB$rule_paths$baseline$theta[1]; ra0 <- LB$rule_paths$baseline$ratio[1]
## the claims in this chapter
guard(abs(sd_min$ratio - rd("audit.rds")$neutral_ratio) < 0.02 && sd_min$tenor == 10,
      "the spread of ROE is smallest at the rate-neutral ratio with ten-year reinvestment")
guard(all(lfr$efficient == (lfr$tenor == 10 & lfr$ratio >= rd("audit.rds")$neutral_ratio - 1e-9)),
      "the efficient static settings are the ten-year line from the rate-neutral ratio up")
guard(g0(p10, "win") == 1 && abs(g0(p10, "d_roe_up") - g0(p10, "d_roe_down")) < 0.001,
      "ten-year reinvestment beats the plan in every episode, rising or falling rates alike")
guard(g0(st_lab(0.8, 5), "d_roe_mean") > 0 && g0(st_lab(0.8, 5), "d_roe_p5") < -0.02 &&
      g0(st_lab(0.8, 5), "d_roe_up") < 0 && g0(st_lab(0.8, 5), "d_roe_down") > 0, "a high static hedge is a rate view")
guard(abs(g0(rl[["R1"]], "d_roe_mean")) < 0.001 && g0(rl[["R1"]], "d_roe_p5") < -0.01 && abs(g5(rl[["R1"]], "d_roe_mean")) < 0.001,
      "R1 adds nothing on average, with a costly tail, with or without an anticipating curve")
guard(g0(rl[["R2"]], "d_roe_mean") > 0 && g0(rl[["R2"]], "d_roe_mean") < g0(p10, "d_roe_mean"),
      "R2 pays but less than always reinvesting at ten years")
hq25 <- "25% of HQLA in 10-year bonds"
guard(g0(rl[["R3"]], "d_roe_mean") > g0(hq25, "d_roe_mean") && g0(rl[["R3"]], "cet1_min_fv") > g0(hq25, "cet1_min_fv") &&
      abs(g0(rl[["R3"]], "d_eve200") - g0(hq25, "d_eve200")) < 0.01 && g0(rl[["R3"]], "d_roe_p5") < g0(hq25, "d_roe_p5") &&
      g0(rl[["R3"]], "win") < 0.95 && g0(rl[["R3"]], "d_roe_up") < g0(rl[["R3"]], "d_roe_down") / 5 && r3_gain_up < 0 && r3_gain_dn > 0,
      "R3: more ROE and a better capital trough than a static quarter at the same EVE, a worse tail from realised losses when rates rise")
guard(g0(rl[["R6"]], "win") == 1 && g0(as25, "win") == 1 && g0(rl[["R6"]], "d_roe_mean") < g0(as25, "d_roe_mean") &&
      abs(g0(rl[["R6"]], "d_eve200")) < 0.005 && abs(g0(as25, "d_eve200")) < 0.005 && g0(as25, "cet1_min_fv") > g0("Plan", "cet1_min_fv"),
      "R6 and the static asset swap beat the plan everywhere with no EVE; the rule earns less from today's tight spread")
guard(g0(rl[["R7"]], "win") == 1 && g0(buf170, "win") == 1 && g0(rl[["R7"]], "d_roe_mean") < g0(buf170, "d_roe_mean") &&
      g0(buf170, "d_roe_p5") > 0.004, "R7 and the static buffer beat the plan everywhere; the rule pays for liquidity in stress")
guard(g0(rl[["R4"]], "d_roe_mean") > 0 && g0(rl[["R4"]], "cet1_min_fv") > g0("Plan", "cet1_min_fv") &&
      g0("70% payout", "breach") > 0.05 && g0(rl[["R4"]], "breach") == 0, "R4: a little ROE and a higher capital trough; a flat 70% breaches")
guard(abs(g0(rl[["R5"]], "d_roe_mean")) < 0.001, "R5 does nothing in this engine")
guard(g0(rl[["all"]], "d_roe_mean") > 0.025 && g0(rl[["all"]], "win") > 0.9 && g0(rl[["all"]], "coe_hit") > 0.6 &&
      g0("Plan", "coe_hit") < 0.05 && g0(rl[["all"]], "d_eve200") > 0.15 && g0(rl[["all"]], "cet1_min_fv") < 0.12 &&
      g0(rl[["all"]], "cet1_min_fv") >= CFG$cet1_min, "all seven rules: about three points of ROE, at an EVE cost and close to the CET1 floor")
guard(max(abs(d5[c(rl[["R2"]], st_lab(0.8, 5)), "d_roe_mean"] - d0[c(rl[["R2"]], st_lab(0.8, 5)), "d_roe_mean"])) < 0.001,
      "an anticipating curve barely moves the hedge strategies")
guard(drv[["gdp_mean"]] > 0 && drv[["d_repo_mean"]] < 0 && abs(drv[["d_unemp"]]) < 0.001 && LB$drivers_r2 > 0.9,
      "ROE across episodes: growth up, rates down, no unemployment channel")
```


The scenarios ask *what if X happens*. A positioning decision also has to
survive what nobody wrote down, and the most honest set of those outcomes a
South African bank has is its own history. The lab replays every complete
twelve-quarter macro episode since 2008 -- `r n_ep` overlapping windows, from
`r li$episode[1]` to `r li$episode[n_ep]` -- from today's starting point, and runs each
through the whole chain: the sector models, NGFB's share dynamics and the
engine. Rates, the long bond, inflation and unemployment move by the change
they made in the episode; GDP, house prices, the rand and equities grow as
they grew, compounded from today's levels, so that an episode starting in the
base-effect quarters of 2020–21 does not shift its whole path. It is
historical simulation, the market-risk workhorse, applied to a balance sheet:
no distribution is assumed, but only history's episodes can occur,
consecutive windows share eleven of their twelve quarters, and the sample
holds one global financial crisis and one pandemic.

Each strategy is judged as an ALCO would judge it: its average ROE across the
episodes, its downside (the 5th percentile), how often it beats the plan, and
the risks the three-year ROE does not price -- the CET1 trough with any bonds
held at fair value, and the change in the economic value of the hedge and
bond books for a 200 bps rise, the yardstick of the IRRBB outlier test. Bonds
bought for the buffer are held at fair value through OCI, as banks usually
hold their liquidity portfolios: their carry runs through NII, a sale's
realised gain or loss through profit (IFRS 9 recycles it from OCI), the
unrealised mark-to-market through the OCI reserve and so CET1, and, because
Level 1 assets count at market value, through the LCR. The rules' parameters
were set in advance as round numbers, not fitted to the episodes: fitted on
the same sixty paths, any rule would look better than it is.

| Strategy | What it does |
|---|---|
| Plan | `r pct(lpar$plan_ratio)` of non-maturity deposits received fixed, maturing tranches reinvested at five years; HQLA in Treasury bills; 50% payout |
| Static hedge | a hedge ratio from 0% to 80% set now (5-year swaps at today's rate, laddered like the book) and maturing tranches reinvested at 3, 5, 7 or 10 years |
| Static HQLA, buffer, payout | a quarter or half of earning HQLA in 10-year government bonds bought now; a quarter in 5-year bonds asset-swapped to floating; Treasury bills released to repay wholesale funding until the LCR proxy is 170%; a 30% or 70% payout |
| R1 hedge ratio with the policy rate | the plan's ratio plus 10 points of deposits for each point the policy rate stood above its `r num(lpar$r_star, 2)`% neutral level last quarter, within 20–80% |
| R2 reinvestment tenor with the policy rate | maturing tranches reinvested at ten years when the policy rate is at least half a point above neutral, at three years when half a point below, at five otherwise |
| R3 HQLA duration with the curve's slope | a quarter of earning HQLA in 10-year bonds when the 10-year yield less the floating benchmark is at its post-2008 median (`r num(lpar$slope_med, 2)` pp), an eighth of HQLA more or less for each point above or below, within 0–50% |
| R4 payout with growth and capital | 70% of earnings while GDP grew last quarter and CET1 is above the 12.5% target, 30% otherwise |
| R5 unsecured growth with the labour market | card and personal-loan growth 5 points a year faster while unemployment is falling and growth is above 1%, 5 points slower when unemployment has risen by more than a point over the year or GDP contracts |
| R6 asset swap with the bond–swap spread | none of earning HQLA in asset-swapped 5-year bonds while the spread is below 0.5 pp, a quarter at 1 pp, half at 1.5 pp or more (linear between) |
| R7 liquidity buffer with stress | bills released to an LCR proxy of 170% in calm quarters; rebuilt to 185% after a quarter in which GDP contracted or the rand lost more than 15% over the year |
| All seven | R1–R7 together; if the two bond books and the release would take more than 90% of earning HQLA out of bills, the bond books are scaled down pro rata |

: The strategies. Every rule acts on what was known at the end of the previous quarter. {.striped}

## Sixty macro histories

```{r lab-episodes}
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| fig-cap: "The macro episodes replayed from the jump-off (grey: each a 12-quarter window of South African history since 2008, applied to today's starting point) and the scenarios (colour)."
sp <- LB$scen_paths
vars <- c(repo = "Repo rate (%)", gdp_yy = "Real GDP (% y/y)", gov10y = "10-year government yield (%)", unemp = "Unemployment rate (%)")
el <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sp), function(k) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(vars), function(v)
  data.frame(path = k, date = sp[[k]]$date, var = vars[[v]], value = sp[[k]][[v]],
             kind = if (k %in% names(sc_col)) k else "episode")))))
el$var <- factor(el$var, levels = vars)
es <- el[el$kind != "episode", ]; es$kind <- factor(es$kind, levels = names(sc_col))
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = el[el$kind == "episode", ], aes(date, value, group = path), colour = ink[["muted"]],
            alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = es, aes(date, value, colour = kind, linetype = kind), linewidth = 0.75) +
  facet_wrap(~ var, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sc_col, labels = sc_short, name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(baseline = "solid", upside = "solid", downside = "solid", downside_cuts = "22"),
                        labels = sc_short, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r lab-episodes-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
qs <- function(x) num(stats::quantile(x, c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)), 1)
twin(data.frame(Statistic = c("Minimum", "25th percentile", "Median", "75th percentile", "Maximum"),
                `Repo rate, average change from the jump-off (pp)` = qs(li$d_repo_avg),
                `Real GDP growth, average (%)` = qs(li$gdp_mean), `Real GDP growth, trough (%)` = qs(li$gdp_min),
                `Unemployment, change over the episode (pp)` = qs(li$d_unemp),
                `10-year yield, change over the episode (pp)` = qs(li$d_gov10y), check.names = FALSE),
     "Table view: the episodes in numbers")
```

The episodes span far more than the three scenarios. The policy rate averages
anywhere from `r num(-min(li$d_repo_avg), 1)` points below today's to `r num(max(li$d_repo_avg), 1)` above
(`r lup` episodes with higher rates on average, `r ldn` with lower, `r lfl` broadly flat), real
GDP growth averages between `r num(min(li$gdp_mean), 1)`% and `r num(max(li$gdp_mean), 1)`%, and the deepest
quarter is the pandemic's `r num(min(li$gdp_min), 0)`%. The 3.5% floor on the policy rate binds in
`r sum(li$repo_floored)` episodes, those that replay the 2008–09 cuts from today's lower
starting point, and the zero floor on inflation in `r sum(li$cpi_floored)`.

## The plan across the histories

```{r lab-plan}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "NGFB's plan across the episodes: three-year average ROE against the episode's average policy rate relative to the jump-off, coloured by average real GDP growth. Diamonds: the scenarios. Dotted: the 14.5% cost of equity."
pe_ep$gbin <- cut(pe_ep$gdp_mean, c(-Inf, 0, 2, Inf), labels = c("GDP growth below 0%", "0-2%", "above 2%"))
sc_pts <- pe[pe$kind == "scenario", ]
sc_pts$d_repo_avg <- vapply(sc_pts$path, function(k) mean(sp[[k]]$repo) - lpar$repo_jo, 0)
ggplot(pe_ep, aes(d_repo_avg, roe)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = CFG$coe, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "13") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = gbin), size = 2.2, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_point(data = sc_pts, aes(fill = path), shape = 23, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(div_lo, ink[["muted"]], div_hi), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sc_col, labels = sc_short, name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = "policy rate, average over the episode less the jump-off (pp)", y = "ROE, three-year average") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

```{r lab-plan-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
pt <- pe_ep[order(pe_ep$start), ]
twin(data.frame(Episode = pt$path, `Repo, average change (pp)` = num(pt$d_repo_avg, 2), `GDP growth, average (%)` = num(pt$gdp_mean, 1),
                `Plan ROE` = pct(pt$roe, 1), `CET1 trough (fair value)` = pct(pt$cet1_min_fv, 1), check.names = FALSE),
     "Table view: the plan in each episode")
```

NGFB's plan averages `r pct(g0("Plan", "roe_mean"))` across the episodes, a little below the
baseline, between `r pct(min(pe_ep$roe))` (`r worst_ep$path`, through the pandemic) and
`r pct(max(pe_ep$roe))` (`r best_ep$path`, the rebound from it), with a 5th percentile of
`r pct(g0("Plan", "roe_p5"))`. It earns the 14.5% cost of equity in `r sum(pe_ep$roe >= CFG$coe)` of the `r n_ep`
histories. Two macro numbers explain almost all of the spread
($R^2$ = `r num(LB$drivers_r2, 2)` across the episodes): each point of average GDP growth adds
`r ubps(drv[["gdp_mean"]])` of ROE, and each point by which the policy rate averages above today's costs
`r ubps(drv[["d_repo_mean"]])`, the liability sensitivity the hedge gives NGFB. Unemployment adds
nothing once growth is known, because the engine has no unemployment channel
([What didn't work](#what-didnt-work)). The regression is descriptive: overlapping windows
make its precision look better than it is.

In symbols, the regression across the episodes is

$$\overline{\text{ROE}}_e \;\approx\; a \;+\; b_{\text{gdp}}\,\bar g_e \;+\; b_{\text{repo}}\,\overline{\Delta r}_e ,$$

with $\bar g_e$ the episode's average GDP growth and $\overline{\Delta r}_e$ the
amount by which its policy rate averages above today's.

Every strategy below is judged the way an ALCO would judge it: its average
ROE across the episodes, its bad case (the 5th percentile), how often it beats
the plan, and two risks the three-year ROE does not price. The first is the
CET1 trough with any bonds at fair value, so that the OCI reserve counts. The
second is interest-rate risk, measured the way the IRRBB outlier test measures
it (BCBS 2016), as the change in the economic value of the hedge and bond
books for a 200 bp rise:

$$\frac{\Delta \text{EVE}}{\text{CET1}} \;=\; \frac{200 \times \text{PV01}}{\text{CET1}} ,$$

where PV01 is the change in the books' value for a one basis point parallel
move.

## Static positioning: the hedge frontier

```{r lab-frontier}
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Static positioning of the structural hedge across the episodes: average ROE against its spread (standard deviation across episodes), for each hedge ratio (labels) and reinvestment tenor (lines). The plan is ringed. Changes are made at the jump-off with 5-year swaps at the market rate; maturing tranches are reinvested at the tenor shown."
lf <- lfr[order(lfr$tenor, lfr$ratio), ]
lf$tenor_lab <- factor(lf$tenor_lab, levels = paste(c(3, 5, 7, 10), "years"))
pl0 <- lf[lf$strategy == plan_st, ]
ggplot(lf, aes(roe_sd, roe_mean, colour = tenor_lab, group = tenor_lab)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.6) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = pl0, shape = 21, size = 5, stroke = 0.9, colour = ink[["primary"]], fill = NA) +
  geom_text(data = lf[lf$tenor == 10, ], aes(label = pct(ratio, 0)), nudge_x = 0.0009, size = 3, colour = ink[["secondary"]],
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = seq_ramp[2:5], name = "reinvestment") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(0.1)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(0.1)) +
  labs(x = "spread of ROE across episodes (standard deviation)", y = "average ROE")
```

```{r lab-frontier-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
lt2 <- lfr[order(lfr$ratio, lfr$tenor), ]
twin(data.frame(`Hedge ratio` = pct(lt2$ratio, 0), Tenor = lt2$tenor_lab, `Average ROE` = pct(lt2$roe_mean, 2),
                `Spread (sd)` = pp(lt2$roe_sd, 2), `5th percentile` = pct(lt2$roe_p5, 1),
                `vs plan, average` = bps(lt2$d_roe_mean), `EVE change for +200 bps vs plan (% of CET1)` = spct(-lt2$d_eve200, 1),
                Efficient = ifelse(lt2$efficient, "yes", ""), check.names = FALSE),
     "Table view: every static hedge setting")
```

Three things stand out.

* **ROE varies least near the rate-neutral ratio.** The spread across the
  episodes is smallest at `r sd_min$strategy` (`r pp(sd_min$roe_sd, 2)`, against the plan's
  `r pp(g0("Plan", "roe_sd"), 2)`); both more and less receive-fixed widen it, because the
  hedge then dominates or the endowment does.
* **Longer reinvestment pays at every ratio, whichever way rates go.** At the
  plan's ratio, reinvesting at ten years instead of five adds `r bps(g0(p10, "d_roe_mean"))` on
  average and beats the plan in every episode (`r bps(g0(p10, "d_roe_up"))` when rates rise,
  `r bps(g0(p10, "d_roe_down"))` when they fall): it is the swap curve's term premium, which the
  constant term spreads hold at its 2023–2026 level in every episode, so a
  flatter curve would pay less. Every efficient static setting reinvests at
  ten years. The cost is outside the ROE: a 200 bps rise would take a further
  `r pct(g0(p10, "d_eve200"), 1)` of CET1 off the books' value.
* **More hedge is a rate view.** Receiving fixed on 80% of deposits at five
  years adds `r bps(g0(st_lab(0.8, 5), "d_roe_mean"))` on average, but `r bps(g0(st_lab(0.8, 5), "d_roe_up"))` when rates rise and `r bps(g0(st_lab(0.8, 5), "d_roe_down"))`
  when they fall, with a 5th percentile of `r bps(g0(st_lab(0.8, 5), "d_roe_p5"))`. Its average is positive because
  the extra swaps are struck at the jump-off's 5-year rate (`r num(lpar$jo_swap[["swap5y"]], 2)`%), above the
  floating rate the episodes imply from here on average -- the same bet
  [More levers](#levers) found in the scenarios.

## Rules that read the macro picture

```{r lab-table}
#| echo: false
show_st <- c(rl[["R1"]], rl[["R2"]], rl[["R3"]], rl[["R4"]], rl[["R5"]], rl[["R6"]], rl[["R7"]], rl[["all"]],
             st_lab(0.65, 5), st_lab(lpar$plan_ratio, 10), "25% of HQLA in 10-year bonds", "50% of HQLA in 10-year bonds",
             as25, buf170, "70% payout", rl[["oracle"]])
show_st <- show_st[show_st %in% rownames(d0)]
grp <- ifelse(show_st %in% lab_rules, "Rule", ifelse(show_st == rl[["oracle"]], "Bound", "Static"))
kt(data.frame(Type = grp, Strategy = show_st, `Average` = bps(g0(show_st, "d_roe_mean")),
              `5th percentile` = bps(g0(show_st, "d_roe_p5")), `Beats the plan` = pct(g0(show_st, "win"), 0),
              `NII, 3 years, average` = srbn(g0(show_st, "d_nii_mean")),
              `CET1 trough, worst episode` = pct(g0(show_st, "cet1_min_fv"), 1),
              `Episodes below the CET1 floor` = pct(g0(show_st, "breach"), 0),
              `EVE for +200 bps vs plan (% of CET1)` = spct(-g0(show_st, "d_eve200"), 1), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llrrrrrrr",
   caption = sprintf("Change in NGFB's three-year average ROE against the plan across the %d episodes, with the risk each strategy adds. CET1 trough: the lowest quarter in any episode, with bonds bought for HQLA at fair value. EVE: the change in the value of the hedge and bond books for a 200 bps parallel rise, against the plan's, at the end of the horizon (the deposits' own behavioural duration is the same under every strategy). Plan: %s in the worst episode, %s of episodes below the %s floor.",
                   n_ep, pct(g0("Plan", "cet1_min_fv"), 1), pct(g0("Plan", "breach"), 0), pct(CFG$cet1_min, 1)))
```

```{r lab-dots}
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-cap: "Change in ROE against the plan across the episodes: the average (dot) and the 5th to 95th percentile (line)."
dd <- lb[lb$phi == 0 & lb$kind == "episode" & lb$strategy %in% show_st, ]
ds <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(dd, dd$strategy), function(d) data.frame(strategy = d$strategy[1],
  mean = mean(d$d_roe), lo = unname(stats::quantile(d$d_roe, 0.05)), hi = unname(stats::quantile(d$d_roe, 0.95)))))
ds$type <- ifelse(ds$strategy %in% lab_rules, "Rule", ifelse(ds$strategy == rl[["oracle"]], "Hindsight bound", "Static"))
ds$label <- ds$strategy
ds$label <- factor(ds$label, levels = ds$label[order(ds$mean)])
ggplot(ds, aes(mean, label, colour = type)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lo, xend = hi, yend = label), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Rule = ent_col[["NGFB"]], Static = ink[["secondary"]], `Hindsight bound` = div_lo), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(1e4 * x), " bps")) +
```
