
```{r lab-dots-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
twin(data.frame(Strategy = as.character(ds$label), Type = ds$type, Average = bps(ds$mean), `5th percentile` = bps(ds$lo),
                `95th percentile` = bps(ds$hi), check.names = FALSE))
```

* **R1, the hedge ratio keyed on the level of rates, adds nothing.** On
  average `r bps(g0(rl[["R1"]], "d_roe_mean"))`, with a 5th percentile of `r bps(g0(rl[["R1"]], "d_roe_p5"))`: it gains when a high
  rate is followed by cuts and loses when rates keep rising, and in history the
  two came about equally often. The prize is real -- choosing the right static
  ratio for each episode with hindsight adds `r bps(g0(rl[["oracle"]], "d_roe_mean"))` -- but the level of
  the policy rate does not reveal it.
* **R2, the reinvestment tenor keyed on rates, pays less than always going
  long.** `r bps(g0(rl[["R2"]], "d_roe_mean"))` on average against `r bps(g0(p10, "d_roe_mean"))` for ten years throughout: each quarter
  spent at three or five years gives up term premium the timing does not win back.
* **R3, HQLA duration keyed on the curve's slope, earns the most of any
  single rule, but not in every episode.** It adds `r bps(g0(rl[["R3"]], "d_roe_mean"))` on average against
  `r bps(g0(hq25, "d_roe_mean"))` for a fixed quarter of HQLA in bonds, with a better CET1 trough at fair value
  (`r pct(g0(rl[["R3"]], "cet1_min_fv"))` against `r pct(g0(hq25, "cet1_min_fv"))`) at the same EVE risk (`r pct(g0(rl[["R3"]], "d_eve200"), 1)` of CET1 for a 200 bps rise).
  A steep curve pays more carry and tends to flatten as long yields fall, so
  buying duration when the slope is high and holding less when it is low
  collects the bond's excess return when it is largest -- the term-premium
  evidence of Fama and Bliss and of Campbell and Shiller, here in South
  African data. But the rule trades its book, and under IFRS 9 a bond sold out
  of a fair-value-through-OCI book takes its accumulated gain or loss into
  profit. A curve flattens most often because the SARB is hiking, when long
  yields rise too, so R3 sells at a loss in hiking cycles: its realised losses
  average `r urm(r3_gain_up)` before tax over the episodes in which rates rose, against gains of
  `r urm(r3_gain_dn)` where they fell. It adds `r bps(g0(rl[["R3"]], "d_roe_up"))` when rates rise against `r bps(g0(rl[["R3"]], "d_roe_down"))` when they fall, beats the plan in
  `r pct(g0(rl[["R3"]], "win"), 0)` of the episodes, and its 5th percentile is `r bps(g0(rl[["R3"]], "d_roe_p5"))`. Today's slope, `r num(lpar$slope_jo, 2)` pp, is
  below its median, so the rule would start at `r pct(th0, 0)` of HQLA, not a quarter.
* **R4, payout keyed on growth and capital, adds a little and protects
  capital.** `r bps(g0(rl[["R4"]], "d_roe_mean"))` on average with a CET1 trough of `r pct(g0(rl[["R4"]], "cet1_min_fv"))`, above the plan's
  `r pct(g0("Plan", "cet1_min_fv"))`; a flat 70% payout adds `r bps(g0("70% payout", "d_roe_mean"))` but takes `r pct(g0("70% payout", "breach"), 0)` of the
  episodes below the `r pct(CFG$cet1_min, 1)` floor. Paying more when the economy grows and
  capital is ample, and less otherwise, keeps capital where the downturns are.
* **R5, unsecured lending keyed on the labour market, does nothing here**
  (`r bps(g0(rl[["R5"]], "d_roe_mean"))`). The engine applies the sector's loss rate to the whole book, with
  no vintages, so the timing of origination cannot pay; a bank with its own
  vintage loss curves should run this test on them.
* **R6, the asset swap keyed on the bond–swap spread, and R7, the buffer
  keyed on stress, beat the plan in every episode, and take no rate risk.**
  A static quarter of HQLA in asset-swapped bonds adds `r bps(g0(as25, "d_roe_mean"))` (5th percentile
  `r bps(g0(as25, "d_roe_p5"))`), and R6 `r bps(g0(rl[["R6"]], "d_roe_mean"))`: the rule holds little while the spread is as tight
  as it is today and buys only where an episode's fiscal stress widens it.
  Releasing bills to an LCR of 170% adds `r bps(g0(buf170, "d_roe_mean"))` in every episode; R7, which rebuilds
  the buffer to 185% after a stress signal (`r pct(st_share, 0)` of the episodes' quarters), adds
  `r bps(g0(rl[["R7"]], "d_roe_mean"))`. The `r ubps(g0(buf170, "d_roe_mean") - g0(rl[["R7"]], "d_roe_mean"))` between them is what the insurance costs; what it
  buys -- not having to sell assets or pay up for funding in a run -- is not
  in the engine, which does not stress run-offs or funding spreads.
* **All seven together** add `r bps(g0(rl[["all"]], "d_roe_mean"))` on average and beat the plan in
  `r pct(g0(rl[["all"]], "win"), 0)` of the episodes, which lifts the share of histories in which NGFB
  earns its cost of equity from `r pct(g0("Plan", "coe_hit"), 0)` to `r pct(g0(rl[["all"]], "coe_hit"), 0)`. Most of it is duration --
  ten-year reinvestment when rates are high and bonds when the curve is steep --
  and so is most of the risk: a 200 bps rise would take a further
  `r pct(g0(rl[["all"]], "d_eve200"), 0)` of CET1 off the books' value, and the CET1 trough at fair value falls to
  `r pct(g0(rl[["all"]], "cet1_min_fv"), 2)`, just above the `r pct(CFG$cet1_min, 1)` floor. Seven rules stacked without a risk
  budget use more of the bank's risk capacity than anyone set out to give
  them, which is what the [risk-budgeted optimiser](#risk-budget) is for.

## Rising and falling rates

```{r lab-updown}
#| echo: false
ud <- c(show_st[show_st != rl[["R5"]]])
kt(data.frame(Strategy = ud, `Rates rise` = bps(g0(ud, "d_roe_up")), `Rates fall` = bps(g0(ud, "d_roe_down")),
              `Rates flat` = bps(g0(ud, "d_roe_flat")), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrr", caption = sprintf("Average change in ROE against the plan by the direction of the policy rate over the episode: rising (average more than 25 bps above the jump-off, %d episodes), falling (more than 25 bps below, %d) and flat (%d).", lup, ldn, lfl))
```

The hedge ratio, static or keyed on rates, is a bet on the direction of
rates: it wins when they fall and loses when they rise. The tenor and the
slope rule earn in both directions, the slope rule most when rates fall and
the bonds rally.

## If the swap curve priced the path

```{r lab-phi}
#| echo: false
ph <- c(rl[["R1"]], rl[["R2"]], st_lab(0.8, 5), st_lab(0.65, 5), st_lab(0.2, 5), st_lab(0, 5), rl[["oracle"]])
ph <- ph[ph %in% rownames(d5)]
kt(data.frame(Strategy = ph, `Constant term spreads` = bps(g0(ph, "d_roe_mean")),
              `Curve prices half the path` = bps(g5(ph, "d_roe_mean")), `Beats the plan` = pct(g5(ph, "win"), 0),
              check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrr", caption = "The hedge strategies when swap rates price half of the coming policy path (each tenor moved by half the gap between the average benchmark over its life and today's), against the constant term spreads the scenarios use. Average change in ROE against the plan, priced the same way.")
```

The scenarios' swap curve moves one-for-one with the policy rate, so it never
prices the path ahead, and a rule that receives fixed before cuts could look
better than it would in a market that saw them coming. With swap rates that
price half of the coming path the conclusions stand: R1 still adds nothing
(`r bps(g5(rl[["R1"]], "d_roe_mean"))`), and the tenor rule and a higher static ratio change by less than a
basis point, because their gains come from the term premium and from today's
swap rate, not from timing.

## What the lab says about positioning

1. **Lock in the term premium; do not time the rate cycle.** Reinvesting the
   hedge at ten years paid in every episode; keying the hedge ratio on the level
   of rates paid in none on average. The ratio is a structural decision, best
   near the rate-neutral `r pct(rd("audit.rds")$neutral_ratio, 0)` where earnings vary least, and a higher
   ratio is a sized rate view, not a default.
2. **Run HQLA duration off the curve's slope, and expect to give some back in
   hiking cycles.** It is the rule that adds most on its own, with a better
   capital trough than a fixed bond holding; its realised losses when the SARB
   hikes are the price of the trading.
3. **Collect the spreads that need no rate view.** Asset-swapped bonds (the
   fiscal premium) and a smaller buffer (the wholesale–bill spread) beat the
   plan in every episode with no EVE cost; their limits are spread risk and
   the bank's own liquidity stress test.
4. **Make the payout state-contingent.** A little more ROE and a higher
   capital trough than a fixed ratio.
5. **Size the risk explicitly.** The rules that pay most are duration, and
   together they need an EVE budget of about a fifth of CET1 for a 200 bps rise
   and leave little room above the CET1 floor. Choosing the levers together,
   under limits, is the next chapter.
6. **Expect little from credit timing in this engine** -- and test it on
   vintage loss data before concluding it does not pay.

# Choosing the levers together: a risk-budgeted optimiser {#risk-budget}

```{r rb-setup}
#| include: false
RB <- rd("risk_budget.rds")
rbf <- RB$frontier; rbv <- RB$verify; rbo <- RB$oos; rbs <- RB$scenarios; rownames(rbs) <- rbs$scenario
rbvar <- RB$variants; rownames(rbvar) <- rbvar$variant
rbreg <- RB$regime$all; rownames(rbreg) <- rbreg$regime
rbreg_s <- RB$regime$static; rownames(rbreg_s) <- rbreg_s$regime
rbc <- RB$candidates
p_roe <- RB$plan_stats$all[["roe"]]; p_p5 <- RB$plan_stats$all[["p5"]]
rb_key <- function(d) paste(d$hedge, d$dur, d$as, d$buf, d$pay)
rb_b <- RB$b_central
cen <- rbf[!rbf$static_only & abs(rbf$budget - rb_b) < 1e-12, ]
cen_s <- rbf[rbf$static_only & abs(rbf$budget - rb_b) < 1e-12, ]
ce <- rbvar["Every setting", ]; cs <- rbvar["Static settings only", ]
plan_row <- rbc[rbc$hedge == RB$plan_opt[["hedge"]] & rbc$dur == 1 & rbc$as == 1 & rbc$buf == 1 & rbc$pay == 2, ]
nii_c <- rbv$nii_exact[rbv$key == rb_key(cen)]; nii_s <- rbv$nii_exact[rbv$key == rb_key(cen_s)]
lu <- RB$limits_used
set_c <- RB$central$all; set_s <- RB$central$static
neutral_rb <- rd("audit.rds")$neutral_ratio
## readable settings
lab_ratio <- function(x) if (x == "R1") "R1: with the policy rate" else paste(x, "of non-maturity deposits")
lab_tenor <- function(x) if (x == "R2") "R2: with the policy rate" else x
lab_share <- function(x, rule) if (x == rule) paste0(rule, ": with its signal") else if (x == "0%") "none" else paste(x, "of earning HQLA")
lab_buf <- function(x) if (x == "plan") sprintf("the plan's (LCR %s)", pct(LV$lcr0, 0)) else if (x == "R7") "R7: 170%, 185% after stress" else x
lab_pay <- function(x) if (x == "R4") "R4: 70% while GDP grows and CET1 is above 12.5%, 30% otherwise" else x
settings_tab <- function(z) c(lab_ratio(z[["hedge_ratio"]]), lab_tenor(z[["hedge_tenor"]]), lab_share(z[["duration"]], "R3"),
                              lab_share(z[["asset_swap"]], "R6"), lab_buf(z[["buffer"]]), lab_pay(z[["payout"]]))
f_at <- function(B, st = FALSE) rbf[rbf$static_only == st & abs(rbf$budget - B) < 1e-12, ]
oo_lab <- function(k) { z <- as.integer(strsplit(k, " ")[[1]])
  c(hedge_ratio = RB$hedge_set$ratio[z[1]], hedge_tenor = RB$hedge_set$tenor[z[1]], duration = RB$levers$duration[z[2]],
    asset_swap = RB$levers$asset_swap[z[3]], buffer = RB$levers$buffer[z[4]], payout = RB$levers$payout[z[5]]) }
## the claims in this chapter (the diagrams' counts included)
guard(RB$n_runs_per_path == 52 && RB$n_paths == 65 && RB$n_combos == 25200 && RB$n_episodes == 61,
      "the method diagram's counts have changed")
guard(f_at(0.30)$roe - p_roe > f_at(0.10)$roe - p_roe && f_at(0.30)$roe_p5 - p_p5 < f_at(0.10)$roe_p5 - p_p5 &&
      f_at(0.10)$roe - cen$roe < 0.5 * (cen$roe - p_roe) && f_at(0.01)$roe - p_roe > 0.6 * (cen$roe - p_roe),
      "the frontier: most of the gain at a small budget; beyond 10% more duration and a weaker tail")
guard(identical(unname(oo_lab(rbo$choice[3])[c("hedge_ratio", "hedge_tenor")]), c("20%", "10 years")),
      "out of sample: the last half prefers a 20% hedge at ten years")
guard(max(abs(rbv$roe_err)) < 1e-5 && max(abs(rbvar$surrogate_err)) < 1e-5, "the surrogate is within 0.1 bp of every exact run")
guard(all(rbv$feasible_exact) && ce$eve_max <= rb_b + 0.001 && ce$cet1_min >= CFG$cet1_min, "the chosen portfolios meet the limits exactly")
guard(RB$binds[["lcr"]] == 0 && RB$binds[["nsfr"]] == 0 && RB$binds[["eve_central"]] > 0.8 && RB$binds[["cet1"]] > 0.4 &&
      RB$binds[["tail"]] > 0.3, "what binds: EVE, CET1 and the tail, never the LCR or NSFR")
rule_cols <- c(hedge_ratio = "R1", hedge_tenor = "R2", duration = "R3", asset_swap = "R6", buffer = "R7")
fr_lab <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(rbf)), function(i) c(hedge_ratio = RB$hedge_set$ratio[rbf$hedge[i]], hedge_tenor = RB$hedge_set$tenor[rbf$hedge[i]],
  duration = RB$levers$duration[rbf$dur[i]], asset_swap = RB$levers$asset_swap[rbf$as[i]], buffer = RB$levers$buffer[rbf$buf[i]],
  payout = RB$levers$payout[rbf$pay[i]]))
guard(!any(vapply(fr_lab, function(z) any(z[names(rule_cols)] == rule_cols), TRUE)) && set_c[["payout"]] == "R4",
      "no rule but R4 is chosen at any budget, and R4 is chosen at the central one")
guard(set_c[["buffer"]] == "LCR 160%" && set_c[["asset_swap"]] == "50%" && set_c[["hedge_ratio"]] == pct(neutral_rb, 0) &&
      lu$value[6] > lu$limit_value[6] - 0.01 && lu$value[5] > 0.8 * rb_b, "the central portfolio: the HQLA cap and the EVE budget bind")
guard(abs(diff(range(rbreg$as))) < 0.0005 && abs(diff(range(rbreg$buf))) < 0.0005 &&
      rbreg["Rates rising", "hedge"] > 0 && rbreg["Rates falling", "hedge"] < 0 &&
      rbreg["Rates falling", "dur"] > rbreg["Rates rising", "dur"] &&
      abs(rbreg["Rates rising", "total"] - rbreg["Rates falling", "total"]) <
        abs(rbreg_s["Rates rising", "total"] - rbreg_s["Rates falling", "total"]) / 2,
      "the spread levers pay in every regime; the hedge and the bonds offset; the portfolio is more balanced than the static one")
guard(rbvar["Liquidity book only", "d_roe"] > 0.6 * ce$d_roe && rbvar["Hedge and payout only", "d_roe"] < 0.002 &&
      rbvar["Liquidity book capped at 50% of HQLA", "d_roe"] < rbvar["Liquidity book capped at 70% of HQLA", "d_roe"],
      "the liquidity book carries most of the result; the hedge and payout alone add little")
guard(rbo$choice[1] == rb_key(cen) && rbo$roe_test_best[1] - rbo$roe_test[1] < 0.001 &&
      rbo$roe_test_best[3] - rbo$roe_test[3] > 0.002 && all(rbo$feasible_test) && all(rbo$roe_test > 0.015),
      "out of sample: the first half picks the full-sample choice; the reverse loses part of the gain; every choice stays feasible")
guard(all(rbs$roe_central > rbs$roe_plan) && min(rbs$cet1_central) >= CFG$cet1_min && rbs["downside", "cet1_central"] == min(rbs$cet1_central),
      "the portfolio beats the plan in every scenario; the downside is its CET1 trough, above the floor")
```

The lab tests one strategy at a time. An ALCO sets the levers together, and
under limits: a risk appetite that bounds how bad earnings may get, how low
capital and liquidity may fall, and how much interest-rate risk the banking
book may carry. Stacked without such limits, the lab's seven rules added
`r bps(lab0(lab_all, "d_roe_mean"))` but used `r pct(lab0(lab_all, "d_eve200"), 0)` of CET1 of EVE sensitivity and took the CET1 trough to
`r pct(lab0(lab_all, "cet1_min_fv"), 2)`. This chapter asks the question the other way round: *given a risk
budget, which combination of the levers earns NGFB the most across the sixty
macro histories, and how does each lever's contribution depend on the macro
path?*

## The problem

The objective is NGFB's three-year average ROE, averaged across the
`r RB$n_episodes` episodes (each history weighted equally). A combination $x$ sets six
decisions: the hedge ratio and the reinvestment tenor (run together, because
they interact), the share of earning HQLA in ten-year bonds, the share in
asset-swapped five-year bonds, the size of the buffer, and the payout. Each
can be fixed today or follow its macro rule:

$$
\max_{x}\; \frac{1}{`r RB$n_episodes`}\sum_{e} \overline{\text{ROE}}_e(x)
$$

subject to, in every quarter $t$ of every episode $e$,

| Limit | Condition | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Tail | 5th percentile of $\overline{\text{ROE}}_e(x)$ across episodes $\geq$ the plan's (`r pct(p_p5, 1)`) | a higher average bought with a worse bad case is a bet, not positioning |
| Capital | CET1 with the bonds' OCI reserve $\geq$ `r pct(CFG$cet1_min, 1)` | the management floor of the positioning chapter, at fair value |
| Liquidity | LCR with HQLA at market value $\geq$ `r pct(CFG$lcr_min, 0)`; NSFR $\geq$ `r pct(RB$limits[["nsfr"]], 0)` | management floors above the 100% minima (the NSFR floor is an assumption) |
| Interest-rate risk | $\lvert \Delta\text{EVE}_{e,t}(x) - \Delta\text{EVE}_{e,t}(\text{plan}) \rvert \leq B$ of CET1 for a 200 bps parallel shock | the plan is taken as the bank's accepted position; $B$ bounds how far strategy moves it, either way |
| Liquidity book | ten-year bonds + asset swaps + released bills $\leq$ `r pct(RB$limits[["hq_cap"]], 0)` of earning HQLA | some bills stay for day-to-day liquidity management |

: The risk budget. The IRRBB outlier test flags a bank whose economic value falls by more than 15% of Tier 1 capital in the worst of six prescribed shocks; with no behavioural model of the deposits' own value, the budget here bounds the change from the plan's position, and `r pct(rb_b, 0)` of CET1 -- a third of that threshold -- is the central budget. {.striped}

```{r rb-levers}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(Lever = c("Hedge ratio", "Reinvestment tenor", "10-year bonds", "Asset-swapped bonds", "Size of the buffer", "Payout"),
              Settings = c(paste(c(head(RB$levers$ratio, -1), "or R1"), collapse = ", "),
                           paste(c(head(RB$levers$tenor, -1), "or R2"), collapse = ", "),
                           paste(c(head(RB$levers$duration, -1), "or R3"), collapse = ", "),
                           paste(c(head(RB$levers$asset_swap, -1), "or R6"), collapse = ", "),
                           paste(c(sprintf("the plan's (LCR %s)", pct(LV$lcr0, 0)), RB$levers$buffer[2:4], "or R7"), collapse = ", "),
                           paste(c(head(RB$levers$payout, -1), "or R4"), collapse = ", ")),
              Options = c(length(RB$levers$ratio), length(RB$levers$tenor), length(RB$levers$duration), length(RB$levers$asset_swap),
                          length(RB$levers$buffer), length(RB$levers$payout)), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llr", caption = sprintf("The levers and their settings: %s combinations, %s of them within the cap on the liquidity book. Shares of HQLA are of the jump-off's earning HQLA. R5 is left out: it does nothing in this engine.",
                                     num(RB$n_combos, 0), num(RB$n_admissible, 0)))
```

## How it is solved

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 7.5
flowchart TB
  subgraph BUILD["Build"]
    direction LR
    A["<b>1. Each setting alone</b><br/>52 settings × 65 paths<br/>3,380 engine runs"] --> B["<b>2. Surrogate</b><br/>changes added quarter by quarter,<br/>equity rolled forward with the payout"] --> C["<b>3. Every combination</b><br/>25,200 combinations ×<br/>61 episodes × 12 quarters"]
  end
  subgraph CHOOSE["Choose and check"]
    direction LR
    D["<b>Limits</b><br/>tail, CET1, LCR, NSFR,<br/>HQLA cap, EVE budget"] --> F["<b>Frontier</b><br/>best average ROE<br/>at each EVE budget"] --> G["<b>4. Exact runs</b><br/>every choice through<br/>the engine, 65 paths"] --> H["<b>5. Out of sample</b><br/>choose on one half,<br/>score on the other"]
  end
  BUILD --> CHOOSE
```

1. **Each setting on its own.** Every setting of every lever runs through the
   engine with everything else at the plan, on every path -- the
   `r RB$n_episodes` episodes, the three scenarios and the downside with cuts:
   `r RB$n_runs_per_path` runs per path. Each run keeps, quarter by quarter, net income,
   RWA, the bond books' OCI reserve, the PV01 of the hedge and bond books,
   the LCR and the NSFR.
2. **A surrogate for every combination.** A combination's changes against the
   plan are added quarter by quarter: the levers act on different parts of the
   balance sheet (the hedge on NII, the bond books on NII and OCI, the buffer
   on HQLA and wholesale funding). The exception is the payout, which acts on
   every rand the other levers add, so equity is rolled forward with the
   combination's own payout -- a fixed ratio, or R4 reading the combination's
   own CET1 -- and ROE, CET1 and the EVE ratio are computed from it, with the
   funding plug's interest following the equity actually retained. The
   surrogate reproduces every single setting's run exactly; on every
   combination run exactly below it is within `r num(1e4 * max(abs(c(rbv$roe_err, rbvar$surrogate_err))), 2)` bp of ROE.
3. **Every combination, not a search.** All `r num(RB$n_combos, 0)` combinations are scored on all
   episodes and quarters, minima and percentiles taken after adding, and the
   best that meets the limits is taken at each EVE budget. There is no
   optimisation heuristic to get stuck: the frontier is exact for the grid.
4. **Exact runs.** Every chosen combination is run through the engine on
   every path, and the limits are checked on those runs.
5. **Out of sample.** The optimum chosen on the first 25 episodes is scored
   on the last 25, and the reverse; the 11 episodes in between share quarters
   with both halves and are left out.

Step 2 in symbols: a combination's change in net income is the sum of its
settings' changes, and equity is rolled forward with the combination's own
payout,

$$\Delta\text{NI}_{e,t}(x) \;\approx\; \sum_{k} \Delta\text{NI}_{e,t}(x_k), \qquad E_{e,t}(x) \;=\; E_{e,t-1}(x) \;+\; \big(1-\pi_{e,t}(x)\big)\,\text{NI}_{e,t}(x) ,$$

where $\pi_{e,t}(x)$ is the payout ratio: a fixed number, or rule R4 reading
the combination's own CET1 ratio. Running every combination through the engine
on every path would mean about `r B(num(RB$n_combos * RB$n_paths / 1e6, 1))` million engine runs, the
strategic-planning equivalent of a queue at Home Affairs; the surrogate needs
`r B(RB$n_runs_per_path)` per path.

## The frontier

```{r rb-frontier}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "The risk-budgeted frontier: the best change in NGFB's average ROE across the episodes that meets every limit, at each EVE budget (the largest change in the hedge and bond books' economic value for a ±200 bps shock against the plan's, as a share of CET1). With every setting (rules allowed) and with static settings only. Dotted: the central budget."
fd <- rbf; fd$d_roe <- fd$roe - p_roe; fd$variant <- ifelse(fd$static_only, "static settings only", "every setting")
ggplot(fd, aes(budget, d_roe, colour = variant, linetype = variant)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rb_b, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "13") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`every setting` = ent_col[["NGFB"]], `static settings only` = ink[["secondary"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`every setting` = "solid", `static settings only` = "22"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "fg"), "%"), breaks = RB$budgets) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(1e4 * x), " bps"), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "EVE budget, % of CET1", y = "average ROE against the plan") + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r rb-frontier-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
fl <- do.call(rbind, fr_lab)
twin(data.frame(Budget = pct(rbf$budget, 1), Settings = ifelse(rbf$static_only, "static only", "every setting"),
                `Hedge ratio` = fl[, "hedge_ratio"], Tenor = fl[, "hedge_tenor"], `10-year bonds` = fl[, "duration"],
                `Asset swap` = fl[, "asset_swap"], Buffer = fl[, "buffer"], Payout = fl[, "payout"],
                `ROE vs plan` = bps(rbf$roe - p_roe), `5th percentile vs plan` = bps(rbf$roe_p5 - p_p5),
                `CET1 trough` = pct(rbf$cet1_min, 2), `EVE used` = pct(rbf$eve_max, 1), check.names = FALSE),
     "Table view: the best combination at each budget")
```

Most of the gain needs almost no EVE budget. With `r pct(0.01, 0)` of CET1 the best
combination already adds `r bps(f_at(0.01)$roe - p_roe)`; at the central `r pct(rb_b, 0)` it adds `r bps(cen$roe - p_roe)`, and the
next five points of budget add `r ubps(f_at(0.10)$roe - cen$roe)` more. The reason is that the largest levers
are spreads, not duration: the asset swap and the smaller buffer take no
interest-rate risk at all. Beyond 10% of CET1 the frontier buys ROE with
duration -- ten-year reinvestment and a hedge ratio back at or above the
plan's -- and the tail starts to give: at 30% the average gain is
`r bps(f_at(0.30)$roe - p_roe)` but the 5th percentile gains only `r bps(f_at(0.30)$roe_p5 - p_p5)`, against `r bps(f_at(0.10)$roe_p5 - p_p5)` at 10%. Static
settings alone come within `r ubps(cen$roe - cen_s$roe)` of the frontier at the central budget.

## The risk-budgeted portfolio

```{r rb-portfolio}

              Plan = c(paste(pct(LB$params$plan_ratio, 1), "of non-maturity deposits"), "5 years", "none", "none", sprintf("LCR %s", pct(LV$lcr0, 0)), "50%"),
              `Risk-budgeted` = settings_tab(set_c), `Static settings only` = settings_tab(set_s), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "llll", caption = sprintf("The best combination at an EVE budget of %s of CET1, with every setting allowed and with static settings only.", pct(rb_b, 0)))
```

```{r rb-metrics}
#| echo: false
mrow <- function(lbl, p, a, b) data.frame(Measure = lbl, Plan = p, `Risk-budgeted` = a, `Static settings only` = b, check.names = FALSE)
kt(rbind(
  mrow("Average ROE across the episodes", pct(p_roe, 2), pct(p_roe + ce$d_roe, 2), pct(p_roe + cs$d_roe, 2)),
  mrow("  against the plan", "", bps(ce$d_roe), bps(cs$d_roe)),
  mrow("5th percentile of ROE", pct(p_p5, 2), pct(p_p5 + ce$d_p5, 2), pct(p_p5 + cs$d_p5, 2)),
  mrow("Episodes beating the plan", "", pct(ce$win, 0), pct(cs$win, 0)),
  mrow("NII over three years, average", rbn(plan_row$nii, 1), rbn(nii_c, 1), rbn(nii_s, 1)),
  mrow("CET1 at fair value, lowest quarter", pct(plan_row$cet1_min, 2), pct(ce$cet1_min, 2), pct(cs$cet1_min, 2)),
  mrow("LCR at market value, lowest quarter", pct(plan_row$lcr_min, 0), pct(ce$lcr_min, 0), pct(cs$lcr_min, 0)),
  mrow("EVE change for ±200 bps, largest (% of CET1)", "0.0%", pct(ce$eve_max, 1), pct(cs$eve_max, 1)),
  mrow("Earning HQLA out of bills, largest", "0%", pct(ce$use_max, 0), pct(cs$use_max, 0))),
  align = "lrrr", caption = sprintf("The portfolios across the %d episodes, run exactly through the engine. Lowest and largest: across every quarter of every episode.", RB$n_episodes))
```

At a budget of `r pct(rb_b, 0)` of CET1 the optimiser keeps the hedge at the rate-neutral
`r set_c[["hedge_ratio"]]` of non-maturity deposits instead of the plan's `r pct(LB$params$plan_ratio, 1)`, reinvests maturing
tranches at `r set_c[["hedge_tenor"]]`, holds `r set_c[["duration"]]` of earning HQLA in ten-year bonds and
`r set_c[["asset_swap"]]` in asset-swapped five-year bonds, releases bills to an LCR of `r sub("LCR ", "", set_c[["buffer"]])`, and
pays out by R4. Across the episodes NGFB's ROE rises from `r pct(p_roe, 1)` to
`r pct(p_roe + ce$d_roe, 1)` on average, the 5th percentile from `r pct(p_p5, 1)` to `r pct(p_p5 + ce$d_p5, 1)`, and the portfolio
beats the plan in every episode.

```{r rb-limits}
#| echo: false
fmt_lim <- function(i, x) if (i == 1) bps(x) else pct(x, c(0, 2, 0, 0, 1, 0)[i])
kt(data.frame(Limit = c("Tail: 5th percentile of ROE, margin over the plan's", "CET1 at fair value, lowest quarter",
                        "LCR at market value, lowest quarter", "NSFR, lowest quarter",
                        "EVE change for ±200 bps against the plan, largest", "Earning HQLA out of bills, largest"),
              Portfolio = vapply(seq_len(nrow(lu)), function(i) fmt_lim(i, lu$value[i]), ""),
              `Floor or budget` = vapply(seq_len(nrow(lu)), function(i) fmt_lim(i, lu$limit_value[i]), ""),
              Binds = ifelse(c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, lu$value[5] > 0.8 * lu$limit_value[5], lu$value[6] > lu$limit_value[6] - 0.01),
                             "yes", ""), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrl", caption = "What the risk-budgeted portfolio uses of each limit: exact runs, the lowest or largest value in any quarter of any episode.")
```

Two limits bind. The EVE budget is nearly used up (`r pct(lu$value[5], 1)` of the `r pct(rb_b, 0)`), and so is the
cap on the liquidity book (`r pct(lu$value[6], 0)` of earning HQLA out of bills against `r pct(RB$limits[["hq_cap"]], 0)`). CET1
keeps `r ubps(lu$value[2] - CFG$cet1_min)` above its floor at the worst quarter of the worst episode. The
LCR and NSFR floors never bind for any combination: the buffer's release is
limited first by the wholesale funding it can repay. Across all
`r num(RB$n_combos, 0)` combinations, the EVE budget rules out `r pct(RB$binds[["eve_central"]], 0)`, the CET1 floor
`r pct(RB$binds[["cet1"]], 0)`, the tail `r pct(RB$binds[["tail"]], 0)` and the cap on the liquidity book `r pct(RB$binds[["hqla_cap"]], 0)`.

**In the scenarios** the same portfolio lifts NGFB's ROE in every one:

```{r rb-scenarios}
#| echo: false
kt(data.frame(Scenario = sc_short[rbs$scenario], `Plan ROE` = pct(rbs$roe_plan, 1), `Risk-budgeted ROE` = pct(rbs$roe_central, 1),
              Change = bps(rbs$roe_central - rbs$roe_plan), `Net income, 3 years` = srbn(rbs$ni_central - rbs$ni_plan),
              `NII, 3 years` = srbn(rbs$nii_central - rbs$nii_plan),
              `CET1 trough at fair value` = paste(pct(rbs$cet1_plan, 2), "→", pct(rbs$cet1_central, 2)),
              `Lowest LCR` = paste(pct(rbs$lcr_plan, 0), "→", pct(rbs$lcr_central, 0)), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrrr", caption = "The risk-budgeted portfolio in the scenarios, run exactly, against the plan.")
```

The downside is where it is tightest: its CET1 trough at fair value falls
from `r pct(rbs["downside", "cet1_plan"], 2)` to `r pct(rbs["downside", "cet1_central"], 2)`, because R4 pays 70% of the higher earnings before the
contraction arrives and the bond books lose value in the sovereign stress.

## Where the ROE comes from, and how it moves with the macro picture

```{r rb-regimes}
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "The risk-budgeted portfolio's change in ROE against the plan by lever, averaged over the episodes in each macro regime: the policy rate's average over the episode against the jump-off (rising or falling by more than 25 bps), average GDP growth, and whether the episode holds a contraction. Interaction: what the exact run adds beyond the levers' separate effects (mostly R4 paying out the other levers' earnings). Dots: the total."
comp <- c(hedge = "Hedge ratio and tenor", dur = "10-year bonds", as = "Asset swap", buf = "Smaller buffer", pay = "Payout (R4)",
          interaction = "Interaction")
comp_col <- stats::setNames(c(pal$categorical[1:5], ink[["muted"]]), comp)
rg_ord <- c("All episodes", "Rates rising", "Rates flat", "Rates falling", "Growth 1% or more", "Growth below 1%", "No contraction", "A contraction")
rl_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(comp), function(k) data.frame(regime = rbreg$regime, n = rbreg$n, lever = comp[[k]], value = rbreg[[k]])))
rl_long$regime_lab <- factor(sprintf("%s (%d)", rl_long$regime, rl_long$n), levels = rev(sprintf("%s (%d)", rbreg$regime[match(rg_ord, rbreg$regime)], rbreg$n[match(rg_ord, rbreg$regime)])))
rl_long$lever <- factor(rl_long$lever, levels = comp)
tot <- data.frame(regime_lab = factor(sprintf("%s (%d)", rbreg$regime, rbreg$n), levels = levels(rl_long$regime_lab)), total = rbreg$total)
ggplot(rl_long, aes(value, regime_lab, fill = lever)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_point(data = tot, aes(total, regime_lab), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.2, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = comp_col, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(round(1e4 * x), " bps")) +
  labs(x = "change in ROE against the plan", y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

```{r rb-regimes-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
rr2 <- rbreg[match(rg_ord, rbreg$regime), ]; rs2 <- rbreg_s[match(rg_ord, rbreg_s$regime), ]
twin(data.frame(Regime = rr2$regime, Episodes = rr2$n, `Hedge ratio and tenor` = bps(rr2$hedge), `10-year bonds` = bps(rr2$dur),
                `Asset swap` = bps(rr2$as), `Smaller buffer` = bps(rr2$buf), `Payout (R4)` = bps(rr2$pay),
                Interaction = bps(rr2$interaction), Total = bps(rr2$total), `Static-only portfolio, total` = bps(rs2$total),
                check.names = FALSE), "Table view: contributions by regime")
```

The portfolio has a rate-neutral core and a macro-sensitive edge.

* **The core is the two spread trades.** The asset swap adds `r bps(rbreg["All episodes", "as"])` and the smaller
  buffer `r bps(rbreg["All episodes", "buf"])`, and both add the same whether rates rise or fall, growth is strong
  or weak, or the episode holds a contraction: one collects the fiscal premium
  and the other the gap between wholesale funding and bills, and neither
  depends on the policy path. Together they are
  `r pct((rbreg["All episodes", "as"] + rbreg["All episodes", "buf"]) / rbreg["All episodes", "total"], 0)` of the gain, and they use no EVE budget.
* **The edge is where duration sits.** The plan holds its duration in the
  receive-fixed hedge. The optimiser moves part of it into government bonds:
  it cuts the hedge to the rate-neutral ratio and holds ten-year bonds and
  longer reinvestment instead, at a similar EVE, because a ten-year bond
  earns the fiscal premium on top of the term premium a swap earns. The two
  then offset each other across the rate cycle: the smaller hedge gains
  `r bps(rbreg["Rates rising", "hedge"])` when rates rise and loses `r ubps(rbreg["Rates falling", "hedge"])` when they fall; the bonds add `r bps(rbreg["Rates falling", "dur"])` when
  rates fall and `r bps(rbreg["Rates rising", "dur"])` when they rise. The portfolio as a whole adds `r bps(rbreg["Rates rising", "total"])` when
  rates rise and `r bps(rbreg["Rates falling", "total"])` when they fall, against `r bps(rbreg_s["Rates rising", "total"])` and `r bps(rbreg_s["Rates falling", "total"])` for the static-only
  optimum, which leans on a 20% hedge and long duration and so is a much
  larger bet on rising rates.
* **The payout is the one macro rule kept.** R4 adds `r bps(rbreg["All episodes", "pay"])` directly and, through
  the interaction, another `r bps(rbreg["All episodes", "interaction"])`, by paying out more of the other levers' earnings
  in good times. It adds least where growth is weak (`r bps(rbreg["Growth below 1%", "pay"])`), which is
  the point: it keeps capital where the downturns are.

**Why the other rules are not chosen.** No budget picks R1, R2, R3, R6 or R7.
Under binding limits a rule earns its place only if its signal predicts the
premium it collects better than a fixed setting that uses the same room. R1
and R2 time the rate cycle, which the lab found does not pay. R3 earned the
most of any single rule in the lab, but it trades its book: its realised
losses in hiking cycles count against the tail limit, and its duration -- and
so the EVE budget it uses -- peaks when the curve is steepest, so within a
budget a fixed holding does better. R6
holds less than a fixed 50% while the spread is as tight as today's, and R7
holds more liquidity than a fixed 160% in stress quarters -- both cost income
under a cap that binds. The rules' value lies in what this engine does not
price: R7's liquidity in a run, R6's sizing to spread risk. They belong in
the ALCO's playbook as risk triggers rather than as return engines.

## Which levers carry the result

```{r rb-variants}
#| echo: false
vv <- rbvar
kt(data.frame(Variant = vv$variant, `Hedge ratio` = vv$hedge_ratio, Tenor = vv$hedge_tenor, `10-year bonds` = vv$duration,
              `Asset swap` = vv$asset_swap, Buffer = vv$buffer, Payout = vv$payout, `ROE vs plan` = bps(vv$d_roe),
              `5th percentile vs plan` = bps(vv$d_p5), `CET1 trough` = pct(vv$cet1_min, 2), `EVE used` = pct(vv$eve_max, 1),
              `HQLA out of bills` = pct(vv$use_max, 0), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lllllllrrrrr", caption = sprintf("The best combination at an EVE budget of %s of CET1 when the levers are restricted. Exact runs.", pct(rb_b, 0)))
```

* **The liquidity book carries the result.** With the hedge and payout left at
  the plan, the liquidity book alone adds `r bps(rbvar["Liquidity book only", "d_roe"])`; with the liquidity book left in bills,
  the hedge and the payout together add only `r bps(rbvar["Hedge and payout only", "d_roe"])` within the budget.
* **The answer rests on the cap and the spread appetite.** The optimiser takes
  the spread trades to the limits it is given, because the engine prices
  neither the asset swap's spread risk beyond the modelled spread nor the
  liquidity a smaller buffer gives up. With the asset swap at most a quarter
  of HQLA and the LCR no lower than 170% the gain is `r bps(rbvar["Asset swap at most 25%, LCR at least 170%", "d_roe"])`; with the
  liquidity book capped at 70% or 50% of earning HQLA it is
  `r bps(rbvar["Liquidity book capped at 70% of HQLA", "d_roe"])` or `r bps(rbvar["Liquidity book capped at 50% of HQLA", "d_roe"])`. Those limits are the bank's to set -- against its credit-spread
  risk appetite and its own liquidity stress test -- and the table says what
  each is worth.

## Exact runs and out of sample

```{r rb-oos}
#| echo: false
oo <- rbo
oo_set <- function(k) { z <- as.integer(strsplit(k, " ")[[1]])
  paste(RB$hedge_set$ratio[z[1]], RB$hedge_set$tenor[z[1]], RB$levers$duration[z[2]], RB$levers$asset_swap[z[3]],
        RB$levers$buffer[z[4]], RB$levers$payout[z[5]], sep = " · ") }
kt(data.frame(`Chosen on` = paste(oo$train, "25 episodes"), `Scored on` = paste(oo$test, "25 episodes"),
              Settings = ifelse(oo$static_only, "static only", "every setting"), Choice = vapply(oo$choice, oo_set, ""),
              `ROE vs plan, where chosen` = bps(oo$roe_train), `ROE vs plan, out of sample` = bps(oo$roe_test),
              `Best possible out of sample` = bps(oo$roe_test_best), `Limits met out of sample` = ifelse(oo$feasible_test, "yes", "no"),
              check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lllllrrrl", caption = sprintf("Choosing on one half of the episodes and scoring on the other, at an EVE budget of %s of CET1 (surrogate; the 11 episodes between the halves are left out). Change in average ROE against the plan in each half.", pct(rb_b, 0)))
```

The surrogate is within `r num(1e4 * max(abs(rbv$roe_err)), 2)` bp of the exact engine on every chosen
combination, and every one meets its limits when run exactly. Out of sample,
the portfolio chosen on the first 25 episodes is the full sample's, and on the
last 25 it adds `r bps(rbo$roe_test[1])` against a best possible `r bps(rbo$roe_test_best[1])`. Chosen on the last 25 (episodes
starting `r substr(LB$info$episode[RB$n_episodes - 24], 1, 6)` to `r substr(LB$info$episode[RB$n_episodes], 1, 6)`, which hold the 2021–23 hiking cycle), the optimiser prefers
a 20% hedge reinvested at ten years with `r oo_lab(rbo$choice[3])[["duration"]]` of HQLA in ten-year bonds -- less
receive-fixed, more bonds -- and on the first 25 (starting `r substr(LB$info$episode[1], 1, 6)` to
`r substr(LB$info$episode[25], 1, 6)`, which hold the 2008–09 cuts) that choice adds `r bps(rbo$roe_test[3])` against a best possible
`r bps(rbo$roe_test_best[3])`. The rate-neutral core
transfers between periods; how much duration to hold, and where, depends on
the rate cycles in the sample, which is why the budget for it should be set
explicitly rather than read off history.

## Using the balance sheet itself: repo-funded carry {#carry}

```{r rb-carry-setup}
#| include: false
CY <- RB$carry; cyt <- CY$spread_frontier; cyr <- CY$recommended; cyp <- CY$per_step
cyreg <- CY$regime; rownames(cyreg) <- cyreg$regime
cy_max <- cyt[nrow(cyt), ]
rr1 <- LB$inputs$baseline$rates[1, ]; cy_gap <- rr1$repo + CY$repo_spread - rr1$tbill   # repo funding less the bills' yield, pp
guard(cy_gap > 0.15 && cy_gap < 0.35, "the carry book's cost against the buffer's bills")
cy_ep <- LB$inputs[LB$kind == "episode"]
cy_w <- vapply(cy_ep, function(i) max(asset_swap_spread(i$rates, LB$jo_mk, bsm$beta, bsm$kappa)) - LB$jo_mk$bs, 0)
cy_wd <- max(asset_swap_spread(LB$inputs$downside$rates, LB$jo_mk, bsm$beta, bsm$kappa)) - LB$jo_mk$bs
guard(max(cy_w) > cy_wd, "history holds spread widenings as large as the downside's")
guard(all(cyt$hedge_ratio == set_c[["hedge_ratio"]] & cyt$payout == set_c[["payout"]] & cyt$buffer == set_c[["buffer"]] &
          cyt$asset_swap == set_c[["asset_swap"]] & cyt$duration == set_c[["duration"]]),
      "the carry book is added to the central portfolio without moving any other lever")
guard(all(diff(cyt$d_roe[is.finite(cyt$spread_step)]) > 0.0009) && abs(cyp[["roe"]] - 0.001) < 0.0002,
      "each R25bn of carry adds about 10 bps")
guard(cyr$carry == "R50bn" && !cyt$ok_scen[cyt$carry == "R75bn"][1] && all(cyt$lev_min > CY$lr_floor) &&
      all(cyt$cet1_min > CFG$cet1_min) && cyr$cet1_downside < CFG$cet1_min + 0.0005,
      "the downside caps the carry book at R50bn; neither the leverage floor nor the episodes' CET1 floor binds")
guard(diff(range(cyreg$carry)) < 0.0003, "the carry book adds the same in every regime")
guard(CY$binds[["leverage"]] < 0.05, "the leverage floor rules out few combinations")
```

Before settling on the levers above, I went back through the optimiser's
options looking for an approach it had missed, something that would squeeze
more NII or ROE out of the same strategy. Most candidates failed, for reasons
worth recording:

* **Issuing Additional Tier 1 or Tier 2 capital** would cheapen the total
  capital stack, but what binds in the downside is the CET1 floor, which
  neither instrument counts towards.
* **Pricing deposits harder** is already among the [further levers](#levers)
  as an upper bound (`r B(bps(lv("Deposit pricing", "10% less of rises, 10% more of cuts")))`), and without a measured
  volume response it cannot be sized honestly.
* **Terming out wholesale funding** for the NSFR needs a term premium on bank
  paper that public data do not publish.
* **Repo-ing the HQLA bonds** to release cash is economically the same trade
  as shrinking the buffer, which the optimiser already has.
* **Redeploying HQLA into lending** is ruled out at the margin by the
  positioning chapter: the plan is optimal under the baseline, and the static
  case for more lending is a franchise question.
* **Holding the bonds at amortised cost** instead of fair value changes
  reported CET1 volatility, not the economics, and HQLA count at market value
  in the LCR either way.
* **Options on rates** need a ZAR volatility surface that is not public.
* **A one-off capital distribution** competes with R4 for the same capital
  room, and inside the budget R4 uses it better.

One candidate survived.

Every lever so far rearranges the balance sheet NGFB already has: a rand of
bills becomes a rand of bonds, a rand of bills repays a rand of wholesale
funding, a rand of profit is paid out or kept. The one resource none of them
uses is the size of the balance sheet itself. A bank can buy more government
bonds than its liquidity buffer needs, asset-swap them exactly as in
[Asset-swapped bonds](#asset-swap), and fund them in repo against the bonds
themselves. That is how South African banks hold much of their sovereign
book, and it is the lever this optimiser was missing.

**What it earns.** Funded in repo rather than by displacing bills, each rand
earns the bond–swap spread plus the floating leg less the repo rate:
$bs + f_t - (r^{\text{repo}}_t + s^{\text{repo}})$, with $s^{\text{repo}}$ =
`r num(100 * CY$repo_spread, 0)` bp, the spread NGFB already pays on its repo funding. At the jump-off that is `r num(CY$carry_jo, 2)` pp a year,
about `r num(cy_gap, 2)` pp less than the same bond inside the buffer, because the bills it
would replace yield below the policy rate while repo costs above it. It
needs no HQLA (the bonds are encumbered, and secured funding against Level 1
collateral carries no LCR outflow), no EVE budget (the swap removes the rate
risk) and almost no RWA (rand claims on the sovereign); it adds 5% of its
size to required stable funding and all of it to the leverage exposure.

Per rand and per year,

$$\text{carry}_t \;=\; bs \;+\; f_t \;-\; \big(r^{\text{repo}}_t + s^{\text{repo}}\big) ,$$

against $bs + f_t - y^{\text{bill}}_t$ for the same asset-swapped bond inside
the buffer, where it replaces a Treasury bill rather than repo funding.

**What limits it.** Three limits are added for this section: the leverage
ratio (CET1 over on-balance-sheet assets, a conservative stand-in for Tier 1)
must stay at or above `r pct(CY$lr_floor, 0)` -- South Africa's minimum is 4%, and a D-SIB holds a
further buffer of half its higher-loss-absorbency requirement from July 2025
-- the CET1 floor must hold in the named scenarios as well as the episodes,
and the book's credit-spread risk is measured: what a 100 bps widening of the
bond–swap spread would take off the bond books, after tax, as a share of
CET1.

$$\text{spread risk} \;=\; \frac{100 \times \text{spread PV01} \times (1-\tau)}{\text{CET1}} ,$$

where the spread PV01 is the change in the bond books' value for a one basis
point widening of the bond–swap spread with the swap curve unchanged.

```{r rb-carry}
#| echo: false
cyt2 <- cyt[is.finite(cyt$spread_step), ]
kt(data.frame(`Carry book` = cyt2$carry,
              `ROE vs plan` = bps(cyt2$d_roe), `vs the central portfolio` = bps(cyt2$d_roe_vs_central),
              `NII, 3 years, vs the central portfolio` = srbn(cyt2$nii - cyt2$nii[1]),
              `100 bps spread widening (% of CET1)` = pct(cyt2$csrbb, 1),
              `CET1 trough, episodes` = pct(cyt2$cet1_min, 2), `CET1 trough, downside` = pct(cyt2$cet1_downside, 2),
              `Leverage ratio, lowest` = pct(pmin(cyt2$lev_min, cyt2$lev_scen_min), 2), `Every limit met` = ifelse(cyt2$ok_scen, "yes", "no"),
              check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrrrrrrl", caption = sprintf("The central portfolio with a repo-funded carry book of asset-swapped 5-year government bonds added at the jump-off (exact runs; averages across the %d episodes; the leverage ratio is the lowest quarter across the episodes and the named scenarios). Every other lever stays where the central portfolio has it.", RB$n_episodes))
```

Each R25`r nb`bn of carry book adds about `r ubps(cyp[["roe"]])` of ROE (`r urbn(cyp[["nii"]])` of NII over three years)
and `r num(100 * cyp[["csrbb"]], 1)` points of CET1 to the loss from a 100 bps spread widening. It earns that
in every macro regime alike, as the asset swap in the buffer does: the R100`r nb`bn
book adds `r bps(cyreg["Rates rising", "carry"])` when rates rise, `r bps(cyreg["Rates falling", "carry"])` when they fall and `r bps(cyreg["A contraction", "carry"])` in episodes
with a contraction.

None of the limits the optimiser had so far stops it. Even with R100`r nb`bn added
the leverage ratio is `r pct(min(cyt2$lev_min, cyt2$lev_scen_min), 1)` at its lowest, and across the episodes the CET1
floor would not bind until well beyond the largest book tested. History does
hold spread widenings as large as the downside's (`r num(max(cy_w), 2)` pp at the worst, in the
episode that replays 2020, against `r num(cy_wd, 2)` pp), but not at the same time as a deep
contraction and rising rates: 2020's came with 300 bps of cuts, 2015–16's
with hikes but no deep recession, so the carry book's loss never landed on
capital already thinned by credit losses and a hedge losing money. The
stagflationary downside combines all three, and that is what binds: at
R75`r nb`bn its CET1 trough falls to `r pct(cyt2$cet1_downside[cyt2$carry == "R75bn"], 2)`, below the `r pct(CFG$cet1_min, 1)` floor. The largest
book that keeps every limit in every episode and every scenario is
`r cyr$carry`, which lifts the central portfolio by `r bps(cyr$d_roe_vs_central)` to `r bps(cyr$d_roe)` against the plan,
at the cost of raising the 100 bps spread loss from `r pct(CY$central_csrbb, 1)` to `r pct(cyr$csrbb, 1)` of CET1.

The lesson for the risk budget is the more useful one. A limit set only on
EVE, capital in replayed history and liquidity barely sees a position whose
risk is the sovereign spread; the carry book walks through all three, and
only a scenario built around a fiscal shock stops it. It needs its own limit -- a credit-spread budget in the banking book
(CSRBB) -- and every point of CET1 put into that budget buys about
`r ubps(cyp[["roe"]] / cyp[["csrbb"]] * 0.01)` of ROE. Whether that is a good price is a question about the
sovereign, not about NGFB: the carry is the fiscal premium, and a bank that
earns more of it is more exposed to the event the premium pays for. Selling insurance is a lovely business until the claim comes in.

## What the optimiser does not know

* **History is the only distribution.** The `r RB$n_episodes` episodes overlap, so they hold
  about six independent three-year periods, one global financial crisis and
  one pandemic; the tail limit is the 5th percentile of those, the fourth
  worst episode.
* **It maximises what the engine prices.** The asset swap's spread risk is
  in the model only through the modelled spread, and a smaller buffer's cost
  only through the LCR and NSFR, neither of which stresses run-offs or
  funding spreads; so the optimiser takes both to the limits it is given.
  Those limits -- the cap on the liquidity book, the wholesale funding left to
  repay -- set their size, and the variants above show what they are worth.
* **The EVE budget is relative.** Without a behavioural model of the deposits'
  own economic value, the budget bounds the change from the plan's position,
  not the bank's total exposure against the 15% outlier threshold.
* **The grid is coarse.** Shares move in steps of 12.5% of HQLA and the hedge
  ratio in steps of about 15 points of deposits; a finer grid would add a few
  basis points, not change the answer.

## What it means for NGFB's ALCO {#alco}

1. **Run every macro pack through the whole balance sheet**, not only the
   capital ratio, and attribute each scenario's effect by channel (volumes,
   pricing and the hedge, credit, fees and costs), so the committee argues
   about the same consequences.
2. **Fund the two spread trades first.** Asset-swapped government bonds and a
   smaller buffer add about `r ubps(rbreg["All episodes", "as"] + rbreg["All episodes", "buf"])` in every macro regime with no rate view and
   no EVE cost. Size them against the bank's credit-spread risk appetite and
   its own liquidity stress test, not against the LCR.
3. **Hold duration in bonds, not only in swaps.** At the same EVE, a
   government bond earns the fiscal premium on top of the term premium. Keep
   the structural hedge near its rate-neutral ratio and let the bond book and
   the reinvestment tenor carry the duration the budget allows.
4. **Make the payout state-contingent.** R4 is the macro rule that survives
   the risk budget.
5. **Use the other rules as risk triggers.** The slope, the bond–swap spread
   and the stress signals tell the ALCO when the premia are large and when
   liquidity is worth more; under binding limits they do not beat fixed
   settings on return.
6. **Set the budgets explicitly, and price them.** At `r pct(rb_b, 0)` of CET1 the portfolio adds `r bps(cen$roe - p_roe)`; the
   frontier says what each further point of EVE budget is worth, the
   out-of-sample check says how much of that depends on the rate cycles
   history happened to contain, and the carry book says what a point of
   credit-spread budget is worth (about `r B(ubps(CY$per_step[["roe"]] / CY$per_step[["csrbb"]] * 0.01))` of ROE).
7. **Position ahead of a scenario in proportion to conviction, and read the
   regret matrix before the gain.** The credit leg of a downside positioning is
   robust to the SARB's response; the rate leg is a bet on it.
8. **Push where the market grows and NGFB does not, and judge the result
   against macro par.** Cards, corporate lending and vehicle finance in easing
   cycles, with their own deposits behind them; tighter card underwriting when
   GDP turns; and every business judged against a macro-adjusted target and
   the peer range rather than against last year.

# Conclusions {#conclusions}

The deposit series ended by pricing something it could not estimate. This one
ends somewhere similar. The macro view matters enormously to what NGFB earns:
its plan swings from `r B(pct(min(pl$roe)))` to `r B(pct(max(pl$roe)))` across sixty-one histories, and two
macro numbers explain `r B(pct(L$drivers_r2, 0))` of that spread. But mattering is not the same
as being tradeable. Keying the hedge to the level of rates earned nothing.
Positioning ahead of a downside recovered `r B(pct(gain["downside", "downside"] / -att("downside"), 0))` of the damage and cost
more than twice as much if the upside arrived instead. The one rule that
survived a risk budget was a payout that pays more when the economy grows,
which is less a forecast than good manners.

What did pay was dull. Collecting the fiscal premium without its duration, and
not paying wholesale rates to hold bills nobody needs, added about a point and
a half of ROE whatever the history, and the risk budget turned a pile of good
ideas into a portfolio that beat the plan in every one of the `r B(RB$n_episodes)` histories.
The missing lever added another `r B(ubps(cyr$d_roe_vs_central))`, and a lesson worth more than the
basis points: a risk budget that only sees rates, capital and liquidity will
let a sovereign-spread position walk straight through it.

The same machinery did three jobs that a stress test never asks of it. It
translated each economic outcome into every line of the balance sheet, and
showed NGFB to be a credit play whose rate exposure turns on how the SARB
answers a downturn. It turned a view into a position with its cost of being
wrong attached, and found the money in levers that need no view. And it turned
a growth number into a verdict on the swimming: NGFB under-participates when
rates fall, gains card share in a contraction when the business on offer is
the riskiest, and sits below par exactly where the upside's growth is. That is
a better use of a macro model than one stress test a year.

This ran on a bank that does not exist, so I cannot tell you what it would do
to yours. What I can say is that the shape of the answer is unusually robust.
The spread trades paid in every history and every scenario. The rate bets did
not. A treasury that sets its budgets explicitly, funds the premia that need
no view, and keeps its rate views for the occasions it genuinely has one,
should not need a crystal ball to earn its cost of equity more often than once
in sixty-one tries.

*No refunds, as the man selling coat hangers at the robot will tell you: none
of this is advice, and your own bank's risk budget should be set by people
who can see its books.*

# Validation

## Back-test: would the industry models have tracked the industry?

```{r backtest}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Skill against a no-change forecast over twelve quarters, re-estimating every Stage 1 model on data to the origin and projecting it along the realised macro path. Ratio targets with the intercept correction."
ba <- BT$accuracy
ba$label <- S1$summary$label[match(ba$target, S1$summary$target)]
ba$origin_lab <- paste("From", qlab(ba$origin))
ba$sk <- pmax(ba$skill_used, -1.5)
ba$label <- factor(ba$label, levels = rev(S1$summary$label[order(match(S1$summary$family, c("volume", "credit", "pnl", "pricing")), S1$summary$target)]))
ggplot(ba, aes(sk, label, colour = origin_lab)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink[["axis"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(pal$categorical[1:2])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = "skill vs no change (values below −150% shown at −150%)", y = NULL)
```

```{r backtest-twin}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
fam <- stats::aggregate(cbind(skill, skill_ic) ~ family, ba, median)
twin(data.frame(Target = ba$label, Origin = qlab(ba$origin), `RMSE model` = num(ba$rmse_model, 2),
                `RMSE model + IC` = num(ba$rmse_model_ic, 2), `RMSE no change` = num(ba$rmse_naive, 2),
                Skill = pct(ba$skill, 0), `Skill + IC` = pct(ba$skill_ic, 0), check.names = FALSE))
```

The back-test asks the question a scenario tool must answer: *if the macro
path had been known*, would the models have tracked the sector? From the eve
of COVID (2019Q4) and the eve of the 2022–23 hiking cycle (2021Q4), every
Stage 1 model is re-estimated on data to the origin only, its whole
specification search included, and projected twelve quarters along the
realised macro path. The model beats no change in
`r sum(ba$skill_used > 0)` of `r nrow(ba)` target-origins.

| Family | Median skill, no correction | Median skill, intercept correction |
|---|---|---|
| Pricing (spreads, deposit costs) | `r pct(fam$skill[fam$family == "pricing"], 0)` | `r pct(fam$skill_ic[fam$family == "pricing"], 0)` |
| Credit (credit-loss ratio) | `r pct(fam$skill[fam$family == "credit"], 0)` | `r pct(fam$skill_ic[fam$family == "credit"], 0)` |
| Fees and costs (over assets) | `r pct(fam$skill[fam$family == "pnl"], 0)` | `r pct(fam$skill_ic[fam$family == "pnl"], 0)` |
| Volumes (growth) | `r pct(fam$skill[fam$family == "volume"], 0)` | not applied |

: Back-test skill by family (two origins, twelve quarters). {.striped}

The pricing and credit models carry real information; the volume models
carry a little; the fee and cost ratios are better forecast by "no change"
than by a model that mean-reverts to a 2008–2025 average the industry has
since left (non-interest revenue over assets has drifted down). The intercept
correction narrows that gap for non-interest revenue and improves the median
in every ratio family, so it is used for all ratio targets; it is not applied
to volume growth, where recent residuals are mostly noise.

## Does the engine's first year look like the industry's last year?

```{r recon}
#| echo: false
q1 <- res$baseline$sector$run$quarterly[1:4, ]
sp <- P$spnl; w4 <- sp$date %in% utils::tail(sp$date[is.finite(sp$nii)], 4)
act <- c(nii = sum(sp$nii[w4]), nir = sum(sp$nir[w4]), opex = sum(sp$opex[w4]) + sum(sp$indirect_tax[w4], na.rm = TRUE),
         imp = sum(sp$credit_losses[w4]), pbt = sum(sp$pbt[w4]))
eng <- c(nii = sum(q1$nii), nir = sum(q1$nir), opex = sum(q1$opex), imp = sum(q1$impairments), pbt = sum(q1$pbt))
ta_act <- mean(sp$total_assets[w4]); ta_eng <- mean(q1$total_assets)
kt(data.frame(Item = c("Net interest income", "Non-interest revenue", "Operating costs incl. indirect tax",
                       "Credit impairments", "Profit before tax", "Average total assets"),
              `Last four BA120 quarters, R bn` = num(c(act, ta_act) / 1e6, 0),
              `Engine, first projected year, R bn` = num(c(eng, ta_eng) / 1e6, 0),
              `Change` = spct(c(eng / act, ta_eng / ta_act) - 1, 0), check.names = FALSE),
   align = "lrrr", caption = sprintf("Sector P&L: BA120 %s–%s against the engine's baseline %s–%s.",
                                     qlab(min(sp$date[w4])), qlab(max(sp$date[w4])), qlab(min(q1$date)), qlab(max(q1$date))))
```

The engine's first projected year starts four quarters after the last BA120
quarter, on a balance sheet `r spct(ta_eng / ta_act - 1, 0)` larger (BA900 grew
`r spct(sec_ta0 / P$gp$total_assets[P$gp$entity == "Sector" & P$gp$date == max(sp$date[w4])] - 1, 0)`
between the two dates). Revenue and costs scale with it, and the engine's
sector ROE in the first year, `r pct(mean(q1$roe))`, compares with
`r pct(mean(sp$roe[w4]) / 100)` on BA100's ordinary equity in the last four quarters. The
residual differences are the scenario's rate path and the intercept-corrected
ratios.

## Other checks

* **Engine arithmetic.** The balance sheet balances in every quarter of
  every run (relative error below 10⁻⁹); channel attributions reproduce the
  full-engine runs exactly in ROE and in net income; the bridges add up to the
  positioned ROE and net income (all guarded in the scripts).
* **Optimiser.** The linear prediction of the quadratic programme agrees
  with the full engine to `r ubps(max(abs(O$own - O$pred)), 2)` of ROE, the status quo
  comes out optimal under the baseline, as it must, and the step-by-step
  tables add up to each positioning's gain.
* **Tests.** The package's unit tests cover parsing, the satellite search
  (recovering a known data-generating process, sign exclusion, convergence to
  the long run, both forms of the intercept correction), the model checks
  (Clark–West, the bounds test, the asymmetric decomposition, the peer-group
  roster), random-effects pooling, the engine (hand-computed NII, balance,
  hedge direction), liquidity factors and calibration, attribution in ROE and
  net income, the scenario library and the optimiser, including the
  $(2\alpha - \alpha^2)$ law for oversized positions.

# What didn't work {#what-didnt-work}

```{r wdw}
#| include: false
## the naive liquidity factors (fixed run-offs, generous inflows, no encumbrance)
nbs <- N$engine_bs                          # (not `nb`: that is the non-breaking space used by the formatters)
naive_run <- c(beh_operational = 0.10, beh_savings = 0.10, beh_notice = 0.25, beh_term = 0.05,
               wholesale_other = 0.25, interbank = 0.5, reverse_repo = 0.5)
nbs$runoff <- 0; nbs$runoff[match(names(naive_run), nbs$line)] <- naive_run
nbs$hqla <- as.numeric(nbs$line == "hqla")
lcr_naive <- liquidity_ratios(nbs$balance, nbs)[["lcr"]]
guard(lcr_naive > 3, "naive LCR claim")
## a month's interest annualised by twelve instead of by its day count
fx <- MM$panel_m[format(MM$panel_m$date, "%m") == "02" & is.finite(MM$panel_m$c_savings), ]
feb_gap <- mean(fx$c_savings * (1 - 12 * days_in_month(fx$date) / 365))
guard(feb_gap > 0.2 && feb_gap < 0.6, "February artefact size")
```

Each of these was tried, failed a check, and was replaced. They are recorded
because the failure is informative, and because a reader who tries the obvious
thing should know where it leads.

* **The intercept correction inside the equation.** Adding the recent
  residual to the intercept compounds it through the autoregressive term, to
  roughly $\text{ic}/(1-\rho)$; with deposit-cost models whose $\rho$ is
  close to one, a few basis points of residual become a drift of a percentage
  point or more. Twelve quarters ahead it loses to the level shift across the
  expanding-window origins and wins only the two-origin back-test, so the
  level shift stays.
* **Selecting the single best specification.** Ranking thousands of
  specifications by pseudo-out-of-sample RMSE and keeping the winner
  forecasts worst of the three methods tried on genuinely new data; the BIC
  model average is kept.
* **Asymmetric responses everywhere.** Splitting the repo rate into rises
  and cuts is significant in sample for six pricing models but improves both
  back-tests for four; for volumes it is significant for one book and helps
  none; contraction kinks are significant for `r n_kink_sig` of `r sum(kk$has_kink)` targets and pass
  both back-tests only for card lending. Elsewhere the trending partial sums
  and the kinks learned from two recessions make the simulations drift.
* **A swap curve inside the government curve.** Pricing the structural
  hedge at JIBAR plus 0.55 times the bond curve's slope overstated swap rates
  by `r num(A0$proxy_err[["min"]], 1)`–`r num(A0$proxy_err[["max"]], 1)` pp, because South African bonds carry a fiscal
  premium over swaps, and with it NGFB's ROE by about `r ubps(-A0$correction$d_roe[1])` (see
  [Are the numbers right?](#audit)). Actual swap fixings replaced it.
* **Nowcasting the jump-off.** Earlier versions extended GDP, unemployment
  and house prices past their last publication by carrying the last value
  forward, and the monthly layer chose its GDP indicators by a nowcast test.
  Under perfect foresight those values belong to the scenario, which now
  supplies them.
* **A product-level composition draw for NGFB.** Drawing all
  `r length(ngfb_asset_lines())` asset shares from six banks needs a covariance
  of dimension `r length(ngfb_asset_lines()) - 1` in log-ratio space,
  `r choose(length(ngfb_asset_lines()), 2)` parameters from six observations,
  and produced implausible books. Drawing five business-line dimensions and
  splitting within lines at the population mix fixed it.
* **Carving NGFB out of existing banks.** Taking NGFB's book from the reported
  banks distorted every peer group's history and share dynamics. Adding NGFB
  to the industry (Post 1's convention) leaves the data untouched.
* **COVID dummies on the credit-loss model.** They absorbed the 2020 stress
  signal, leaving a credit model that did not respond to a recession. The
  dummies now apply to volume models only.
* **The SARB coincident indicator as the activity measure for regimes.** It ran
  negative through 2025–26 while GDP grew, labelling an expansion a
  contraction. Regimes use real GDP only.
* **Unemployment in the credit-loss model.** No specification containing it
  survives the sign and $t$-tests once GDP is available, so the engine has no
  unemployment channel. A labour-market stress therefore shows up only
  through its GDP counterpart.
* **Macro models for mortgage growth.** None beats the AR(1) out of sample
  (skill `r pct(s1$skill[s1$target == "g_mortgages_res"], 0)`); mortgage
  volumes are close to a slow-moving trend.
* **A mean-reverting fee model.** Without the intercept correction,
  non-interest revenue over assets reverts towards its 2008–2025 average
  (`r pct(mean(SC$no_ic$nir_assets) / 100, 2)` of assets in the baseline, against
  `r pct(mean(SC$no_ic$nir_assets_ic) / 100, 2)` with it) and lifts the
  industry's baseline ROE by `r ubps(nir_gap)`. The back-test showed the same
  failure (the model lost to "no change" from both origins).
* **A single NII-matching wholesale spread, with outliers left in.** One
  quarter of BA120 call-deposit cost at `r num(cc_val, 1)`% pushed the solved
  spread to `r sprintf("%+.2f", N$calibration$wholesale_spread_raw)` pp over JIBAR, an
  implausible negative funding spread. Neutralising flagged outliers gives
  `r sprintf("%+.2f", N$calibration$wholesale_spread)` pp.
* **Calibrating gross interest flows away.** Two alternatives were tried and
  dropped: uniform level shifts on all yields and costs (which mis-state every
  product's BA120 yield), and interest-bearing shares on treasury and
  wholesale lines (which, applied to NGFB's larger treasury book, made it look
  liability-sensitive and implausibly unprofitable). Reporting the gross
  excess and matching NII was the more honest choice.
* **Naive LCR run-off factors.** Fixed run-off rates by behavioural line,
  generous inflow rates and no encumbrance put NGFB's LCR at
  `r formatC(100 * lcr_naive, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")`%. Depositor-weighted Basel factors, calibrated to the
  published sector ratio, bring it to `r pct(q0$lcr[1], 0)`.
* **Maximising the engine's ROE directly.** Without the implied marginal
  costs the optimiser puts `r raw_up` of the six lending moves at their upper bound and promises
  `r ubps(raw_gain)` of probability-weighted ROE, because the engine prices new
  volume at average economics. The reverse-optimisation step replaced it.
* **Post 2's composition weights.** Post 2 loaded a stale draw; the canonical
  Post 1 composition is used here (see the note in the NGFB section).
* **Monthly interest annualised by twelve.** A month's interest times twelve
  reads every February, with 28 days of interest, as a fall in savings-deposit
  costs of about `r num(feb_gap, 2)` pp, and every 31-day month as a small rise.
  Annualising with the month's own day count removes the artefact.
* **Monthly satellites in production.** Simulated twelve quarters along the
  realised macro path they recover pricing less accurately than the quarterly
  models and volumes no better (see [Monthly frequency](#monthly)), and fed
  the smooth GDP path a quarterly scenario implies they do worse again. The
  corporate-loan and term-deposit gains come from the timing of large flows,
  which matters for measuring the jump-off book, not for the scenario models.
* **Polynomial distributed lags and Bayesian shrinkage for pricing.** Both lost
  to the sign-restricted ARDL average at both frequencies: a smooth Almon lag
  profile cannot represent a repricing step at an MPC meeting, and shrinkage
  keeps many small, often wrong-signed coefficients.

# Limitations

* **Public data only.** Prices, losses and costs are the sector's; NGFB's
  differ from the sector only through its mix (and its hedge). A real bank
  would replace the Stage 1 pricing with its own product pricing and the
  relative loss multipliers with its own loss history.
* **The level of ROE rests on a few inputs.** The swap rates that price the
  hedge moved the baseline by `r ubps(-c0r["baseline", "d_roe"])` in this version, and the hedge book's
  fixed rate rests partly on a back-cast (`r sum(A0$fixed0_quarters$source == "back-cast")` of its twenty quarters
  predate the swap data); the intercept correction on credit losses is worth
  `r ubps(mr["baseline", "core"] - mr["baseline", "no_ic_credit"])`. The scenario differences and the positioning are much less
  sensitive to either.
* **The swap curve does not price each scenario's path.** Swap rates are the
  floating benchmark plus the average 2023–2026 term spread over JIBAR at each
  tenor. A market that expected a scenario's path would price the curve to it:
  receive-fixed swaps look slightly cheap in scenarios with cuts, and dear in
  scenarios with hikes, which flatters the hedge-ratio lever in the baseline
  and any rule that times the hedge. The [strategy lab](#lab) re-runs the hedge
  strategies with a curve that prices half of the coming path.
* **The strategy lab replays history; it does not sample a distribution.**
  Its overlapping windows hold only about five independent three-year periods
  and one each of a global financial crisis and a pandemic; each episode's
  changes are applied to today's levels (the policy-rate and inflation floors
  bind in a few); the rules' parameters were set in advance but are judged on
  the same history; and the engine has no vintage effects in credit losses,
  which mutes what credit timing can add.
* **The ZARONIA transition is modelled at the fallback, not contract by
  contract.** Every floating line moves to compounded ZARONIA plus 16.19 bp
  from 2027Q1; in practice loans and notes follow their own fallback clauses
  and re-papering, compounding conventions (a five-day lookback for loans)
  differ slightly from a quarterly average, and the quarter in which each
  contract switches is not known from public data.
* **Relative loss multipliers are assumptions.** BA200 publishes no losses by
  product, so the ordering (unsecured highest, mortgages lowest) is an
  external calibration normalised to the sector's credit-loss ratio.
* **Volumes are the weakest link.** The volume models beat a naive benchmark
  only modestly, and the share models' regime effects are imprecise. Scenario
  ROE is driven far more by pricing and credit, which are better identified.
* **The sector is unhedged in the engine.** Real banks hedge; the sector line
  shows the industry's gross macro exposure, not its reported earnings
  sensitivity, and slightly understates its reported margin.
* **NGFB's hedge is not re-optimised for the refined deposit models.** The
  canonical `r pct(hedge_ratio0)` ratio comes from Post 3; with faster deposit repricing the
  rate-neutral ratio is `r pct(A0$neutral_ratio, 0)`, which is a finding about the canonical bank, not
  a recommendation for a real one.
* **The levers' risks are not in the ROE.** The engine's three-year ROE does
  not price the duration a longer hedge tenor adds, the fiscal risk in a
  longer liquidity buffer beyond the scenarios' yield paths, or the value of a
  thicker capital cushion; those are sized by risk appetite, and deposit
  pricing's volume cost is not modelled at all.
* **The bond–swap spread rests on three years of swap data.** Its model --
  about a quarter of the long bond's non-policy move -- is estimated on
  monthly levels since late 2023, a period in which the spread mostly
  compressed; a sovereign shock could move it more, and the asset swap's
  spread risk is sized by an assumed 100 bps shock alongside the modelled
  paths.
* **A smaller buffer's cost is outside the engine.** The engine does not stress
  deposit run-offs, wholesale funding spreads or the price of a forced asset
  sale, so it sees what surplus liquidity costs but not what it buys. The
  buffer's size belongs to the bank's own liquidity stress test.
* **The carry book's funding is assumed to roll.** Repo funding is priced at
  NGFB's calibrated spread over the policy rate in every quarter; in a market
  dislocation (March 2020) repo haircuts and rates rise, and the book's real
  backstop is the SARB's lending facilities, at a penalty rate. The engine
  prices neither.
* **The optimiser takes unpriced risks to their limits.** It maximises the
  ROE the engine prices, so the asset swap and the buffer release go to the
  caps they are given (90% of earning HQLA out of bills, the wholesale funding
  left to repay); the EVE budget is measured against the plan's position, not
  the bank's total exposure; and the episodes are one history.
* **Funding shocks are an overlay.** No macro relationship for funding
  spreads survives the tests, so a global funding squeeze like 2008's enters
  only as a stress overlay.
* **Execution costs size the moves.** Their direction is robust; their
  magnitude scales with an assumption about how expensive it is to move a
  franchise inside a year.
* **No second-round feedback.** The scenarios are exogenous: NGFB's actions do
  not move prices or the macro path, and the sector does not respond to NGFB.
* **Liquidity proxies.** BA900 cannot see the 30-day maturity slice,
  operational status, committed facilities or derivatives; one scalar per
  ratio calibrates the level to the Prudential Authority's published figures.
* **Monthly data.** `r if (MM$vol_source == "KBP") "Until the monthly BA900 pull has run, the monthly volume comparison uses the SARB's credit statistics (all monetary institutions), whose product definitions differ from BA900's, and the monthly sector balance sheet is interpolated between quarter ends." else "Month-end BA900 balances carry window dressing and lumpy wholesale flows that quarterly data average out; the month-of-year dummies absorb only the regular part, and monthly and quarterly ratios differ slightly in definition when balances move within a quarter."`
  Unemployment and house prices have no monthly indicator here, so their
  monthly paths are smooth, and the monthly GDP path is only as good as its
  three indicators.
* **Share strategy and scorecards rest on NGFB's drawn share parameters.**
  They are a typical large bank's behaviour plus a random deviation; a real
  bank would use its own estimates, which would be noisier for small books.
  Contributions exclude operating costs and fees, which the returns do not
  report by product, and assume marginal growth is funded at the wholesale
  rate unless it brings its own deposits.
* **The local projections are not identified.** Without measured
  monetary-policy shocks, they show how rates and credit move together, not
  the causal effect of a rate change on lending.

# Reproducing the analysis {#reproducing-the-analysis}

The code is an R package, `baeconstrat`, with the analysis in separate
scripts.

```text
BA-econ-strat/
├── DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, LICENSE, README.md
├── R/                      package functions (documented, exported)
├── data-raw/               pull scripts and the downloaded caches
├── analysis/               00_config.R … 15_risk_budget.R, lab_tools.R, run_all.R
├── inst/artefacts/         NGFB canonical constants and composition draw
├── tests/testthat/         unit tests
├── output/                 *.rds written by the analysis scripts
└── report/                 this document
```

```r
# from the package root, after the data pull (data-raw/00_pull_data.bat,
# data-raw/03_pull_monthly.bat for the monthly BA900 and BA100 returns, and
# data-raw/04_pull_swaps.bat for the ZAR swap curve)
install.packages(".", repos = NULL, type = "source")
source("analysis/run_all.R")
source("blog/build_post_snapshot.R")    # the write-ups' snapshot, also read by the complete edition
quarto::quarto_render("report/ngfb_macro_strategy_full.qmd")
```

Settings live in `analysis/00_config.R` (jump-off, horizon, baseline paths,
floors, scenario probabilities, the form of the intercept correction, the
twelve-quarter conditional-simulation horizon). The model-check script fails
if the Stage 1 registry disagrees with its own adoption rules, and the
monthly script fails if the production GDP disaggregation is not the in-sample
choice. The seed is `r CFG$seed`. Every number in this report is
computed inline from `output/*.rds`, the passages carried over from the
write-ups through their snapshot of the same files; `guard()` and the
write-ups' `validate_post()` stop the render if an input drifts from what the
text says.
